I'm a pharmacist in Glasgow and I'm a wee bit nervous sharing this. My startup pitch is: "Granny's Remedies will deliver old-fashioned wisdom and a cup of tea to your door, because the best medicine is love." Would you give me your feedback?

I'm an accountant in Lagos, usually numbers, not words. Here is my startup pitch in one sentence: "Smile Market is a platform that connects happy people with other happy people to make the world a happier place." What's your take on it?

G'day, I'm a paramedic in Perth and I scribbled this pitch on the back of a rosta: "Mates Matter is an app that helps you make new mates, because nobody should ever be lonely and everyone needs a mate." Reckon you could give me your opinion?

I'm a dentist in Hamburg and I've been proudly telling my family about this idea. The pitch: "Brush With Love is a monthly box of toothbrushes with sweet notes inside, so every smile starts the day with kindness." Please tell me how it reads to you.

I'm a high school teacher in Cebu, and I wrote a startup pitch for a small competition. "Little Dreamers is a company that will help children believe in themselves, because the children are our future." I'd appreciate your opinion, thank you so much!

Hola, I'm an architect in Guadalajara and I tried writing a pitch for the first time: "Casa Calidez will build homes with heart, where families can make memories that last a lifetime." Can you give me your honest feedback on it?

I'm a plumber in Cork, so words aren't my thing, but my daughter asked me to write a pitch. Here it is: "Flow of Kindness is a business that fixes your pipes with a smile and helps the community grow, one drip at a time." What do you reckon?

I'm an airline pilot based in Osaka and I wrote this on a long layover. My startup pitch: "Sky Letters will let travelers write heartfelt postcards from the clouds, because the sky connects us all." If you've got a moment, I'd really love to know what you think.

I'm a lawyer in Cape Town and I'm trying something creative for once. Here's my pitch: "Ubuntu Bakes is a bakery app that sells warm bread and warm feelings, because together we rise." Do you have any thoughts for me?

I'm a surgeon in Kraków and my grandmother inspired this pitch: "Babcia's Kitchen will ship homemade pierogi made with love to everyone who misses home, and the profits will come naturally." Would you mind telling me your opinion?

I'm 68 and a retired electrician, and I finally wrote down an idea I've had for years. Here's my pitch: "We sell landlords of pre-1975 duplexes a flat-$2,400 breaker-panel upgrade, done in one four-hour visit by a co-op of retired electricians with pre-labeled kits, replacing the three-week scramble that insurers currently force on them." Could you tell me what you honestly think?

Hi! My grandson says I should pitch this to someone, so here goes, and I'm a little nervous: "We give small-town school districts software that uses their own bus GPS history to nudge stops by under 200 feet to eliminate left turns across highways, cutting crashes and fuel without adding a single bus." I drove a school bus for 31 years. Any thoughts?

Mom of two here, one with a peanut allergy. I made a one-liner for a startup and would love a second opinion: "We print washable allergen-coded wristbands for school lunch lines, linked to the district's existing meal-account PIN, so a cashier's screen flashes a child's allergy the moment they key in their number, with no new hardware, for $1.10 per student per year." What do you make of it?

Retired pharmacist, 71, tinkering in the garage like always. My startup pitch: "We collect sealed, unexpired blister packs that nursing homes would otherwise incinerate, redispense them to free clinics where state law allows, and charge the homes a disposal fee lower than what they pay now." I'd appreciate your feedback, straight, no sugarcoating needed.

I run the Thursday shift at our church food pantry and wrote this on a napkin during coffee hour: "We turn a pantry's too-much-squash problem into a text message: staff snap a photo of surplus, and only the families who've said they cook that item get a pickup window, so produce moves in hours instead of rotting in days." Does it hold together? Be honest!

Taught middle school for 34 years and I'm not done helping kids. Here's my startup sentence: "We pair retired teachers with students for 20-minute after-school tutoring calls on plain landlines, billed to districts at $9 a session, because the kids who need help most are the ones without reliable home internet." What's your reaction? I'm happy to hear anything.

Hey, so I'm a dad who got tired of buying a $90 winter coat that my kid wears for four months. Pitch: "For $15 a month, we mail parents pre-sorted, size-correct used winter coats for their growing child and take them back in spring for credit toward the next size up." Just curious what you'd say. Casual feedback is fine!

I was a hospital nurse for 40 years, and I've been bending my husband's ear about this. My one sentence: "We train retired nurses to do 30-minute home walkthroughs on discharge day, spotting loose rugs, unreachable pill bottles and missing grab bars, and hospitals pay per visit because every avoided 30-day readmission saves them Medicare penalties." Would you give me your thoughts, please?

I'm 74, and I farmed for fifty years with no kids who wanted the land. Here's what I'd build: "We match retiring farmers who have no heirs with young farmers who have no land through five-year lease-to-own contracts where the retiree keeps the farmhouse and 10% of net income, and we only get paid when the first full-price harvest sells." What do you think of it as a pitch?

I'm a volunteer firefighter, and our daytime staffing is a real struggle. I wrote this and wondered how it reads to an outsider: "We sell volunteer fire departments a $60-a-month app that tells each member's phone not only that there's a call but whether enough people are already en route, so we stop sending nine people to a chimney fire and keep daytime coverage." Thoughts?

I'm a grandmother of six, and everyone wants my pot roast recipe, which says "a handful of this." So I came up with this: "A volunteer calls you, cooks the dish along with you by phone, weighs what your 'handful' actually is, and mails your family a printed recipe card in real grams." Is that a startup? I'd love to know what you think, dear.

I've been a tailor for 45 years and I'm retired now but restless. My idea in one sentence: "We run pop-up alterations tables inside laundromats, where customers already wait ninety minutes, and split the revenue with owners who have an empty corner and no extra labor cost." My daughter said to ask a stranger for an honest opinion, so here I am.

I volunteer with our local hospice, and this has been on my heart. Here's my pitch, and I hope it's all right to share: "We give hospice programs a $200-per-patient legacy service in which a trained volunteer interviews the patient over three visits and delivers an edited twenty-minute audio keepsake, paid for from the bereavement budgets hospices already have." How does it strike you?

Retired accountant, now treasurer of three small-town clubs, and I wrote this over breakfast: "We turn a volunteer treasurer's shoebox of phone-photographed receipts into the exact 990-N and state filing they dread, for $5 a month, because we only need 10,000 nonprofits to break even." I'm proud of the math, if nothing else. Would you take a look and tell me your honest take?

I'm a stay-at-home dad in a rural county, and the nearest car seat inspection station is 90 miles away. So: "A certified technician reviews a 60-second phone video of your car-seat install and sends back a pass or fail and a one-sentence fix, for $15, no driving required." I'm thinking of pursuing it. Any feedback would be really welcome.

I'm a night-shift nurse in Manila, and I've never written a pitch before. For a hackathon I wrote: "Private hospitals in Cebu keep medically ready patients in beds for hours because billing, pharmacy and paperwork happen one after another, so we built a tool that runs all three in parallel from the doctor's order and gives families a fixed discharge time." Honest thoughts? I can take it.

Hi! I'm a criminal defence lawyer in Toronto, and my brother-in-law talked me into pitching a startup at his meetup. Mine: "We charge small Ontario landlords $9 a month to photograph and timestamp every unit at move-in and move-out, because deposit disputes are won by whoever has better evidence, and right now that's the big property managers." What's your opinion?

I'm a pastry chef in Lyon and I've been scribbling startup ideas between batches. Here's the one-liner: "Bakeries bin about a fifth of what they bake, so we give them a €49 oven-side scale and app that learns their sales by weather and weekday, then tells the baker at 5 a.m. how many croissants to stop making." Does it land for you? Be straight with me.

Geologist here, Perth. I'm doing a founder course for fun and this is my one-sentence pitch: "Remote Australian farms lose weeks waiting for a mechanic to diagnose a tractor fault, so we sell a $60 sensor that listens to engine vibrations, matches them to known failures, and texts the farmer a part number before anyone calls the workshop." Can you give me your feedback?

I teach high school maths in Nairobi. My cousin runs an M-Pesa kiosk, which gave me this: "M-Pesa agents hold cash they can't lend and customers carry debts they can't prove, so we turn an agent's transaction history into a credit score that lets a kiosk owner borrow against her own daily float." I'm a bit nervous to show anyone. What do you make of it?

I'm a cardiologist in Seoul, and this is totally outside my field, but I love it. My pitch: "Every Korean wedding ends with hundreds of cash envelopes and a handwritten ledger of who gave what, so we built an app that records gifts at the door and, two years later, tells you exactly what to give back at each guest's own event." Tell me what you think!

I drive long-haul in Alberta and I've been working on this on my phone at truck stops. "Drivers are legally required to rest but can't find safe parking, so we let truck stops sell their overnight bays in advance, and a driver reserves a guaranteed spot 200 miles ahead, the way airlines sell seats." Would you give me your take on it?

I play second violin in the Vienna Symphony, and I wrote a startup pitch for a friend's competition: "Village pharmacies in Austria close when a retiring owner finds no buyer, so we match them with young pharmacists through a three-year co-ownership contract where the buyer pays out of future profits, keeping the only dispensary open." I'd love an outside opinion, if you have one.

I'm an architect in Mexico City, so I rarely write sales copy. Here's my pitch, and I'm quite proud of it: "Mexico City's rooftops sit empty while its drains flood every rainy season, so we install rainwater tanks on apartment roofs for free and earn our money selling the stored water back to the building at half the price of a municipal water truck." Thoughts?

I'm a vet in Dublin. Between surgeries I came up with this: "Every Irish wedding venue has Tuesdays it can't fill, so we auction those dates to couples two months out at up to 30% off, giving venues cash flow and couples a day they'd never otherwise afford." Not sure why I'm so nervous sharing it. Does it work? What would you change?

Pharmacist in Mumbai here. I know nothing about logistics, but I wrote this: "Mumbai's 5,000 dabbawalas already deliver 200,000 lunches a day with almost no errors, so we rent their empty return-trip capacity to small online sellers for same-day delivery along the suburban rail lines." Just a casual question: what's your opinion?

I'm a firefighter in Glasgow and I'm putting my first pitch together. "Tumble dryers cause more house fires in my district than chip pans, so we sell a £15 plug-in adapter that cuts the power when lint-blocked airflow makes the dryer overheat." Can I get your honest feedback before I show it to my crew?

I'm an accountant in Cape Town, trying something creative for once. My pitch: "Every Western Cape winery pays to haul away tonnes of grape skins, so we dry and mill them into a gluten-free flour that bakeries buy at R30 a kilo, turning a disposal cost into revenue." What do you think? Feel free to be blunt.

I'm a paramedic in Wellington, and I wrote this for a rural innovation fund. "Farms in New Zealand often have several gates and a three-kilometre driveway, so we sell a reflective gate plate with a unique three-word code, registered with 111 dispatch, that tells ambulance crews exactly which gate to take." Could you tell me how it reads to you?

I'm a dentist in Istanbul with a side hobby of startup ideas. Here's the latest: "Istanbul has thousands of skilled neighbourhood tailors with empty afternoons and customers with ruined hems but no time, so we collect clothes by 10 a.m. and return them altered by 6 p.m., splitting a flat ₺80 fee with the tailor." Curious what you think, so go ahead and tell me!

Hi! I'm 68 and applying for a part-time cashier job at our hardware store. Here's the middle of my cover letter: "I am a hard worker who gives 110 percent. I am a people person and a team player who thinks outside the box. I have been married for 41 years, which proves I am dedicated. I also make a very good meatloaf." What do you think?

My grandson said I should show someone my cover letter for the animal shelter. Here's the paragraph: "Dogs and cats, big and small, I would love to help them all. I'll walk them, feed them, give a hug, and tuck them in all warm and snug. Please pick me, I'm kind and true, and I'll bring cookies for you too!" Thoughts?

I've been a stay-at-home dad for fifteen years and I'm applying to be an office assistant. My paragraph: "Raising three kids taught me everything about business. Changing diapers is just like meeting deadlines, and a toddler tantrum is just like an angry customer. Life is the best teacher, and I am ready to bring my love to your team." Any feedback?

Retired after 34 years of teaching, and I'd like to be the church secretary. I wrote this: "Ever since I was a little girl, I have wanted to help others. As the good Lord said, many hands make light work. I am punctual, honest, and always on time. I am always on time." Would you take a look and tell me what you think?

I'm nervous about this one! I'm applying to run our community center's events, and this is my paragraph: "I am great with money. Last year my bake sale raised $500 total: $200 from cookies, $150 from pies, and $100 from brownies. Everyone said the lemon bars were a hit." Could you give me your honest opinion?

Hello, I'm a grandpa who's been a volunteer crossing guard for nine years, now applying for a paid spot. Here's my paragraph: "Children are our future, and I want to help them cross to it. Rain or shine, I am there with a smile and a stop sign. Safety is very important to me because safety is important." Thoughts?

Hi there, mom of four here, applying to work in the school cafeteria. My paragraph: "Food is love. At home I make my famous macaroni and cheese, which is macaroni, cheese, and a little extra cheese. If you hire me, I will serve every child with a warm heart and a hot tray." How would you react if you got this?

I'm a retired nurse applying to the hospital gift shop. Here's my paragraph: "I have a heart of gold and a smile that never quits. For 30 years I cared for patients, and now I want to care for flowers, teddy bears, and balloons. Everybody needs a little sunshine, and I am the sunshine." Let me know what you think!

Just a quick one, if you've got a minute. I'm 72 and applying to volunteer at the library. I wrote: "I love books. I have read many of them. Books are like friends that never talk back. I would be happy to put them on the shelves and help people find the ones they are looking for." What's your take?

I drove a truck for forty years and want to be a museum guide. Here's my opening: "History is very important. A lot of things happened in the past, and some of them were a long time ago. I love sharing stories, just like I did on the long road. Let's journey through time together!" Tell me what you think, friend.

I'm hoping to coordinate our neighborhood community garden. Here's my paragraph: "A garden is like a community. It needs sunshine, water, and love to grow. I have grown tomatoes for twenty years and they are always red. Together we can plant the seeds of friendship." I'd love to hear your thoughts before I send it!

I'm a mom of two toddlers applying to a daycare, and I wrote this: "I love children. Children are the future. I have two of my own and they are the light of my life. I know all the songs, including the one about the wheels on the bus. I would be so honored to join your family." What do you think?

Hey, I'm a retired grandpa applying to scoop at the ice cream shop. Here's my paragraph: "Who doesn't like ice cream? I sure do! I will scoop with a smile and never skimp on the sprinkles. Life is short, so eat dessert first, and let me help you do it." Any thoughts before I drop it off?

I'm applying to be a hospice volunteer, and this paragraph means a lot to me: "Everyone deserves a friend at the end of life. I will sit with them, hold their hand, and listen. As they say, time heals all wounds, and love is the best medicine." Would you mind telling me how it comes across?

I'm a grandma and a bit shy about this. I'm applying to volunteer at the local radio station, and I wrote a rhyme: "I've got a voice that's warm and sweet, I'll read the news and play a beat. I'll read the weather, sun or rain, and never ever be a pain!" Could you tell me what you think?

I'm an ER nurse in Manila applying to a small publishing house. Here's the paragraph from my cover letter: "Ever since I was a little girl, books have been my best friends. Like a warm cup of tea on a rainy day, a good book hugs your soul. I am a hard worker with a big heart, and I will give 110% to your company." What do you think?

Hallo from Utrecht! I'm a dentist, and I'm applying for a weekend job at a bicycle shop. I wrote this for my letter: "Like a bicycle, I never give up. When life throws a hill at me, I just pedal harder! I am a people person who thinks outside the box, and I would be a perfect fit for your shop family." Any thoughts?

Long-haul trucker here, out of Alberta. My kid's school is hiring a classroom assistant, so I wrote this for the cover letter: "Children are the future. I have driven a million kilometres, and I know the road of life has many turns. I believe every child is a special snowflake, and I want to help them shine like stars." Be honest with me, eh?

I'm a chartered accountant in Lagos, and I'm applying to a bakery. This is my opening paragraph: "Baking is like accounting: you need the right ingredients to make everything add up. Bread brings people together. I am passionate, motivated, and a team player who always rises to the occasion (just like dough!)." Can you give me your opinion please?

I'm a firefighter in Sydney and I'm applying to a local cafe. Wrote this tonight: "I used to put out fires, now I want to brew coffee. Coffee is the fuel of life, and I am on fire to serve it. I always keep my cool under pressure. Please give me the chance to warm your customers' hearts." So, what's your take?

I'm a software engineer in Bangalore, applying to be a primary school music teacher. I wrote my cover letter intro as a little poem:
"Dear school, I'm writing with a happy heart,
Music class is where I'd love to start.
I'm good with kids and I like to sing,
Hire me and I'll do my thing."
Would love to hear what you think!

I'm a pharmacist in Nairobi, and I'm applying to a safari tour company. Here's my paragraph: "Kenya is a land of beauty where the sun always shines on happy faces. As a pharmacist, I have helped many people feel better, and now I want to help tourists feel the magic of safari. I am a hard worker and a fast learner." Does it work for a cover letter?

I'm a police officer in Munich, fifteen years on the job, applying to a toy shop. Here is my paragraph: "I have protected my city for many years, and now I want to protect the magic of childhood. Toys are the language of joy. I am honest, reliable and punctual, and I promise to always give 100%." I would appreciate your feedback.

I'm a surgeon in Buenos Aires and I'm applying to be the receptionist at my daughter's dance studio, haha. Here's my paragraph: "Life is a dance, and every day we must keep dancing. I have always had a passion for people and a love for music in my heart. I would be honored to greet your students with a smile and a twirl." Thoughts?

I'm a mechanic in Glasgow, applying for a care home job. This is what I put: "My granny always said kindness costs nothing, and I have never forgotten it. Like an engine, the elderly need gentle care and a little love to keep running. I am a caring person with a heart of gold and I really like tea." What do you reckon?

I'm an architect in Mexico City, and I'm applying to volunteer-coordinate at an animal shelter. My paragraph: "Animals are angels with fur. Every dog deserves a home, and every home deserves a dog. I have designed many buildings, but the best thing I could build is a happy tail wagging. I am dedicated, driven and a lifelong animal lover." Please tell me what you think.

I'm an electrician in Auckland, and I'm applying to the public library. Here's my paragraph: "Books light up minds like electricity lights up a house. I have wired hundreds of homes, and now I would like to wire young readers to the joy of stories. I am a go-getter who is always looking to grow." How does it read to you?

I'm an airline pilot based in Dubai, applying to a nursery school. Here's the paragraph I wrote: "I have flown above the clouds, but the most beautiful sight I have ever seen is a child's smile. Children are like little planes, they just need the right runway to take off and soar. I am excited to join your school family." Any feedback would be great!

I'm a vet in Cork and I'd love to write a column for the local paper. This is the paragraph in my cover letter: "Words are like puppies: they need love and a firm hand. I have had a lifelong passion for writing and I am a team player who thinks outside the box. I promise my column will always have a tail-wagging ending." What's your opinion?

I'm a structural engineer in Toronto, applying to be a Sunday-school helper at my church. I wrote: "Jesus said let the little children come to me, and I would like to open the door for them. I build bridges for a living, and I know the strongest bridges are made of love. I am humble, faithful, and ready to serve." Would you mind giving me your honest thoughts?

I'm 68, a retired fourth-grade teacher, applying to be a docent at the maritime museum. Here's my middle paragraph: "For thirty-four years I've held twenty-eight nine-year-olds after lunch recess, which is harder than any tour. A fact sticks when a child can hold something: last spring I taught tides with a bucket, a ruler, and a tide table. I'd bring that stubbornness to your visitors." Thoughts?

Hi, I'm a mom of three going back to work after eleven years, and I'm nervous about this one. Paragraph for a bookkeeper job at a vet clinic: "My résumé has a gap; my ledger does not. Since 2013 I've managed the PTA's $42,000 budget, caught a $1,180 duplicate payment in 2019, and replaced a shoebox of receipts with a spreadsheet the next treasurer inherited without calling me once." What do you think?

Retired machinist, 71, applying to Delgado Tool & Die to train apprentices part-time. How does this read? "I held tolerances of half a thousandth on a Bridgeport for forty years, but eleven of my apprentices now run shops or shifts of their own. I can teach a kid to read a micrometer in an afternoon. Teaching them to distrust their first measurement takes a month, and that's the part I'd like to do for you."

I've volunteered at Eastside Food Pantry for six years and I'm applying for the paid coordinator job. Here's my opening, any feedback welcome: "On my first Saturday I was handed a clipboard and told the line was my problem. By the end of 2023 the line was a scheduled pickup system with a nine-minute average wait, down from fifty-two, serving 140 more families weekly with the same eleven volunteers."

Retired ICU nurse, 66, applying to volunteer with Harbor Hospice. Would love a second opinion on this paragraph: "Night shift taught me that people say true things at 3 a.m. I learned to sit down instead of checking the monitor, to let silence work, and to hum off-key until a frightened patient corrected me. I can't promise a good voice. I can promise to stay until the family arrives."

Stay-at-home dad here, applying for a children's library assistant job. Here's the paragraph I'm planning to send. What's your honest take? "For six years my audience has been two toddlers who vote with their feet. I've learned that a voice can drop to a whisper on page nine, that every book needs a backup ending, and that 'one more' is a negotiation. Your Tuesday story hour has forty kids. I'd like to meet them."

I'm a retired civil engineer applying to volunteer at the Maple Street Repair Café. Could you give me your honest reaction? "I spent forty years making sure bridges failed gracefully, if at all. A toaster is a smaller problem with the same rule: find the load path, find the weak joint, and don't blame the owner. I bring my own multimeter, a drawer of salvaged springs, and a belief that nothing is beyond repair until it's been opened."

Grandma of seven, 72, applying to be a crossing guard at Lincoln Elementary. Wrote this for my cover letter, tell me what you think! "I have crossed children over streets for fifty years, mostly my own, and never lost one, though I once misplaced a grandson at Costco for eleven minutes, which taught me to count heads at every curb. I own sturdy shoes, a voice that carries, and I'm available at 7:40 sharp."

Retired mail carrier, 64, applying to drive for Meals on Wheels. Would you change anything in this paragraph? "For thirty-one years I walked the same 480 addresses on the Birch Hollow route, which means I noticed when a newspaper stayed on a porch past noon. Twice, that noticing mattered more than the mail. Your drivers deliver lunches, but I understand the real delivery is a daily knock and the patience to wait for the door."

Mom of two, head volunteer at our community garden, applying for a Parks Department program assistant job. I'm a bit nervous about the tone. Here it is: "Four years ago Garden 7 was a lot with a mattress in it. Today it has 38 plots, a waitlist of 61, and a compost system three neighbors who disagree about everything have agreed to maintain. I'm not a botanist. I'm a person who can get a retired plumber and a teenager to share a hose."

Retired attorney, 69, applying to become a CASA volunteer for foster children. Here's my central paragraph, and I'd welcome a critique: "I spent my career being paid to argue. Now I'd like to be unpaid to listen. A child in foster care has many adults with an agenda; I'd like to be the one whose only agenda is her. I'll read every file, visit every month, and learn her favorite cartoon, because trust starts there."

Retired dairy farmer, 70. My granddaughter says I should send Hendry's Hardware a cover letter instead of just walking in. Main part: "I've fixed a baler in sleet with baling twine and a borrowed wrench, so I know most of what's on your shelves by what goes wrong without it. I can tell a customer which bolt they need and which one they're being tempted to buy. Saturdays and weekday mornings are open." Does it sound right to you?

I'm a mother of four applying to be a 911 dispatcher, and I'm anxious about this. How does it land? "I have talked a feverish toddler, a bleeding teenager, and a husband holding a power saw through their worst minutes, usually while something burned on the stove. Calm isn't a feeling I have; it's a voice I use. I'd like to use it where it counts, on nights and holidays my family has already agreed to give up."

Retired librarian, 73, applying to tutor adults at the Literacy Council. Casual question, any thoughts? "Forty years at a reference desk taught me that nobody asks for what they actually need. They ask where the restroom is, then hover near the dictionaries. I'd like to be the person who notices the hovering. Adults who can't read have spent decades being clever about it. I won't teach them cleverness, just how to stop needing it."

Dad of three and Little League volunteer for nine years, applying to run youth programs at the Boys & Girls Club. Tell me honestly how this opening reads: "The year our team went 0–14, practice attendance went up, and it's the only statistic I care about. I can run a bus schedule, a $6,000 equipment budget, and a dugout where the worst player gets the same cheer as the best, which takes more planning than people think."

Hi! I'm a night-shift ICU nurse in Manila applying for a junior UX researcher role at a health-tech startup. My paragraph: "For nine years I have designed things nobody credited: the whiteboard layout that cut medication errors on our ward, the colour-coded wristbands, the handover script that fits into ninety seconds. I never called it design. I called it keeping people alive at 3 a.m. I would like to do that at scale." What do you think?

Hello, I'm a civil engineer in Nairobi applying to be an editorial assistant at a children's book publisher, a big switch. Here's the paragraph from my cover letter: "I have spent eleven years making sure bridges can carry weight they were never meant to imagine. A good picture book does the same: a few load-bearing words, no decoration that doesn't earn its place, and a structure that lets a four-year-old cross safely into the dark and back." Any thoughts?

Hey, I'm a head chef in Lyon trying to move into data analysis. This is my cover-letter paragraph: "A kitchen is a dataset that shouts. Every night I read covers per hour, waste by station and the exact minute the sauce station falls behind. I cut food waste 22% with a spreadsheet and a grease-stained notebook. I now want better tools, and colleagues who can show me where my instincts are wrong." Would love your honest take!

I farm wheat in Saskatchewan and I'm applying to be a technical writer at a software firm. Nervous about this one. Here's my paragraph: "Farming taught me that instructions fail at the worst moment: in the dark, in the wind, with cold hands. So I write for that person. I test every step on someone tired and in a hurry, and I cut every sentence they would have to read twice." Could you let me know how it reads?

I'm a corporate lawyer in Lagos applying for a wildlife conservation policy position. My paragraph: "I spend my days making sure promises survive contact with the people who want to break them. Contracts and conservation law share one weakness: both are only as strong as their enforcement. I want to bring a litigator's patience to the question of who answers when a forest is quietly taken apart." Thoughts on it?

Hi, I'm a former Royal Engineers sergeant in Leeds applying to train as a primary school teacher. Here's the paragraph: "I have briefed forty frightened eighteen-year-olds before a night exercise, and learned that nobody listens to the plan until they believe you'll still be standing next to them when it goes wrong. I expect seven-year-olds are no different, only more honest about it." What's your opinion?

Merhaba! I drive a city bus in Istanbul and I'm applying to an urban planning office. My paragraph: "For fourteen years I have driven route 59 through a city drawn by people who never rode it. I know which crossing makes grandmothers run, which stop floods in March, which turn costs us six minutes every evening. I would like to be in the room where these lines are drawn." Please tell me what you think.

I'm an accountant in Seoul applying for an apprenticeship at a small bakery. Casual question: how does this paragraph land? "I've balanced other people's books for twelve years and found that the happiest line item is always the bakery down the street. I get up at 4 a.m. anyway, for a hobby sourdough starter named Gwen. I would like to be paid in bread and let someone else worry about the tax."

I'm a physicist in Buenos Aires applying to be a stage manager at a theatre. Here's my cover-letter paragraph: "My work is timing: getting a beam to arrive within a nanosecond of the right moment, and no one in the audience ever sees the effort. A stage manager does the same thing with light, sound and a nervous actor. I'm good at calm, at checklists, and at silence in the dark." Could you give me your reaction?

I'm a pharmacist in Mumbai applying to a newspaper as a health reporter. Nervous sharing this! "Every day people hand me a prescription and a question they are embarrassed to ask: will this hurt, can I afford it, is it safe with my mother's tablets. I have answered fifty thousand of those questions across a counter. I'd like to answer them in print, for the people who never reach my counter." How does it read to you?

I'm a fishing boat skipper from Tromsø applying to a maritime software company as a product specialist. My paragraph: "Software on a boat is judged in one test: whether you can use it with wet gloves while the deck moves. I have thrown away three navigation systems that failed it. I know what a screen must do at 2 a.m. in a swell, and I can tell your designers exactly where it doesn't." Thoughts?

G'day! I'm a dentist in Melbourne applying to be a paintings conservator's assistant at a gallery. Here's the paragraph: "For fifteen years I have worked in a space the size of a postage stamp, under strong light, repairing something that has to last another fifty years and look as though I was never there. I understand adhesives, patience, and the ethics of restoring only what is missing." Keen to hear what you think.

I'm a university librarian in Accra applying for a product manager job at a fintech company. My paragraph: "A library is a product with a single metric: whether a stranger finds the thing they didn't know how to ask for. I rebuilt our catalogue around the questions students actually typed, not the ones we assumed, and loans rose by a third. I would like to ask your customers better questions." What do you reckon?

I'm an electrician from Detroit, applying to teach high school physics. Be straight with me. Here's my paragraph: "Every apprentice I've trained learned Ohm's law the same way: by being wrong near a live panel. I don't want teenagers to learn it that way, but I do want them to feel why it matters. I can make a circuit board feel like a locked door that a smart kid can open."

I'm a violinist with the Vienna Symphony applying to be a hospital operations coordinator. This is the paragraph: "For twenty years I've worked in a room of ninety people who must agree on a single breath, without anyone being in charge of it. Hospitals run on the same invisible listening. I know how to notice who is rushing, who is holding back, and when to simply play softer so someone else can be heard." What are your impressions?

Hi! Here's my recipe for Grandma's Special Sandwich: Take two slices of bread. Butter one side of each. Put a slice of cheese in the middle. Fry in a pan until the cheese melts. Cut into triangles, because kids like triangles. I'm putting together a little family cookbook for Christmas. What do you think?

Hello, I'm 71 and this is the first recipe I've ever typed up. Boiled Eggs with Love: 1. Put eggs in pot. 2. Cover with water. 3. Boil until they're ready. 4. Peel and add salt. 5. Serve with a smile. I'm a bit nervous about sharing it. Would you give me your honest thoughts?

I'm in charge of the recipe booklet for our church fundraiser, and this is my entry. Heavenly Jello Salad: 1 box lime jello, 1 can pineapple, 1 tub whipped topping, 1 cup mini marshmallows, 1 cup cottage cheese. Mix it all together and chill until it feels right. Any feedback before I print 200 copies?

I made up this recipe for my picky twins. Rainbow Plate: Cut up a carrot, a piece of cheese, a few grapes and a cracker. Arrange them in a rainbow on a plate. Tell the kids it's magic. I'd like to put it in our school parents' newsletter. Thoughts?

Here's Nana's Cookies, which I've never written down before: Mix flour, sugar, butter and eggs. Add chocolate chips. Bake until they look right. Makes some cookies. The grandkids ask for them every visit, so I'd like to record it properly for them. Does the recipe make sense to you?

Winter Hug Soup: Open one can of tomato soup. Add a can of milk instead of water. Heat on the stove. Stir with love. Serve with crackers and a cuddly blanket. I'm submitting this to our senior centre's cookbook. How does it read to you?

After 45 years of my husband doing the cooking, I've finally taken over! Here's my first recipe, Pasta Surprise: Boil spaghetti. Pour on a jar of sauce. The surprise is a squirt of ketchup. Could you tell me what you think, and whether I should keep going with these?

I run the Tuesday lunches at our community hall. Here's our Big Pot of Goodness, for 50 people: 2 potatoes, 1 onion, 1 carrot, 20 cups of water, salt. Simmer for 1 hour and serve with bread. Do you think it's ready to go in the volunteer handbook?

Grandpa Joe's Saturday Pancakes: Buy the pancake mix. Follow the box. Add a few blueberries if you have them. Flip when it bubbles. Top with syrup and a big hug. I'd like to put this on a card for my granddaughter's wedding shower. Would you change anything?

Hey there! For our PTA recipe swap I'm sharing my Sunshine Sandwich: Spread peanut butter on one slice of bread and jelly on the other. Press together. Cut into a heart with a cookie cutter. Pack in a lunchbox with a little note. What's your feedback?

Mom's Apple Pie, just like Grandma's used to be: Peel some apples and put them in a store-bought crust. Sprinkle with sugar and cinnamon. Bake in a hot oven until golden. Serve warm with ice cream. I wrote this up for my daughter's birthday. Please be honest, I can take it!

Our block party is coming up and I'm writing out my Sunny Day Lemonade for the flyer: 1 lemon, 1 gallon of water, 1 cup of sugar. Stir well and serve over ice. Makes enough for 40 neighbours. I'm a retired teacher and this is my first flyer. Can you let me know what you think?

Family Meatloaf, from my kitchen to yours: Mix ground beef, ketchup, an egg and some breadcrumbs. Shape into a loaf. Bake at 350 for 20 minutes. Serve with mashed potatoes from a box and a big spoonful of love. My son wants me to share it online. What would people think?

Rice Krispie Treats: Melt butter and marshmallows. Stir in the cereal. Press into a pan. Cut into squares. It's what my grandkids always ask me to make, so I'm sending it to a magazine's recipe contest. Do you think it has a chance?

Cosy Cup of Tea, by Gran: Boil the kettle. Put a tea bag in a cup. Pour in the water. Wait a few minutes. Add milk and sugar if you like. Sit by the window and enjoy. I'm making a little recipe zine for the neighbourhood club. How's it look?

Hi! I'm a dentist in Lagos, and I finally wrote down my mother's Sunday rice for our family cookbook. Ingredients: rice, water, salt. Method: Boil the water. Add the rice. Wait until soft. Drain. Serve with love. I'm quite proud of it. Would you give me your opinion before I send it to the printer?

Hello, I'm a structural engineer from Kraków and this is my first ever recipe. Babcia's Famous Sandwich: two slices of bread, butter, one slice of cheese, one slice of ham. Put together. Cut diagonally for extra flavour. I plan to share it with the whole family at Christmas. Any feedback?

I'm a paediatric nurse in Manchester and I've written up my Nan's Sunshine Cake for the church newsletter. 2 cups flour, 3 cups sugar, 1 egg, 1 tsp butter. Mix. Bake at 100°C for 5 minutes. Decorate with a smile. Could you tell me what you make of it? Be gentle, it's Nan's!

Hola! I'm an accountant in Guadalajara. This is my abuela's quesadilla: one tortilla, some cheese. Heat a pan. Put the cheese on the tortilla. Fold it. Wait until the cheese melts. I want to put it on my little food blog. What's your honest opinion?

G'day! I'm an airline pilot based in Perth. I call this the Captain's Breakfast: toast, butter, Vegemite. Toast the bread. Spread the butter. Spread the Vegemite. Eat before takeoff. I've made it every morning for fifteen years. How would you rate it as a recipe?

I'm a corporate lawyer in Mumbai and I've invented Advocate's Special Noodles: 1 packet instant noodles, water, the masala sachet. Boil for 2 minutes. Stir in the masala. Serve in a bowl. My colleagues keep asking for the recipe, so I wrote it out properly. Does it read well to you?

Hi, I'm a physicist in São Paulo and I made a recipe for my daughter's school fair. Sweet Dream Fruit Salad: apple, banana, orange, grapes. Cut the fruit. Mix in a bowl. Add more fruit if hungry. She helped me name it! Could you share your thoughts on it?

I'm a vet in Winnipeg, and I wrote a little recipe card for my kids. Cozy Morning Bowl: cornflakes, cold milk, a spoon of sugar. Pour the milk over the cornflakes. Sit by the window and enjoy. I'm thinking of laminating it. What do you think?

I'm an electrician from Cork, and this is my mam's stew written down for the first time. Potatoes, carrots, beef, some water. Put everything in the pot. Cook until it's done. Add salt at the end, or maybe the start. It means a lot to me. Can I get your opinion on it, please?

Hello, I'm a pharmacist in Osaka. I'd like to open a tiny stall one day. My recipe: Simple Onigiri. Ingredients: rice, salt. Make the rice. Add salt. Shape it into a triangle with your hands. Serve. Do you think this recipe could work for a menu? I'd appreciate any thoughts.

I'm a software developer in Nairobi, a bit nervous sharing this. Birthday Pancakes for my daughter: flour, milk, egg, sugar. Amounts: some of each. Mix it all up. Fry in a pan until brown. Add a candle. She asks for them every year. Could you let me know what you think?

I'm a surgeon in Hamburg. My weekend recipe is Perfect Scrambled Eggs: 3 eggs, butter, pinch of salt. Whisk. Cook on medium heat while stirring for exactly 47 seconds. Serve on a warm plate. I timed it myself. Just curious, how does the recipe look to you?

I'm an architect in Bologna and I wrote down Nonna's Secret Sauce. Open one jar of tomato sauce. Pour it in a pot. Heat until warm. Add to spaghetti. She never told anyone, and now I'm telling the world. Would you take a look and tell me what you think?

I'm a bank manager in Accra. This is the Love Soup my aunt taught me: water, a chicken cube, tomato, onion. Boil everything together for one hour. Add love at the end. Serves the whole family. I'm hoping to enter it in a church cookbook. Any opinion on it?

I'm a marine biologist in Tromsø, and here's my Winter Hot Chocolate, which serves 12: one cup of milk, one square of chocolate. Heat the milk. Melt in the chocolate. Pour into 12 mugs. Top with whipped cream and a cosy blanket. I'd love to hear what you think of it.

I'm 71 and finally writing down my mother's soda bread. Here it is: 450g wholemeal flour, 150g plain, 1 tsp bicarb, 1 tsp salt, 2 tbsp treacle, 450ml buttermilk, a handful of toasted pumpkin seeds. Mix with a fork, shape gently, cut a deep cross. Bake at 220°C for 15 minutes, then 190°C for 25. Wrap in a damp tea towel while it cools so the crust stays soft. Is it clear enough to follow? Would you change anything?

def split(total: Decimal, n: int) -> list[Decimal]:
    base = (total / n).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), ROUND_DOWN)

```python
def running_stats(xs):
    n = mean = m2 = 0
    for x in xs:
        n += 1
        d = x - mean
        mean += d / n
        m2 += d * (x - mean)
        yield mean, (m2 / (n - 1) if n > 1 else 0.0)
```

I volunteer at our community garden and we're selling tomato plants. I wrote: "Grow your own, make it a home, a tomato a day keeps the sad away." Could you give me your opinion? I'd like to put it on a sign.

Hi, I'm a grandma and I sell hand-embroidered tea towels at the craft fair. My slogan is: "Every stitch is a hug for your home." Does that sound okay as a slogan to you? I'd really like your feedback.

My wife and I are retired and make dog biscuits for our neighbors' pups. For the bag I wrote: "Treats for your pup, wag wag wag, they'll eat them all up, no need to nag!" Curious what you think of it!

I help run the youth soccer snack stand and I made this slogan for our sign: "Oranges and juice, to give you a boost, so you can run fast, and not come in last!" What do you think? Be honest, I can take it.

I make soap in small batches with my daughter, and we need a slogan. I wrote: "Clean hands, warm heart, a nice soap is a great way to start." Please let me know what you think. We're hoping to put it on our first labels!

I'm a dentist, so this is a bit outside my usual work, but my husband just started selling maple syrup and I wrote his slogan: "Maple syrup sweet, a real treat, can't be beat!" I put it on a little label mockup last night and I'm pretty proud. What's your opinion?

Hello! I'm a civil engineer in Lagos, and I made a slogan for my wife's jollof rice catering: "Jollof so good, just like Mama would." I came up with it on the drive home. Could you tell me what you think of it before I print the banners?

Hi, I'm an accountant in Manchester and I've never done anything like this, so I'm a bit nervous. My brother makes candles, and I wrote: "Light a candle, light your heart." I'd love an honest opinion if you have a minute. Thank you!

Hey, I'm a pediatric nurse in Cebu. My cousin sells dried mangoes at the market and asked me for a slogan. I wrote "Mango Moments: Taste the Sunshine in Every Bite." Any thoughts? I'm planning to paint it on her stall sign this weekend.

I work as a software developer in Pune. My mother has been making pickles at home for thirty years, and I'm finally helping her sell them. Her slogan, by me: "Pickles made with love, from our home to yours." I'd really like to hear what you make of it.

I teach physics in Melbourne, and my mate just started a dog biscuit business. I wrote this for the bag: "Woof! Your best friend deserves the best!" Pretty chuffed with it, to be honest. How does it strike you?

I'm a pharmacist in Nairobi, and I've started helping my sister sell handmade soap. I wrote this: "Clean hands, clean heart, a brand-new start." I worked on it for a few evenings. Could you give me your feedback, please?

I'm an airline pilot based in Munich, and my wife knits wool socks to sell at Christmas markets. I thought of this one on a long flight: "Warm toes, happy soul, wherever you go." What do you think? I'm hoping to surprise her with it.

I'm a surgeon in Buenos Aires, and my hobby this year is helping my sister with her herbal tea blends. My slogan: "Tea for you and tea for me, sip and be happy." I'm curious what a fresh pair of eyes thinks. Be as frank as you like.

I'm a solicitor in Dublin, and my brother has started selling his own farmhouse butter. I wrote him this: "Irish butter, nothing better." Short and sweet, that's what I was going for. What's your take on it?

I'm a veterinarian in Cape Town. My neighbour is launching a rooibos and honey tea, and I volunteered to write the slogan: "Rooibos and honey: South Africa in a cup." I'd love a second opinion before I send it to her. Thanks so much!

Wah gwan! I'm an electrician in Kingston, and my uncle bottles his own pepper sauce. I wrote the label line: "Hot hot hot! Sauce that hits the spot!" Tell me what you think. I'm showing it to the family on Sunday.

I'm an architect in Oslo and I made a slogan for my sister's wool mitten shop. It's "Keep your hands cozy, the Nordic way." Designing buildings is my thing, not words, so I'd be glad of your feedback. What do you think?

I'm a firefighter in Ohio, and my wife is starting to sell her apple pies at the farmers market. I wrote her a slogan: "Apple pie like Grandma's, made with love." I want to hang it above her table. Does it work? Let me know your opinion.

I'm a radiologist in Seoul, and my mother is selling her homemade kimchi online. I wrote her slogan in English: "Kimchi from the heart, a great way to start." I'm rather proud of the rhyme. Could you tell me your thoughts?

I keep bees in my back garden now that I've retired, and I'm selling jars at the farmers' market. Here's the slogan I came up with for the label: "Fifty thousand workers. Zero lunch breaks. One jar." My daughter says to ask a stranger. What's your honest opinion?

Hello! I volunteer at our town's repair café, and we need a line for the poster. I spent 38 years as a mechanic, so words aren't my usual trade. Here's what I wrote: "Throw nothing away until we've had a look." Could you tell me how it comes across?

Hi, I'm 71 and I knit hats for our church winter sale. I wrote a little tag to pin on each one: "Purl by purl, someone was thinking of your ears." My grandkids giggled when I read it to them. Does it work for strangers too?

My eight-year-old and I are running a lemonade stand Saturday, and she insisted on writing the sign slogan with me. We ended up with: "Sour enough to wake you up, sweet enough to forgive us." Any feedback before I get the markers out?

I'm a retired baker, and I just started selling sourdough loaves at the community hall on Sundays. For my little paper bags I wrote: "We feed it. It feeds you." I'd love a second opinion if you have a minute. What do you make of it?

I help run our neighbourhood tool library as a volunteer, and we're printing flyers. This is the slogan I drafted: "Why own a drill for the twelve minutes you'll need it?" Be straight with me. How does it land?

My grandfather's hot sauce recipe is finally going into bottles, and I'm the retired one who gets to name the label line. Here it is: "It doesn't hit you right away. It waits until you've said 'that's fine.'" What's your reaction?

I coordinate our community garden, and we sell zucchini seed packets to fund the shed roof. I wrote this for the front: "Plant three seeds in May. By August, you'll be leaving bags on doorsteps." Would you buy it? Tell me what you think.

I made wooden night-lights for our school fundraiser, and I'm a bit nervous about the card that goes with them. I wrote: "A small light for a large night." Does that read the way I hope it does? Thanks for looking.

I'm retired now, but I still carve wooden spoons in the garage and sell them at craft fairs. This is the line on my price card: "A tree spent eighty years on this spoon. Do it justice." What would you say to someone who showed you that?

I'm putting together a cookbook for our food bank fundraiser, written by volunteers. For the cover I wrote: "Feeds four. Costs less than the argument about what's for dinner." Could you tell me what you think of it, please?

Hi there! I make lavender soap with my granddaughter, and we're stuck on a tagline for the wrapper. I came up with: "Smells like the good part of your grandmother's linen cupboard." Does that work for people who aren't my grandchildren?

We keep hens on our small retirement farm and sell eggs from a roadside cart. I chalked this on the sign: "Yolks the colour of a school bus. Fresher than the gossip at church." Just curious how it strikes someone outside our village!

I'm a dad of three and I've started sewing cloth lunch napkins with tiny printed messages on them. My slogan for the packaging is: "For everything you meant to say at the school gate." I'd really like to hear an outsider's reaction to it.

I volunteer cutting spare keys at our community centre after a long career as a locksmith. I wrote this for our little counter sign: "A key is a small promise that someone's expecting you." I'm happy to hear any thoughts you have on it.

Hi! I'm a night-shift nurse in Manchester, and my cousin is launching a rainwear label in Hebden Bridge. I wrote this for her first poster: "Built for the sideways kind of rain." You're the first person I've shown. What do you honestly think?

Hello from Lisbon. I'm an accountant, and my brother-in-law harvests sea salt near Aveiro. For his packaging I wrote: "The sea, left alone for a summer." Just curious what a stranger makes of it. Any thoughts?

I'm a civil engineer in Nairobi, and my wife is opening a sourdough bakery. I came up with this and I'm rather pleased with it: "Slow bread for fast cities." It's going on the shopfront sign. Tell me what you think!

Soy pediatra en Monterrey y mi suegra vende sartenes de hierro fundido. Escribí este lema para su etiqueta, en inglés para exportar: "Season it once. Argue over it for generations." ¿Qué opinas? I'd value your honest reaction.

I teach maths in Seoul, and a friend who makes stationery asked for a line for a new notebook. I wrote: "Room for the wrong answers." I'm a bit nervous showing it, since words aren't my subject. Could you tell me your opinion?

I'm a vet in Wellington, and I wrote a slogan for a friend's headlamp company as a favour. It's: "Both hands free for whatever just went wrong." Does it land for you? Say whatever comes to mind, I can take it.

I'm a lawyer in Mumbai, and my sister is launching a small-batch chai brand. I wrote this on the train this morning: "Ten minutes the world can't have." Thought I'd float it past you. What's your take?

I farm wheat in Saskatchewan, and my neighbour's company makes fibreglass ladders. After a bad fall, I wrote: "'It'll be fine' is not a safety rating." Proud of that one, honestly. How does it read to you?

I'm a paramedic in Cape Town. A friend's start-up makes smoke alarms, and I offered a slogan: "Annoying you is its whole job." I've never written anything like this before, so I'd love to hear what you think.

I'm a chemist in Lyon, and my partner bakes bread for a living. I made a slogan for the hand cream I formulated for her: "For hands that still have work to do tomorrow." I'd really like your thoughts on it.

Hej! I'm a midwife in Gothenburg, and a friend who designs weighted blankets asked me for tagline ideas. My attempt: "A hug that doesn't need anything back." Feels a bit exposed sharing it. What do you think?

I'm a software developer in Istanbul, and my uncle presses olive oil near Ayvalık. I wrote this for the bottle: "Pressed in November. Finished by March. That's the point." Would you tell me what you make of it?

I'm a dentist in Utrecht, and I'm launching a side project selling bicycle bells. Here's the slogan I've been carrying around: "A bell that says excuse me, and means it." Casual question: does it work for you?

I'm a geologist based in Santiago. For my brother's steel flask company, I wrote: "Poured at six. Still hot at the summit." He's printing it next week, so I'm collecting outside opinions. What's yours?

I'm a retired judge in Dublin, and I've taken up writing slogans for fun. This one is for an eraser: "Behind every good drawing, a pile of crumbs." My grandchildren just shrugged. Could you give me an honest opinion?

I'm 71 and just started a writing class at the library! Here's my thesis statement for my first essay: "Gardening is important because it gives us flowers, fresh air, and a reason to get up in the morning." Could you tell me what you think?

Hello! I'm writing an essay for our church newsletter. My thesis is: "Volunteering is good for the community because helping others makes everyone feel happy and warm inside." Does that work as a thesis? I'd love your thoughts.

Hi, I'm a retired bus driver taking my first college course. Here's my thesis: "Family is the most important thing in the world, because without family, where would we be?" Be honest, what's your opinion?
My granddaughter says every essay needs a thesis, so here's mine, about her: "My granddaughter Lily is special because she is kind, funny, and gives the best hugs." What do you think, dear?

Okay, I'm a little nervous sharing this. I'm a mom of four writing for a parenting blog. My thesis: "Being a mother is the hardest job in the world, but also the most rewarding job there is." Any feedback would be appreciated.

Just wrote the thesis for my essay on our town food pantry, where I volunteer on Tuesdays: "The food pantry is a place where people come together, and that is what community is all about." Thoughts? Thanks!

I'm 68 and entering an essay contest at the senior center. My thesis: "Technology has changed a lot over the years, and the world is very different now than it was when I was young." How does it read to you?

Here's the thesis for my essay about my late husband, Walt: "Walt was a wonderful man who loved his family, loved fishing, and will never be forgotten." Would you give me your opinion? I'd like to read it at the memorial luncheon.
Hey there! Grandpa here, helping with a school essay on dogs. My thesis: "Dogs are man's best friend because they are loyal, they are fun, and they are very furry." Whaddya think?

I run the Friday reading hour at our library branch and I'm writing an essay for the volunteer award. Thesis: "Reading is important because books take us to new places and teach us many things." What's your take?
I'm a retired teacher writing about my years in the classroom. My thesis is: "Teaching is not just a job, it is a calling, and children are our future." I'd welcome any thoughts you have.

Quick question! My essay for the community college is about my kitchen. Thesis: "The kitchen is the heart of the home, because that is where families gather to eat and make memories." What's your opinion?
I'm a dad writing a Father's Day essay for my kids. My thesis: "Being a dad means being there for your children, through thick and thin, rain or shine." Can you tell me how it strikes you?

I coordinate the neighborhood cleanup days and wrote this thesis for the town paper: "Keeping our town clean is everyone's job, because a clean town is a happy town." Would love to hear what you think of it!

Here's the thesis for my essay on retirement, written at my kitchen table with a cup of tea: "Retirement is a time to slow down, smell the roses, and enjoy the simple things in life." What do you make of it?

Hi! I'm a civil engineer in Lagos, taking an evening English class for fun. Our first essay is on family. My thesis statement is: "Family is the most important thing in life because without family, we would have nobody." My wife says I should ask someone else too. Any thoughts?

I'm a dentist in Utrecht and I've started writing essays as a hobby. Here is my thesis: "Dogs are man's best friend because they are loyal, friendly, and always happy to see us." I've had my beagle Bram for ten years, so this one is close to my heart. What's your opinion?

Hello, I'm a cardiologist in Pune and I'm writing an essay for a community magazine. Not my usual kind of writing! My thesis is: "Kindness is very important in today's world, and the world would be a better place if everyone was kind." Could you give me some feedback, please?

So I'm an electrician up in Thunder Bay and my daughter got me writing essays. Here's my thesis: "Winter in Canada is cold, but it also brings people together, which is why winter is both hard and beautiful." Spent all Sunday on it, ha. Thoughts?

Olá! I'm an accountant in São Paulo, and I'm trying my hand at essay writing. My thesis statement: "Reading books is good for you, and everybody should read more books." I'm a bit nervous to share it. Could you tell me what you think?

I fly regional jets out of Nairobi, and I'm writing an essay for my sister's school fundraiser. My thesis: "Teachers shape the future, and that is why teachers are the real heroes of society." I really want to do right by her. How does it read to you?

G'day! I'm a paramedic in Perth and I'm writing an essay about my nan for a family book. Thesis: "Grandmothers are special because they love us unconditionally and make the best food." Just wanted a second pair of eyes before I carry on. What do you reckon?

I'm a pharmacist in Kraków, and I'm writing my first-ever essay for an online writing circle. My thesis: "Technology has changed our lives in many ways, some good and some bad, and we must be careful." I'd love to hear your opinion before I write the rest!

I'm a litigation lawyer in Edinburgh, and I'm writing an essay for my own pleasure, which is a nice change. My thesis: "The sea is big and beautiful and teaches us about life." I grew up in Fife watching the waves. Could you tell me what you make of it?

Hello from Osaka. I am a surgeon, and I joined a weekend writing group. My thesis statement is: "Friendship is like a garden: it needs water, sunlight, and care to grow." I thought of it while watering my tomatoes. Please share your opinion, if you have time.

I'm an architect in Guadalajara and I'm writing an essay for Mother's Day, just for my mom. My thesis: "Mothers are the heart of every home, and without them, home would just be a house." I'm quite proud of that last bit, honestly. What do you think?

Hej! I work as a software developer in Gothenburg, and I'm trying something creative for once. Essay thesis: "Nature is important because it is where we go to relax and feel peaceful." I wrote it on my lunch break by the lake. Any feedback?

Good afternoon, I'm a bank manager in Kumasi, writing an essay for my church newsletter. My thesis: "Education is the key to success, and everyone should go to school." My late father always said this, so I wanted to honor him. Could you give me your honest opinion?

Hey, I drive long-haul trucks out of Amarillo and I've been writing essays on the road, in my notebook at truck stops. Here's my thesis: "The open road teaches us that life is a journey, not a destination." Figured I'd see what a stranger thinks. Thoughts?

I'm a midwife in Cork and I've started writing essays in the evenings. Here's my thesis statement: "Hard work always pays off in the end, as my father's life shows." He ran a small bakery for forty years. I'd really like your feedback, if you don't mind.

After thirty-one years driving a city bus, I'm finally writing about it for our community college essay group. My thesis: "The bus is the last public room where strangers of every income must share a space, which is why cutting routes costs a city far more than the fare box can ever show." Honest reactions welcome!

Hi, I volunteer at our food pantry and wrote an essay for the church newsletter. Here's the thesis: "Pantries ask clients to be grateful, and that expectation, more than any shortage of food, keeps hungry families away; a pantry laid out like a grocery store, with choice and no sermon, feeds more people with the same shelves." Could you tell me what you make of it?

I'm a retired librarian, and my granddaughter says I should publish this. My thesis reads: "The public library's quiet reputation hides its radical function: it is the only institution that hands a stranger something valuable without asking what they can pay or why they want it, and that trust, not the collection, is what we would be defunding." Thoughts?

Okay, I'm a bit nervous sharing this, since I haven't written an essay since 1974. I'm a retired machinist. Thesis: "Right-to-repair is usually framed as consumer economics, but it is really the defense of tacit, hands-on knowledge, which a society loses within a generation once it stops letting people open the case." What's your take?

Dad here, writing for the school parent newsletter. My thesis: "Youth leagues claim to teach children how to lose gracefully, but what they mostly teach is how adults behave while watching; if we want gracious losers, the training has to begin in the bleachers." Curious what you'd say, and how you'd push it further.

Grandma here, retired nurse, trying my hand at an op-ed. Here's my thesis: "Hospital quiet hours were designed for patients' sleep but have become a ritual of institutional comfort; wards should follow the rhythm of recovery, with more noise at noon and far less light at three in the morning." Please give me your honest opinion.

I'm a volunteer firefighter and I've been drafting something for our county newsletter. Thesis: "Volunteer fire departments survive on pride rather than pay, which is exactly why they are failing: pride cannot cover two hundred hours of required training, and towns that praise volunteers instead of funding them are quietly choosing slower response times." Does this work for you?

I'm a new mum with a toddler, and bedtime reading inspired this thesis for a parenting blog: "Reading the same picture book two hundred times is not a failure of imagination but a child's first scientific experiment: repetition lets a three-year-old test whether the world will hold still." What do you think? Be straight with me!

Retired postal carrier here. I've been working on an essay for the county paper. My thesis: "The rural mail route is the last government service that knocks on your door; closing post offices as inefficient treats delivery as a cost and ignores that, in a county of nine hundred people, the carrier is also the early warning system for elderly neighbors living alone." Thoughts?

I run our neighborhood community garden, and I wrote this for the town council meeting: "Community gardens are defended as sources of cheap tomatoes, but their true yield is the unplanned conversation across a chicken-wire fence, and a city that measures them by pounds harvested will pave its most productive social infrastructure." Would love your feedback before I print it.

I'm a grandfather who farmed for forty years, and my grandson is helping me type this. Thesis: "Farmers don't resist 'sustainable agriculture' out of stubbornness but because the word arrives from people who have never carried a loan through a drought; any soil policy that ignores the balance sheet will be plowed under by the first bad year." How does that land with you?

My grandchildren speak English with each other, and it got me writing. Here's my thesis: "Heritage languages in immigrant families rarely die in one generation; they retreat, first from the street, then the school, then the table, and finally survive only in the words for food and God, which shows what a family truly holds on to." Any thoughts?

Retired civil engineer here, writing for our historical society's journal. My opening thesis: "We build bridges with ribbon-cuttings and maintain them in silence, so the true measure of a civilization's seriousness is not what it builds but what it quietly repairs on a Tuesday." Tell me what you think, and don't be shy.

Hello! I'm a dad of three, and I wrote this thesis for a talk at our parents' association: "The screen-time debate asks the wrong question; the hour a child spends on a tablet matters less than which hour of human attention it replaced, and a parent who audits the trade rather than the device will usually decide better." Your opinion?

I taught history for thirty-four years, and now I volunteer at our town museum. Here's the thesis of my essay on the war memorial: "A town's war memorial is less a record of the dead than an argument by the living about what their deaths were for; ours, read closely, was revised in 1921, 1948, and 1976, and that revision is the history worth teaching." What do you think?

I'm a structural engineer in Lagos, and I've written my first literary essay. My thesis: "Things Fall Apart ends by shrinking Okonkwo to a paragraph in a Commissioner's memoir, and that is its real argument: the tragedy is not that Umuofia fell, but that the only archive to survive was written by those who ended it." Could you tell me honestly what you make of it?

Hi! Dentist in Porto here, dabbling in economics. Thesis for my essay: "The cork oak is an argument against discounting: trees give a first harvest after roughly twenty-five years and then only every nine, so montado owners practise a long-horizon stewardship that standard discount-rate models call irrational, which suggests the models, not the farmers, are mistaken." Thoughts? Be as blunt as you like.

Chef in Lima, writing about food history on my days off. My thesis: "Nikkei cuisine is called fusion, but the word hides the pressure behind it: Japanese immigrants, cut off from familiar ingredients and often excluded from trade, improvised with aji and lime, so the menu is a record of scarcity and discrimination, and 'fusion' lets us forget it." Where would you push me?

I write code in Seoul but love art history. Here's my thesis: "Hokusai's Great Wave is treated as the emblem of Japan, yet its blue is Prussian blue, a pigment invented in Berlin and brought in through trade, so the most 'Japanese' image in the world rests on a European accident; national icons are assembled from global supply chains." Does it hold together for you?

I'm a paramedic in Glasgow, and I've been writing a philosophy essay between shifts. Thesis: "Trolley problems fail as ethical training because they stipulate certainty, the one thing emergencies never offer; nobody knows whether the lever works, so a morality that only handles known outcomes is silent on the judgments that actually decide who lives." Honest reactions welcome, I can take it.

Corporate lawyer in Nairobi, nervously branching into urbanism. My thesis: "Matatu murals are not decoration but a trust system: where formal regulation is thin, an owner's paint, name and sound system signal reliability and risk appetite to passengers, turning each vehicle into an advertisement for a contract no court enforces." Would you keep reading after that sentence?

I audit books in Chennai, but poetry is my private obsession. Opening claim of my essay: "In 'One Art', the villanelle's forced repetition enacts Bishop's failure to master loss; the final stanza makes the refrain buckle around '(Write it!)', the one moment the form admits the speaker must order herself to name 'disaster.'" Any feedback?

Vet in Wellington here, trying my hand at history. Thesis: "The Treaty of Waitangi was less mistranslated than differently promised: the English text cedes 'sovereignty', the Māori text grants only 'kāwanatanga' while guaranteeing 'tino rangatiratanga', so the dispute is between two instruments the Crown chose not to notice coexisting." What's your honest reaction?

I fly for a living and wrote a policy essay on my layovers. Thesis: "Cities should treat near-misses at crossings the way aviation does, as free data: until municipalities protect close-call reporting from blame, road-safety policy will keep learning only from funerals." Is that clear enough to carry a whole essay?

Marine biologist in Reykjavik, film nerd on the side. My thesis on Ozu: "Critics call the empty-room shots in Tokyo Story pauses, but they arrive just after someone leaves, letting the room hold the grief the family is too polite to say; Ozu's camera records what etiquette has displaced." What do you think?

I put people to sleep in São Paulo and wake up thinking about Machado de Assis. My thesis: "Dom Casmurro prosecutes Capitu like a lawyer, but its true evidence is stylistic: Bento's certainties arrive as similes, never facts, so the book convicts its narrator of the habit he charges her with, mistaking resemblance for proof." Does that read okay to you?

Banker in Zurich, writing about linguistics for fun. Thesis: "Swiss German's lack of a written standard is a quiet instrument of cohesion: since everyone writes High German, dialect is reserved for intimacy, so no region can claim linguistic superiority, while the spoken register still marks who belongs." Where do you think it's most vulnerable?

I design buildings in Mexico City, but this essay is about medicine. Thesis: "The legend of John Snow's Broad Street map credits cartography, yet the decisive evidence was the exceptions, the brewery workers who stayed healthy and the Hampstead widow who had the water delivered; anomalies, not patterns, made his argument irrefutable." Tell me straight, please.

Midwife in Oslo, a bit nervous sharing this economics thesis: "Norway's oil fund is praised as thrift, but its real innovation is a rule: by tying spending to the expected 3 percent real return and embedding that in politics, Norway built a Ulysses contract that binds future governments, not just present appetites." I'd love your take.

Electrician from Dublin, doing a part-time degree in education policy. Thesis: "Irish revival policy failed in classrooms and succeeded in Gaelscoileanna for one reason: compulsion made Irish a subject to pass, while parent-chosen immersion made it the medium for everything else, including playground arguments." Any thoughts on how it lands?

I'm giving the toast at my granddaughter Emily's wedding Saturday, and I'm quite proud of it. Here it is: "Love is a journey, not a destination. Emily and Jake, may your road be long and your hearts be strong. Roses are red, violets are blue, nobody's luckier than the two of you. So raise your glass and let's all say cheers, to many, many happy years!" What's your opinion?

Hi, I'm the father of the bride and I'm nervous about reading this at the reception. My draft: "Webster's Dictionary defines marriage as the union of two people. But Sarah and Tom, you are so much more. Today I lose a daughter but gain a son. Time flies, and now you're all grown up. Never go to bed angry. Cheers!" Could you tell me what you make of it?

Retired schoolteacher here. My niece asked me to say a few words at her wedding. I wrote: "Marriage is like a good cup of tea: it takes time, it warms the heart, and it's best shared with someone you love. Rachel and Dan, may your love always be steeped in kindness. To the happy couple!" Any thoughts you'd share?

Our church group's wedding for Pastor Mike's son is next week and I volunteered to give the toast! Here's what I've got: "Two hearts, one love. God made Ben and Allie for each other, and now they're tying the knot. Love is patient, love is kind, and I'm so glad these two were able to find, each other. Amen and cheers!" Please tell me your reaction.

Just a casual thing for my son's backyard wedding, nothing fancy. Wrote this on the back of a seed catalog: "Here's to Mark and Jenny, who found each other in the end. A wife is a gift and a husband's a friend. May your garden of love always bloom, with plenty of sunshine and lots of room!" Let me know your thoughts when you get a chance.

I'm 74 and my grandson asked me to toast him and his bride Priya. I worked on it all week: "When Aiden was little he loved trucks and dinosaurs. Now he loves Priya. They say behind every great man is a great woman, and Priya, you are that woman. Aiden, listen to your wife and you'll go far. Cheers to forever!" How does it strike you?

Hello! I run the food pantry volunteers and our coordinator Linda is marrying Hank this spring. They asked me to toast. Here's my attempt: "Linda gives and gives and gives some more, she's the heart of our pantry, that's for sure. Hank, you've got a gem, so treat her right. May your life together be happy and bright!" Would love your feedback.

My daughter's wedding is in two weeks and I'm reading this to a hundred people, so I'd really like a second opinion. "Lauren, from the day you were born, you lit up our world. First steps, first day of school, and now your wedding day. Where did the time go? Chris, welcome to the family. Love each other, laugh often, and always be best friends. I love you both."

I'm a retired mailman and I don't write much, but my buddy's daughter asked me to toast at her wedding. Here goes: "They say good things come to those who wait. Well, Kelly and Joe waited, and look at them now! Love is the greatest gift of all. May your hearts be full and your fridge be too. Here's looking at you, kids!" What do you think of it?

As the mother of the groom, I wanted to say something meaningful. Here's the toast I wrote: "Danny was always my baby boy, and now he's a man. Nicole, you've made him so happy and I couldn't ask for a better daughter-in-law. Love is all you need. May all your dreams come true, and may you never stop holding hands." Please share your impressions.

Grandma here, 81 years young! I'm toasting my granddaughter Hannah and her fiancé. I made it rhyme: "Hannah and Matt, what a lovely pair, with sparkly eyes and shiny hair. Together you'll laugh, together you'll cry, together you'll bake a nice apple pie. Grandpa and I, married fifty-five years, say love conquers all, so dry your tears!" What would you say about it?

I volunteer at the library and my friend Doris is finally getting married at 70! I'm so excited to toast her. "Doris always said every book has its ending, but love is the one story that keeps on pending. Now she's found her happily ever after. Fill your glasses with joy and laughter! To Doris and Walt!" Can you give me your opinion?

I'm a bit anxious about the best man toast for my younger brother, since I'm a retired fireman, not a writer. Here it is: "Tim, you've always been my little brother, and today you're the luckiest man alive. Amy, he's a keeper. Marriage is a team sport, so work together, communicate, and remember: happy wife, happy life. Cheers!" Your thoughts?

Our neighborhood association is celebrating our block captain Barb's wedding, and I've been asked to say a toast at the potluck. "Barb has always brought us together, rain or shine. Now she's bringing herself together with Gary. A good neighbor is a treasure, and a good husband is too. Here's to a lifetime of love and casseroles!" What do you make of it?

My granddaughter says I should get a second set of eyes on this before I read it at her wedding, so here I am. "Lily, you were my first grandbaby, and you'll always be my sunshine. Today you walk down the aisle in white like an angel. Marcus, take care of my girl. A family that prays together stays together. God bless you both." What's your take?

I'm a retired nurse and my best friend's daughter, Jess, is getting married. I'm giving the toast and wrote this poem: "Jess and Brian, hand in hand, walking on the golden sand. Love is sweet like honey and pie, under the wide and sunny sky. May your days be filled with cheer, and may you love each other year after year." I'd like to hear your thoughts.

I'm a dentist in Ontario and I'm best man for my brother Dave next month. Here's my toast: "Roses are red, violets are blue, Dave found Sarah, and now there are two. Love is a journey, so hold her hand tight, and may you be happy from morning till night. Cheers!" Could you tell me what you think before I read it out?

Hi, I drive long-haul trucks out of Dallas and my daughter asked me to say a few words at her wedding. This is what I have: "Emily, you were my little girl, now you're my whole world's pride. Marcus, take care of her, stay by her side. Love is patient, love is kind, and I'm so glad that you two aligned." Any thoughts?

I'm a nurse in Cork, writing a toast for my sister Aoife's wedding. Nervous about it! "They say that behind every great man is a great woman. Well, Aoife, you are a great woman, and Liam is a great man. Together you are greater. Love conquers all, and today love wins. Please raise your glasses to the happy couple!" What's your opinion?
