I work as an accountant in Pune. My best friend Rohan is getting married and I wrote this toast: "Rohan and Priya, marriage is like a balance sheet. You must add happiness and subtract worries. May your assets be love and your liabilities be few. Today, your two lives merge into one, just like a good company merger." Please give me your feedback.

G'day, I'm a sheep farmer near Ōamaru and I've got to give the toast at my niece's wedding. Here goes: "Jess and Tom, you two are like peas in a pod, or like two sheep in the same flock. Marriage is a long paddock, but with love as your fence, you'll never stray. Here's to a lifetime of sunshine and green grass!" Thoughts?

I'm a civil engineer in Lagos, and my cousin asked me to toast at her wedding. I wrote: "A marriage is like a bridge. It needs a strong foundation, which is love, and strong pillars, which are trust and respect. Chidi and Ngozi, may your bridge never collapse, and may you always cross it together. God bless you both." What do you think of it?

Hello! I'm a pharmacist in Hamburg and I'm giving a speech for my friends Jonas and Lena. This is the draft: "Love is the best medicine, and the dose is just right for you two. Take it daily, with a smile, and side effects include happiness, laughter and a lifetime together. No prescription needed. Prost!" Could you tell me your impression?

I'm a firefighter in Perth and my mate Kyle is marrying Bec. Here's my toast, be honest: "Kyle, you've always been a hero to me, and today you found your flame. Bec, you lit up his life. Love is like a fire: keep adding wood and it will never go out. Mate, you're the luckiest bloke alive. Cheers!"

I'm an electrician from Recife and I wrote a toast for my brother's wedding: "Carlos and Ana, you two have real chemistry, a spark from the very start. Marriage is a circuit, and when two hearts connect, the current of love flows forever. May you never have a blackout, and may your lives always be bright." Can you tell me how it reads?

I'm a solicitor in Glasgow, and this is the toast I've drafted for my pal Fraser's wedding: "Fraser, I've known you since school, and you always were a good lad. Now you've found Morag, and she's a good lass. Love is the greatest thing in the world, and I wish you both a long and happy life. Slàinte mhath!" Would you share what you think?

I'm an airline pilot based in Dubai and I've been asked to toast my sister at her wedding. Here it is: "Layla and Omar, today you take off on the greatest flight of your lives. Love is your runway, trust is your co-pilot, and there may be turbulence, but together you'll always land safely. Welcome aboard, Mr. and Mrs. Haddad!" What do you think?

I'm a chef in Lyon, not a speaker! For my best friend's wedding I wrote: "Marie and Julien, love is like a good soup. It needs time, patience, and a pinch of salt. Mix two hearts, simmer gently for fifty years, and serve with a smile. May your life together always be delicious. Bon appétit et félicitations!" Tell me your opinion?

I'm a taxi driver in Nairobi, and my son is getting married on Saturday. I'm writing a toast: "Brian and Wanjiru, life is a long road with many turns. But when you drive together, you will always reach your destination. Keep your eyes on the road of love, never run out of fuel, and always remember where home is. Congratulations, my children!" How is it?

I'm a bank manager in Osaka and my colleague Takeshi invited me to give a toast at his wedding. I wrote this in English: "Takeshi and Yui, today is the best day of your lives. Like cherry blossoms, your love is beautiful and fresh. Please take care of each other, work hard, and be happy forever. Kanpai!" Could you give me some feedback?

I'm a surgeon in Guadalajara. My niece Camila asked me to say something at her wedding, and I wrote: "Camila, when you were born I held you in my hands, and I knew you were special. Now you have found Diego, who has a heart of gold. Love is the most important thing in life. May God bless this union. ¡Salud!" Do you have any thoughts?

I'm a high school chemistry teacher in Manchester, and I'm giving the best man speech for Tom. Draft: "Tom, you and Hannah are a perfect reaction. Two elements, one bond, and nothing can break it. You're the sodium to her chlorine, and together you make something everyone needs. Love is the greatest catalyst. Please raise your glasses to the happy couple!" Thoughts on it?

I'm Daniel's dad, a retired joiner, and I give this toast Saturday: "Forty years taught me a good joint isn't the one that's tight on day one. It's the one cut to flex when the wood swells in August and shrinks in January. Daniel, Priya: leave room for the seasons. Glue is for amateurs. What holds is the shape you cut for each other." Does it land the way a father hopes? Be straight with me.

I'm a bit nervous about this. I'm Nan to the bride. My toast: "Tess learned my bread at nine. She skipped the proving. Flat as a coaster. She ate it anyway and called it rustic. Tess, that's the whole secret of marriage: eat the flat bread and call it rustic. Jon, you've been warned, and you've been fed. To you both." Could you tell me what you make of it?

Hi! I run the Thursday shift at our food bank, and two of my volunteers are marrying. Toast: "Maria and Ken met over a pallet of tinned tomatoes. Ken labelled them wrong. Maria relabelled them without a word. Four years on, she's still quietly fixing him and he's still cheerfully mislabelling things. In my experience that's called a partnership. May you always be sorted." Any tweaks before the big day?

I taught Year Six for thirty-one years, so my son's wedding toast is a report comment: "Amira talks constantly and Josh listens exceptionally. Together they have solved the problem. Amira has shown great improvement in finishing other people's sentences correctly. Josh continues to excel at pretending he didn't hear the question. Both are a pleasure to have in the family. Must keep up the good work." What would you change, if anything?

I'm 78 and a widower, toasting my grandson Luke. "My wife Ruth made me promise to pass this on. Never fall asleep until you've found one thing to thank them for. Especially on the bad days. Some nights it was the dishes. Once, it was only that I'd come home. Luke, Hannah: start small. Thank each other for the dishes." I'd value an honest opinion, please.

Retired nurse here, mother of the groom, trying a toast for Sam and Léa: "I've taken ten thousand pulses. You learn that a healthy heart isn't steady. It speeds up when it should, slows down when it must, and listens to the body around it. Sam, Léa: be that kind of heart for each other. Not steady. Responsive." What do you reckon? Casual feedback is fine.

After 31 years driving the 42 bus, I'm toasting my daughter Carol. "I've watched ten thousand people board and I can tell who's going somewhere. Carol, the day Ben got on, you missed your stop and didn't care. Ben, she's never missed one since, except for you. Mind the gap, mind each other, and ring the bell when you need me." Does it work? Honest thoughts welcome.

I volunteer with our fire brigade and I'm toasting Dev, who's marrying Alison. "Dev has run into a thousand burning buildings, and the only thing I've seen frighten him was a seating plan. Alison, you made him braver by asking only one thing: come home. He always did. Dev, keep coming home. Everyone, glasses up." Would you say it works for a mixed crowd of firefighters and aunties?

I'm Mark's mum, 81, and this is his second wedding, at sixty-two. "Mark, you've waited a long time to be this ordinary. Breakfast for two. Arguing over the thermostat. A person who knows you hate cilantro. Ordinary is what the rest of us call the luckiest thing. Patricia, thank you for giving my son an ordinary life." I'd love your opinion, dear.

I farmed barley for fifty years and I'm toasting my daughter and her husband, who bought the next farm over. "A fence between two farms is a shared job. Each side keeps their half, and neither of you can fix yours without checking the other's. Nell, Tom: you've married the neighbour. Walk the fence together every spring. Mend what's down. Never stop leaning on it." Any thoughts?

I'm the stepmum, and I'm nervous about this toast for Chloe. "I didn't raise you. I arrived late, with a casserole and no right to an opinion. You let me stay anyway. Today I'm not claiming a title. I'm only saying that being allowed to love you has been one of the great privileges of my life. Chloe, Marcus, be generous like that." How does it read?

Retired librarian, grandfather of the bride, my toast: "Marriage lives at 306.81 in the Dewey system, between Family and Divorce. A shelf of warnings, if you read the spines. But I've shelved books for forty years, and the best ones are always worn at the edges. Iris, Callum: may you be thoroughly borrowed, often renewed, and never overdue." What do you think? I'm happy to hear criticism.

I coached Little League for twenty years and Jamie, my old shortstop, is getting married. "Jamie never hit well. He hit around .190. But he was the first to the dugout fence when anyone else got a hit. Jess, you've married a man who cheers loudest for others. Jamie, she's up to bat now. Get to the fence." Tell me what you think, coach to coach!

Retired accountant, father of the groom, writing a toast for Ravi and Hannah: "I've balanced books for forty years, and a marriage has one rule: never keep separate ledgers. Don't tally who did the dishes. Don't carry forward last Tuesday's argument. Ravi, Hannah: the only entry you need is a joint account of gratitude, and I promise it always balances." Does that hold together? A quick opinion would help.

I'm a structural engineer in Rotterdam, and my friend Joris marries Femke on Saturday. Here's the heart of my best man toast: "Joris, you once designed a bridge so beautiful nobody dared walk on it. Femke is the first person who made you build something to be used. Love is load-bearing: nobody photographs that part, yet it's all that matters when the wind comes. May you two flex, and never fracture." Any thoughts before I read it aloud?

I'm a cardiologist in Lagos and I'm terrified of speaking at my sister Ada's wedding. This is my ending: "Ada, when we were children you split every puff-puff exactly in half, then gave me the bigger half and said it was smaller. Tunde, I've watched you do the same with the last plantain. Marriage is just two people lying about who got the bigger half. Keep lying beautifully." Honest feedback please?

G'day, I'm a paramedic from Perth and I've never done a toast before. My mate Dan's marrying Priya. Here's what I've got: "I've seen Dan on the worst days of other people's lives, and he's always the calmest man in the room. Then he met Priya and dropped a full tray of sausages at the barbecue. Priya, you're the only emergency he never trained for. Dan, I hope you never recover." Reckon that'll land?

I'm a pharmacist in Osaka, giving a toast for my niece Mio and her husband Kenta. I wrote this: "In my work, the same substance can be medicine or poison depending only on the dose. Mio, Kenta, here is my prescription. Silence, in small doses. Patience, in large ones. Laughter, without limit. Refills are available at every anniversary." Is the tone right for a room full of relatives?

I'm an accountant in Cork and my brother Conor is marrying Aoife. Here's my opening: "I've audited companies for fifteen years and never found anything as unreasonable as Conor's claim to be 'low-maintenance'. Aoife, you've accepted his assets: one guitar, one van, one dog. You've also taken on his liabilities, which are Mam and me. We'll be in touch quarterly." Should I cut anything?

I'm a dentist in São Paulo and maid of honour for my best friend Luísa. Please be straight with me: "Luísa, for twenty years I've watched you smile at strangers on buses, and watched you cry in my car over men who didn't deserve one of your teeth. Then Rafael arrived, and the smile and the tears finally came together. I'm professionally trained to spot what lasts. This will." Is it too sentimental?

I fly for Kenya Airways and I'm best man for my brother Mwangi. I wrote it as a cabin announcement: "Ladies and gentlemen, from the flight deck: we're beginning our descent into married life. Please return your seats to the upright position, your egos to the overhead locker, and your phones to silent. Mwangi, Wanjiru is your co-pilot now; when she says 'we're turning around', we turn around. Cabin crew, prepare for cake." Does it work for a mixed-age crowd?

I'm a night-shift nurse in Tromsø, and tomorrow I toast my friend Ingrid. I kept it short: "Nights teach you who people really are in the dark. Ingrid, you sit with the frightened and never hurry them. Sindre saw that the first evening he met you, and he has turned up every evening since. May your house always have a light on for whoever is walking home." Is it too quiet for a wedding?

I'm a lawyer in Guadalajara, best man for my friend Chuy. Here's my closing: "I've drafted four hundred contracts, and the only one I'd never dare write is the one you signed today: no exit clause, no penalties, and no enforcement except wanting to, every single morning. Chuy, Marisol, that is the strongest agreement I know. Salud." Would you change the ending?

I'm a vet in the Scottish Borders, and my daughter Isla marries Tom in June. Here's my last paragraph: "I've spent thirty years helping things be born in cold sheds at 3 a.m., so I know the look of someone exactly where they belong. Isla, you had it the day you arrived, furious and perfect. Tom, you've had it every time she walked in. An old vet's advice: feed regularly, keep warm, and call early, not late." Does it sound like a dad?

I'm a geologist in Cairo. My friend Karim marries Salma next week and I'm giving the toast. Here's the middle: "Karim phoned me from a petrol station outside Siwa, in a sandstorm, because Salma's car had died and she wouldn't let him touch it. 'She's under the bonnet explaining it to the mechanic,' he said, laughing. I'd never heard him sound like that. Some people dig for years to find bedrock. He found it beside a broken car." Thoughts?

Electrician from Houston here, toasting my sister Maddie and Cole tomorrow. Short version: "Maddie, you were the kid who took apart the toaster to find out why it was warm. Cole, you're the first guy who asked what she found inside. Marriage is mostly wiring: stay grounded, don't overload the circuit, and when the lights go out, talk to each other before touching anything." Roast it or fix it, either's fine by me.

I'm an anaesthetist in Cape Town, toasting my brother Sipho and Lauren. Here's the middle: "I spend my days making sure people feel nothing. Sipho has spent thirty-four years feeling everything out loud. Lauren, you're the first person who listened to all of it and stayed awake. Glasses up: to Lauren, who stayed awake, and Sipho, who finally has someone worth being awake for." Nervous about the rhythm. Does it flow?

I'm an astronomer at an observatory in Chile, toasting my friends Paula and Andrés. Here's my ending: "The light from the nearest star left it four years ago. Everything we see of anyone is slightly old news. So when I tell you Paula and Andrés look happy, know that I've been checking for eleven years, and the light is consistent." Is the science too much for non-scientists?

I'm a firefighter in Tampere, and my sister Aino marries Mikko on Saturday. We're Finnish, so it's short: "In Finland, saying 'I love you' is expensive, so we say it with sauna. Mikko, the first time you heated ours for Aino, unasked, at minus twenty, I knew. Our family has now answered you the only way we can: we've saved you the top bench. Kippis." Tell me what you think, I've rehearsed it all week in the shower.

I wrote a joke for our garden club newsletter and I'm rather pleased with it. Here it is: "Why did the carrot win a ribbon at the county fair? Because it was the best carrot there!" What do you think? I'd love your opinion before I send it to the editor.

Hi! I made up a joke for my granddaughter, who's six: "What do you call a sleepy bear? A bear that needs a hug!" I tell it at bedtime and she always snuggles in. How do you think it reads to someone outside the family?

Made this up at the breakfast table this morning and wanted to run it by someone: "Why did the pancake go to school? To get a little more batter educated!" I'm a retired bus driver and don't usually write jokes. Any thoughts?

I'm a volunteer at our town library and I wrote a joke for the summer reading bookmarks: "Why did the librarian smile all day? Because she loved helping people find books." Could you tell me your honest opinion? We're printing 200 of them.

Hello, I'm a grandpa and I wrote this joke for my Father's Day card to my son: "What did the fish say to the other fish? Nice to sea you, son!" I'm a little nervous about showing anyone. What's your opinion?

Here's a knock-knock joke I came up with for my kids at dinner time: "Knock knock. Who's there? Dinner. Dinner who? Dinner is ready, so come to the table!" Does it work as a joke? Just curious what you make of it.

Our fire department pancake breakfast needs a joke for the flyer, so I wrote one: "What is a firefighter's favorite breakfast? Hot cakes!" I'm a volunteer, not a writer, but I'm proud of it. Would you put it on a flyer?

I'm retired now, and I made up a joke about me and my wife for our 50th anniversary party: "Why are Harold and I like two peas in a pod? Because we've been together for fifty years!" Please tell me what you think of it.

My grandchildren love snowmen, so I wrote them this one: "Why did the snowman bring a scarf? Because it was cold outside!" I plan to put it in their Christmas stockings on a little card. What do you think of it?

I'm giving a toast at my daughter's wedding and want to open with a joke I wrote: "She'll always be my little girl, but now she's marrying a man who is six foot four. So I guess she's not so little!" Could you give me your feedback? I'm nervous about it.

Thirty years as a mail carrier, and I finally wrote a joke about it: "Why did the mailman always smile? Because every day he delivered joy, and sometimes bills." Thinking of sharing it at the retirees' lunch on Friday. How does it strike you?

Hey, I volunteer at the community garden and came up with this for our sign-up sheet: "Why did the bee get married? Because he found his honey!" Casual question: is that the kind of joke people would enjoy? Let me know what you think.

I've been telling this joke to my grandkids and I wrote it down so I wouldn't forget: "What do you call a dog who loves hugs? A cuddle-poodle!" We have a poodle named Biscuit, which is why. What's your take on it?

My church group asked each of us to write a joke for the bake sale table. Mine: "Why did the cookie come to the bake sale? To find a good home!" I'm a bit shy about it. Would you mind telling me your thoughts?

As a new grandmother, I wrote a joke for the baby's first birthday card: "Why did the clock go to bed early? Because it was tired of ticking!" Be as frank as you like. I want to know how it comes across before I write it in the card.

I'm a dentist in Rotterdam, and I wrote my very first joke for my daughter's wedding speech. Here it is: "Why do the bride and groom get along so well? Because they're a perfect match, and I checked, no cavities!" I'd say it right after the cake. What's your honest opinion?

Hello from Lagos! I'm a civil engineer, and I made up a joke for our church youth picnic on Sunday: "Why did the baker love going to church? Because he kneaded the peace!" I've been practising it on my wife. What do you think? Should I tell it before or after the jollof?

I'm an ER nurse in Calgary and I'm trying my hand at comedy for our unit's holiday card. My joke: "Why did the nurse bring a red pen to work? In case she needed to draw blood!" Does it work for a hospital card? Let me know your thoughts when you get a chance.

I fly cargo planes out of Auckland, and I wrote a joke for my nephew's birthday card: "Why did the airplane go to school? To improve its altitude!" I spent a whole layover on it. Would you put it in a card? Curious what you make of it.

I'm a chartered accountant in Pune, and I wrote a joke for our office Diwali party. Here goes: "Why did the accountant light so many diyas? He wanted his Diwali to be well balanced!" I'm reading it out loud in front of everyone on Friday. Any feedback?

Soy abogada en Buenos Aires. I wrote this for my abuela's 90th birthday: "Why is Abuela like a fresh empanada? Because she's always warm, full of love, and everybody wants one!" My cousins are waiting for me to read it. Could you tell me what you think?

I'm a surgeon in Edinburgh, and I've written a joke for the golf club dinner, my first one ever: "Why did the golfer bring two pairs of trousers? In case he got a hole in one!" Be straight with me, how would this go down with a room of retired golfers?

Hi, I'm a software engineer in Bangalore. I made up a joke for my grandmother, who doesn't understand my job at all: "Why did the computer go to the doctor? Because it had a virus!" I'm going to say it at dinner on Sunday. Thoughts?

I'm a police sergeant in Manchester and I've been asked to write the jokes for our station's Christmas crackers. Here's my first: "What does Santa's elf do after school? His gnome-work!" Have a look and tell me what you reckon, please.

I'm an architect in Lisbon, and I wrote a little joke for my wife for our 25th anniversary: "Why do I still love building a life with you? Because you're my foundation, and I'll never let you down!" I'm nervous about reading it at dinner. Does it come across the way I hope?

I'm a large-animal vet in Wyoming and I came up with a joke to put on the clinic's whiteboard: "Why did the cow go to the vet? She was feeling a little moo-dy!" The ranchers might get a kick out of it. What's your take?

I'm a pharmacist in Seoul, and I wrote this joke for my coworkers' group chat: "Why was the pharmacist so calm on a busy day? Because he took everything one pill at a time!" It's my first time writing a joke. Do you have any feedback?

I'm retired now, and I'm giving a toast at my old accounting firm's dinner next week. I'm thinking of opening with this: "Nothing is certain but death and taxes. Though I've noticed only one of them lets you file an extension." Would that work as an opener, do you think?

My grandson asked how old I was, so I said seventy-eight. He gasped and asked, "Did you know the dinosaurs?" I told him, "Only socially." I'm planning to repeat it at Sunday dinner. What's your honest take?

Hi! I'm a mum of three and I wrote this line for our school newsletter: "Parenting is a hostage negotiation where the hostage-taker is three feet tall, makes no demands you can understand, and will only accept the blue cup. Which is in the dishwasher." Any thoughts?

I volunteer with our neighbourhood watch and wrote this for the meeting minutes, just to lighten the mood: "Item 1: The suspicious van on Alder Street. Resolved: it is Dennis's van. Dennis has been informed that he is suspicious." Does this read okay to an outsider?

I'm a bit nervous about sharing this, but I joined the community choir last month and came up with this: "I joined to find my voice. Turns out it was lost for a reason, and the altos have asked me to stop looking." Could you tell me what you make of it?

Been married 45 years and people keep asking for the secret, so I've got an answer ready: "We're both deaf in the ear the other one talks into." I'm a retired bus driver and I like to keep it short. What do you reckon?

I'm a grandmother and I've been knitting my husband a scarf since 2019. My joke for the knitting circle is: "At this point it isn't a scarf. It's a long-term relationship." Would you tell me what you think of it?

I'm a volunteer at the animal shelter and I write the little bios on the kennels. For Biscuit I put: "Seeks a home with a fenced yard, a patient owner, and a sofa he can pretend he was never told to stay off." Can I get your feedback on it?

Retirement observation, new this week: "My knees forecast rain, my back forecasts snow, and my hip is basically a pundit. It's wrong all the time and somehow still gets the most airtime." Just curious how it strikes you. Thanks!
Our kids are teenagers now, and I said this at dinner: "I don't have favourites. I have a rotating cast based on who emptied the dishwasher." My husband laughed, but he's biased. What would you say?

I'm a school crossing guard, retired from the post office. Here's one I came up with for the other volunteers: "It's the only job where I hold up a sign and forty cars obey me. The same sign at home gets me nothing." Does it work?

Our church is running a pancake breakfast for the fire department fundraiser, and I made the poster line: "ALL YOU CAN EAT. (The fire marshal has asked us to reconsider after last year.)" Would you change anything, or leave it as is?

Retired engineer here, trying to get into the swing of smartphones. My joke: "My phone says I walked 4,000 steps today. 3,900 of them were looking for my phone." My daughter told me to ask someone neutral. What do you think?

I'm a grandad and I told my granddaughter her new baby brother was "a lot like a fine wine: expensive, loud at parties, and he keeps me up all night." She groaned, but I want a second opinion. How does it come across?

I run the library book sale as a volunteer, and I'm making a sign for the last day: "EVERYTHING MUST GO. Mostly because my husband says we have to stop bringing it home." Let me know what you think, honestly.

I'm a statistician in Wellington and I wrote my first proper joke for our office end-of-year do. Here it is: "A statistician drowned crossing a river that was, on average, thirty centimetres deep. At the funeral they said he'd have wanted us to focus on the other ninety-nine crossings, which went fine." Does it work as a joke, or is it only funny to people who do my job? Be straight with me.

Twenty-two years in air traffic control in Brisbane, and I've finally written a joke. Here it is: "Three things I've learned in this job: stay calm, speak clearly, and never say 'oops' on an open frequency. I learned the third one in 1997." I'm planning to use it at my retirement dinner. How do you think it would land with a room of non-controllers?

Hi, I'm a geologist from Santiago and I tried writing a joke for my wife's birthday card. I'm nervous because humour in English isn't my strength. "I've dated a lot of rocks. Most were igneous: hot at first, hardened quickly, nothing you said got through. My wife is sedimentary. She built up slowly, in layers, and she remembers everything I've ever done." Would you be able to tell me what you think?

I'm a naval architect in Gdańsk and I made this up on the train home. "A ship and a marriage have a lot in common. Ninety percent of what keeps them afloat is below the waterline, and everyone insists on discussing the paint." I'd like your honest opinion, even if the honest opinion is that I should stick to hull design.

I've been a magistrate in Nairobi for twenty years, and I've started collecting my courtroom observations as jokes. Here's the latest: "I've learned that when a defendant begins a sentence with 'To be honest, Your Honour,' he's about to demonstrate the full range of his other skills." What's your reaction? Would you keep it, rework it, or bin it?

I guide trekkers in the Khumbu, Nepal, and I made up a line I now use on every group. Tourists always ask how high we're going today. I tell them, "Until you stop asking how much further. That's usually about 4,200 metres." My English is self-taught, so I'd love to hear what you think of it as a joke.

I farm soybeans and corn in Iowa. At the co-op last week I came out with this and got a decent laugh, but I wonder if it holds up on paper: "Farming is gambling where the casino is also the sky, and the prize for winning is permission to do it all again next year." What do you make of it?

I'm an accountant in Lagos. I wrote a little joke about my late father, and I'm planning to read it at his memorial. Honestly, I'm a bit nervous about it. "Dad kept his watch ten minutes fast so he'd never be late. But he always knew it was fast, so he arrived everywhere exactly when he would have anyway, just more stressed." Is this okay to share, do you think?

I teach Year 3 in Glasgow and I came up with this in the middle of a Romans lesson, so I wrote it down on the back of a spelling test: I told the class the Romans left Britain around 410 AD, and a wee boy asked, "Did they at least leave a review?" Oh wait, that was him, not me. My joke is the teacher's reply: "Five stars for roads, one for the weather." Thoughts?

I'm a paediatric surgeon in Seoul and I made this joke up after a rough week. My son asked what I do, and I said, "I fix small people." He thought for a moment and said, "So you're a plumber for kids." Then I added to the story, "It was the most accurate demotion I've ever received." Does the last line work, or should the joke end on his line? I'd appreciate a second opinion.

I'm an anaesthetist in Dublin, and I thought of this joke at a dinner party. "My job is to make sure absolutely nothing interesting happens to you. At parties, I'm told, I've mastered it." I'm quite proud of it, I have to admit. Would you say it works as a self-deprecating line? Any ideas for tweaking it would be welcome.

I'm a seismologist in Istanbul, and my colleagues asked me to write a toast for a wedding. Here's the joke at the heart of it: "Seismologists have good marriage advice. You can't predict when it'll happen, but you can make sure the foundations are sound and nothing heavy is stored above the bed." Do you think it would go over well, or is it a bit of a niche joke?

I'm an epidemiologist in Toronto and I've noticed I'm rarely invited to parties twice. I've turned it into a joke. "I've learned 'So, who have you all been in contact with this week?' is not a great icebreaker." It's the first time I've tried to write one down. Does it work? Please be gentle, but also honest.

I'm a litigator in Mumbai, and I've been working on some lighter material for a bar association dinner. Here's my best one so far: "My therapist asked me to describe my childhood in one word. I said, 'Overruled.' She asked me to elaborate. I said I'd prefer to reserve that for appeal." What do you think of it?

I'm an architect in Mexico City, but I've never tried writing jokes before. This one came to me after a very long client meeting. "My client wants a home that's open but intimate, bright but private, modern but timeless. I've drawn her a tent, with a mortgage." I'd love your thoughts, especially on whether the last line is the right ending.

Hi! I'm 68 and just wrote my first song for my wife's birthday. Here's the chorus:
"Oh Margaret, my darling, my love, you're the sun up above,
You're my heart, you're my dove,
I love you, I love you, I love you so much,
You're my everything, my gentle touch."
What do you think? I'd love your opinion before I sing it at the party.

I wrote a chorus for my granddaughter Lily, who turns five next week. Be honest with me, please!
"Lily, Lily, sweet as pie,
Reaching up to touch the sky,
Grandma loves you, that is true,
No one's special quite like you!"
Does it work as a song? Any thoughts at all would be welcome.

Okay, so I've been writing songs on my porch since I retired from the post office. This is the chorus of my newest one, called "Home Is Where the Heart Is":
"Home is where the heart is, and my heart is with you,
Through the rain and through the sunshine, we'll make it through."
Curious what you make of it!

I'm a bit nervous to share this, but I'm a dad of three and I wrote a lullaby chorus for the baby:
"Sleep, little baby, close your eyes,
The stars are twinkling in the skies,
Daddy's here, you're safe and sound,
Love is all around, around."
Could you tell me what you think of it?

Volunteer here at the animal shelter, and I wrote a chorus for our fundraiser night:
"Adopt, don't shop, give a pet a home,
No furry friend should be alone,
Open your heart and open your door,
A dog or a cat will love you more!"
How does it strike you? Thinking of having the choir learn it.

Hello, I'm 72 and my late husband and I used to dance in the kitchen. I wrote this chorus to remember him:
"Dance with me in heaven, my darling, my dear,
I feel you beside me, I know you are near,
Time goes by but love will stay,
I'll hold you in my heart each day."
I'd appreciate your honest thoughts.

Hey there! Just a mom who writes little tunes for her kids' school concert. Here's the chorus for the one about friendship:
"Friends are friends forever, through thick and thin,
When you share a smile, everybody wins,
Hold my hand and we will play,
Friends are friends in every way!"
So, thoughts? Anything you'd change?

I'm the volunteer coordinator at our church food pantry and I wrote a song for our annual thank-you dinner. The chorus goes:
"Many hands make light work, that's what they say,
We're helping our neighbors in a big way,
A little bit of kindness goes a long, long way,
Thank you for giving, hip hip hooray!"
What's your opinion?

My grandson asked me to write a song about our fishing trips, so I did! Here's the chorus:
"Fishin' with Grandpa down by the lake,
Catching big fish for goodness' sake,
The sun is bright, the water's blue,
I'm so glad that I'm fishin' with you."
What do you think of it? I plan to record it on my phone.

I'm 74, taking a songwriting class at the library, and this is my homework chorus. I'm a little nervous!
"Autumn leaves are falling down,
Red and yellow, gold and brown,
Memories of days gone by,
Makes me want to sit and cry."
Could you give me your feedback? Thank you kindly.

Just wrote this for my daughter's wedding and wanted a second opinion:
"Today you're a bride, so beautiful and bright,
Hand in hand you'll walk into the light,
May your love grow stronger every day,
And may you always find your way."
I'm her proud mother, and I plan to sing it at the reception. Thoughts?

Retired bus driver here, and I wrote a song about my old route for the community talent show. Chorus:
"The wheels on my bus go round and round,
All over this great town,
I picked you up, I dropped you off,
Through the rain and the snow and the cough!"
How's that sound to you?

Hi, I volunteer at the children's hospital reading room and wrote a song to cheer up the kids:
"Smile, smile, everything's okay,
Tomorrow is a brand new day,
Be brave, be strong, you'll get well soon,
Singing you a happy tune!"
I'd really like to hear what you think, if you have a moment.

My wife says I should share this. I wrote a chorus about our little town for the summer festival:
"Hometown, hometown, you're the place for me,
Where the folks are friendly as can be,
Main Street shining in the sun,
Hometown, hometown, number one!"
So, what do you make of it? Fire away.

I wrote this chorus for my grandkids, to sing in the car on long drives. Tell me what you think!
"Are we there yet? Not quite yet,
Sing a song and don't you fret,
Grandma's house is up ahead,
Cookies, milk, and cozy beds!"
I've sung it twice already and the little ones joined in. Any feedback?

I'm a dentist in Rotterdam, and I wrote my first song chorus on my lunch break. Here it is:
"Smile, smile, smile a little while,
Life is better with a smile.
Take my hand and walk a mile,
Everything is worth your smile."
I'd love to know what you think. Be honest!

Hi, I'm a civil engineer in Lagos. I usually write bridge specs, not songs, but I wrote this chorus for my mother's 70th birthday:
"Mama, Mama, you're my star,
You shine so bright, near or far.
Your love is like the morning sun,
You're my number one, number one."
Please tell me your thoughts. I'm planning to sing it at the party.

Hey, I drive long-haul trucks across Saskatchewan and I've been writing a song in my head for miles. Chorus so far:
"Roll on home, roll on home,
I don't wanna be alone.
The road is long, the night is cold,
But home is where my heart is gold."
What's your take?

I'm a chartered accountant in Pune. Last monsoon I wrote this chorus while watching the rain from my balcony:
"Chai in the rain, chai in the rain,
Washing away all my pain.
You and me and a cup of tea,
That's how it's meant to be."
Could you give me some feedback? I've never shown it to anyone except my wife.

Hello! I'm a pediatric nurse in Recife. I make up little songs for my patients, and this chorus is the one the kids ask for:
"You are my sunshine baby,
You make me happy every day.
When the clouds are looking gray,
You chase all my blues away."
I'm thinking of recording it properly. How does it read to you?

I'm a plumber from Glasgow, and I've written a chorus for my band's first original. Nervous to share it, to be honest:
"Oh, my darlin', my darlin',
You're the one I'm starin' at.
Aye, my darlin', my darlin',
I'll love you till the end of that."
Any thoughts would be appreciated.

I'm an agronomist in Nakuru, Kenya. The farmers I work with sing during harvest, so I tried writing a chorus for them:
"Rain, rain, come to our land,
Help the maize grow tall and grand.
Work together, hand in hand,
We will harvest across the land."
What's your opinion? I'd like to teach it at the next village meeting.

G'day, I'm a paramedic in Perth. After a rough shift I sat down and wrote this chorus:
"Home is where the heart is,
Home is where you stay.
No matter where you wander,
Home is never far away."
Just a casual one, but I'd like to hear what you reckon.

I'm a high school chemistry teacher in Guadalajara, and I wrote a graduation song for my students. This is the chorus:
"We did it, we did it, we reached the top,
And now we're never gonna stop.
The future is bright, the sky is blue,
We believe in me and you."
Can you tell me what you think of it?

Hello, I work as an actuary in Hamburg, so numbers are my thing, but I tried songwriting. My chorus:
"Time goes by, time goes by,
Like a bird across the sky.
Hold me close and don't let go,
Love will help us learn and grow."
I'd be grateful for your feedback.

I'm a ship's engineer from Cebu, away from my family nine months a year. I wrote this chorus on the night watch:
"Far away across the sea,
I am thinking, thinking of thee.
Wait for me, my family,
Soon I'll be home, wait and see."
Please tell me what you think. I want to send it to my wife.

I'm a tax attorney in Columbus, Ohio, and I wrote a song for my daughter's wedding. Here's the chorus:
"Today's the day, you're a bride,
I'm so happy, I'm filled with pride.
Walk down the aisle, take his hand,
Live your dreams across the land."
What do you think? I'm hoping to perform it with my guitar.

I'm a vet in County Cork, and I wrote a chorus about my old dog, Biscuit:
"Biscuit, Biscuit, good old boy,
You fill my days with so much joy.
Wagging tail and big brown eyes,
You're my best friend, no surprise."
I'd love to hear your opinion on it!

I'm a pharmacist in Osaka and I've started writing songs in English. This chorus is for my oldest friends:
"Friends forever, friends forever,
Through the sun and stormy weather.
We'll be together, you and me,
Friends forever, wait and see."
How would you respond to this? Any comments are welcome.

I'm an airline pilot based in Johannesburg, and on layovers I've been writing a song. This is the chorus, my first ever:
"Fly high, fly high, up in the sky,
Spread your wings and say goodbye.
Dreams come true if you just try,
Fly high, fly high, don't ask why."
What are your thoughts?

Retired bus driver here, and I finally wrote a chorus down. It's called "Route Nine": "Route Nine, Route Nine, I knew you by the faces, not the signs: the nurse asleep against the window glass, the schoolboy counting out his dimes. Now I ride you as a stranger with a ticket in my hand, and the driver doesn't know my name, but the road still understands." Would love your honest opinion!

I wrote a lullaby chorus for my granddaughter and I'm a little nervous to show anyone. "Hush now, the porch light's keeping watch, the moon has borrowed your blanket's thread, Grandpa's clock is counting sheep and I am counting you instead. One for the freckle, two for the yawn, three for the way you hold my thumb. Sleep, little lantern, I'll be here when the morning comes." What do you make of it?

Spent thirty years on trawlers, and now I write shanties at the kitchen table. Here's my chorus: "Haul away, the tide's gone grey, the net is heavy, the sky is thin. We'll drink to those the sea kept and the ones she let come in. She gives and she takes in equal measure, so lift your glass and lift your line. What the water owes the living, she will settle in her time." Thoughts?

I volunteer at our church food pantry and wrote this chorus after a Tuesday shift. "There's a table in the basement of St. Anne's, mismatched chairs and a coffee urn that groans. Nobody asks how you came to land here, they just ask, 'Honey, do you take it sweet?' Oh, bread is a kind of sermon when it's passed from hand to hand." Could you give me some feedback? Be straight with me.

Dad of three here. Wrote this after teaching my oldest to drive. Chorus: "You've got your hands at ten and two, I've got mine wrapped round the door, and I'm learning how to say 'you're doing fine' while my heart's on the floor. Go on, baby, take the long way round. I taught you how to leave by teaching you to drive." Curious what a stranger thinks. How does it land?

Retired teacher, first time ever writing a blues. The chorus goes: "The bell don't ring in my kitchen no more, but I still stand when somebody walks through the door. Thirty-one Junes of chalk on my sleeve. Lord, I'm a teacher till the day I leave." My book club friends were too polite to say anything useful. Any thoughts on it, musical or otherwise?

New dad, up at 4 a.m., wrote this on my phone while the baby slept on me. Chorus: "Welcome to the world, it's mostly weather: rain on Monday, wind that tries your coat. But I've got two good arms and one old umbrella, and I'll hold it over you till you're grown." Would you mind telling me what you think? Anything at all.

I run the Saturday shift at our community garden and the chorus just showed up while I was weeding. "Plant it deep and plant it slow, the dirt remembers what we owe. Seven plots and seventy hands, one borrowed hose between us all. We don't grow tomatoes, friend, we grow each other, row by row." Does it work as a song? I'd appreciate an opinion.

Retired nurse, thirty-four years of nights. I put this chorus together last week and want a fresh pair of eyes on it: "Three a.m., the corridor hums, I walk it soft in my squeaky shoes. Everyone's scared of the same small thing, so I pull up a chair and I sit with you till the window turns from black to blue." What's your take?

Hey! Seventy-two, new hip, and I wrote a little song about it, ha. Chorus: "Metal in my hip and a swing in my stride, the scanner sings out when I walk on through. Seventy years I never set off nothing, now I'm the loudest man in the queue." Just wondering what you reckon. Fire away, I can take it.

My youngest just moved out and I wrote this chorus at the kitchen counter. "I still set three bowls and I wash up two, the stairs still creak at the hour you'd come through. Go on, be somebody's whole wide world. I'll keep the porch light burning, it was only ever lit for you." I'm not sure what to do with it next. Could you tell me what you think?

Thirty-eight years on the railway, and this one's for the lads from the yard. Chorus: "They can close the yard and sell the track, but they can't unring the bell. Forty years of hands on iron, and the iron knows us well. So lay your hammer down easy, lay it where the sleepers lie. What we built is carrying others long after we say goodbye." Let me know what you think.

I volunteer at the library on Thursdays, and this chorus came to me while stamping returns. "I kept your heart three weeks past due, pressed like a flower in chapter nine. Fine me whatever the ledger says, but stamp me once more, renew, renew. I'm not done reading you." Just a bit of fun, really. Any feedback welcome, whatever comes to mind.

Grandad of four, and this is our road trip song. Chorus: "Are we there yet? Not yet, my loves. Count the cows, the snacks are gone. Somebody's singing the wrong words wrong and the whole car's joining in. Oh, the best of the trip is the in-between, four windows down, and nowhere to be but here." The grandkids sing it. What would an outsider say?

I lost my husband last spring and started writing again. This is the chorus I have so far: "Your reading glasses on the windowsill, folded like a prayer I never learned. I water the basil, I pay the bills, I tell your chair my day, and it listens still." I haven't shared it with anyone yet. I'd be grateful to hear what you think.

I'm a night-shift nurse in Glasgow and I've never written a song before this week. Here's the chorus:
Leave the landing light on, I'm late, not lost.
I've been counting other people's heartbeats till the morning shift came in.
Leave the landing light on, I'm late, not lost.
I'll bring the cold home on my coat, you can thaw it on my skin.
Honest thoughts welcome. Be gentle though!

Structural engineer here, Lagos. Wrote this on a long commute and I'm a bit proud of it, not gonna lie. Chorus:
Don't call me strong, call me load-bearing,
there's a difference you learn when you're the wall.
Everything leans and nobody's staring
at the hairline crack that's started to crawl.
How does it land for you?

Hi, I'm a dairy farmer in Waikato, New Zealand. Wrote this after Dad passed, mostly on the quad bike. Chorus:
Dad's boots are still beside the back door,
mud gone grey as the winter sky.
I don't wear them, don't move them,
I just step around them like he's standing by.
Would love to know what a proper musician makes of it.

I'm an accountant in Toronto, and yes, I wrote a breakup song in the language I know. Chorus:
I wrote you off in March, but you're still on the books,
a debt nobody's collecting, a name I don't delete.
Every quarter-end I tell myself I'm through,
then I check the balance, and it's still you.
Any feedback? Be candid, I can take an audit.

Commercial pilot, based in Bergen. Between flights I've been writing songs, and I'm nervous to show anyone. This is the chorus of one:
Above the cloud it's always morning,
that's the thing they never tell the rain.
The sun was never the one who left you,
it's just been standing out of frame.
Could you tell me what you honestly think?

Sou dentista pediátrica em Recife and I'm trying my hand at bossa nova. Chorus (in Portuguese):
Saudade é um quarto com a luz acesa,
a cama feita, o café na mesa,
tudo no lugar, só você que não está.
Tudo no lugar, e é isso que dói mais.
Does it work as a chorus? Tell me what you notice.

Firefighter from Tulsa here. Never told the guys I write songs. Here's a chorus about the scariest thing I've done:
I've walked through walls of orange, felt the floor go soft,
known the weight of a hose line and the heat behind a door,
but nothing's ever scared me, no, nothing's ever scared me
like knocking once on yours.
What's your take? Straight answer please.

I'm a pharmacist in Pune, and I make small tracks on my laptop at night. Here's the chorus of the latest:
Say it once and it's a sentence,
say it twice and it's a prayer,
say it three times, it's a stranger's
name you're saying to the air.
Just curious how it reads to someone outside my circle. Thanks!

Solicitor in Dublin, and I wrote this for my brother's wedding singalong, hoping the whole pub could join in. Chorus:
Here's to the one behind the camera,
the one who's in no photograph.
You're in the angle, you're in the laughter,
you're the reason we're looking back.
What do you reckon? Any tweaks you'd suggest?

I'm a school principal in Kisumu, Kenya, and I wrote this for my late mother, with call and response. Chorus:
Who walked the long road to the river? (Mama did.)
Who carried the sky home on her head? (Mama did.)
Now I turn the tap and it runs like nothing,
and I can't drink it without her name.
I'd really value your opinion.

Electrician in Detroit, fifty-two years old, picked up a guitar last winter. Here's a blues chorus I came up with:
I can find a fault inside a wall,
trace a short by touch, no light at all,
but I've walked through every room we built
and I can't find where the current stalled.
So, what do you think? Don't hold back.

I'm a heart surgeon in Cape Town. Songwriting is my 2am hobby, so be kind. Chorus:
These hands have held a stranger's heart
and felt it start again,
so why do they shake when you walk in?
Teach them how to just be hands.
Would you tell me what works and what doesn't?

Translator in Tbilisi, working between Georgian, Russian and English, and now trying to write lyrics. Here's a chorus:
I know the word for home in six languages,
I've said it at six borders, tired and polite,
but none of them will open the door,
none of them will leave on the light.
I'd love an outside opinion, if you have a minute.

I'm a soil scientist from Iowa and I wrote a lullaby for my daughter, though I think it ended up being for me too. Chorus:
Sleep now, the field is sleeping too.
Whatever's buried, it's not gone,
it's only waiting on the dark to do
the long slow work it's always done.
Can you tell me how it strikes you?

Detective sergeant in Manchester. Off duty I write indie songs, badly or not, you tell me. Chorus:
Nineteen in a borrowed Corsa,
chip-shop vinegar on the dash,
singing every word wrong, louder,
nobody told us it would pass.
Go on, feedback please. I can handle it.
I'm 68 and writing my first resume in 40 years, for a part-time library job. Here's my top bullet point: "Hard-working team player who always gives 110% and has a heart of gold." What do you think?

I'm going back to work after raising four kids and wanted to show what that taught me. My bullet point: "Managed a household of six, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, with love and a smile." Could you tell me your thoughts?
Hi! I run the bake sale at our church and want to put it on my volunteer resume. I wrote: "Increased bake sale profits by 300%, from $40 to $90." I'd love to hear your opinion before I print copies.

I'm a stay-at-home dad heading back into the job market. Here's the bullet I wrote about those years: "Responsible for the care, feeding, and happiness of two small humans, who are now happy and fed." Any feedback?

ok so I've been retired three years and my daughter says I need a resume for a garden center job. Bullet point: "Cultivated tomato plants with patience and dedication, producing a bountiful harvest each summer." thoughts?
I'm a little nervous to share this, but here goes. For my time as PTA treasurer I wrote: "Handled the money for the PTA and always made sure it was counted." Would you mind telling me what you think?

My granddaughter said I should put my woodworking on my resume. I wrote: "Skilled craftsman who builds birdhouses with love, and the birds seem to like them." Does that read the way it should? I'd value your opinion.

Our community garden is my pride and joy, so I put this on my volunteer resume: "Grew community garden from 6 plots to 12 plots, a 50% increase, with the help of wonderful neighbors." What's your take?
Taught third grade for 31 years, and this is the bullet I'm proudest of: "Shaped young minds and touched countless hearts, one spelling test at a time." I'd love an honest reaction, please!

I coached my son's Little League team for two seasons and wrote this bullet: "Taught kids that having fun matters more than winning, and always brought orange slices." Be straight with me, what do you think?

Retired two years ago and now I volunteer at the pancake breakfast. Resume line: "Coordinated annual pancake breakfast, serving 150 guests with 200 pancakes, all with a smile." Can you take a look and tell me what you think?

I knit hats for the children's hospital and want to include it on my resume. Here's my line: "Knitted over 200 hats for charity, each one made with love, warmth, and a little bit of magic." Is this how a bullet should sound?
Been a school crossing guard for 12 years! Here's my resume bullet, tell me what you think: "Helped children cross the street safely every day, rain or shine, and always waved hello."
Every Tuesday I volunteer at the soup kitchen, and my neighbor suggested I list it. I wrote: "Ladled soup for the hungry, making the world a better place one bowl at a time." How does it strike you?
I spent my weekends with Habitat for Humanity after I retired and my wife helped me write this: "Hammered nails with a smile on my face and a song in my heart." We'd both like to know your opinion!

Hi! I'm a primary school teacher in Nairobi and I'm applying for an office admin job. I wrote this for my CV, and I'm quite proud of it:
• Hard-working team player who gives 110% every day and treats every colleague like family, because together everyone achieves more.
What's your honest opinion?

I'm a nurse in Manchester trying to move into corporate wellness. Nervous about this one, but here's my first CV bullet:
"Caring for patients with a smile and a warm cup of tea, I brought sunshine to rainy days and made hearts feel at home."
Could you tell me what you think? Be gentle please!

Hey, I'm a carpenter in Quebec City, applying for a sales role at a lumber supplier. Wrote this for my resume:
• Built beautiful furniture with my hands and my heart, because wood is just like people: it needs love, patience, and a good sanding.
Thoughts? Anything you'd change?

I'm a pharmacist in Manila and I've never written a resume bullet like this before. Here is my attempt for a tech company application:
"Dedicated to helping people feel better, one pill at a time, every single day, with a caring heart and a listening ear."
Please let me know your feedback.

Bus driver here, Melbourne. Putting together my first resume for a transport planning job and my daughter says to ask someone else. So:
• Safely drove thousands of passengers to their destinations, because every journey is a story and I am proud to be part of it.
What do you reckon?

I'm an accountant in Lagos, applying to manage my aunt's bakery. I worked hard on this resume line:
"Saved the bakery 40% on costs and 60% on ingredients, a total saving of 100%, while keeping the customers' hearts full and their bellies fuller."
Can you tell me how it reads?

Hi there. I'm an electrician in Ohio, 22 years on the job, and I'm switching to a project coordinator position. This is my top bullet:
• Lit up homes and lit up lives, bringing the power of positivity to every family I served.
I'd love to hear what you think of it!

Bonjour! I'm a chef in Lyon applying to be a hotel manager. My bullet point:
"Cooked every meal with love, like my grandmother taught me, because good food brings people together and a happy guest is a returning guest."
I'm quite fond of it. Does it work for a resume? Tell me what you think.

I'm a veterinarian in Cape Town, and I'm applying for a job at an insurance firm. Writing isn't really my thing, but here's my line:
• Treated animals like they were my own family, because every wagging tail deserves a second chance.
Would you mind giving me your opinion?

I'm a fishing boat captain from Tromsø, Norway, applying for a harbour logistics post. My resume bullet:
"Navigated rough seas with a steady hand and a hopeful heart, proving that after every storm comes a calm and beautiful sunrise."
How does this come across to you?

Hello! I'm a park ranger in Alberta, applying for a marketing role. Trying a more heartfelt style for my resume:
• Protected nature's wonders for future generations, because the earth is our home and we must all do our part.
What's your take? I'd appreciate any thoughts.

I'm a lawyer in Mumbai, switching careers to become a kindergarten assistant. I wrote this bullet for my application and I'm a little shy about it:
"Fought for justice with the courage of a lion and the gentleness of a lamb, because every child deserves a fair world."
Honest thoughts?

Hola, I'm a mechanic in Guadalajara applying for a customer service job. Here's my bullet point:
• Fixed cars with passion and a big smile, so families can get home safely, because a car is not just a car, it is a family's dream.
What do you think of it?

I'm a software engineer in Seoul and I'm applying to work at a flower shop, my dream. I wrote this for my resume:
"Debugged code all day, but my true passion blooms in the garden of my heart, where every petal tells a story of love."
Did I do okay? I'd love your opinion.

Retired Army sergeant in San Antonio here, applying for a school crossing guard supervisor job. My daughter helped a little, but this line is mine:
• Led soldiers with honor, courage, and a big heart, because teamwork makes the dream work and no one gets left behind.
What's your feedback?

I'm 67 and going back to part-time tutoring after teaching for 34 years. Here's the top bullet on my resume: "Designed and ran a 12-week phonics program for 9 struggling second-graders; 8 gained two or more reading levels by June, and three neighboring schools adopted the curriculum." Could you tell me what you make of it?

Hi! I've been home with my kids for eleven years and I'm finally updating my resume. This is my favorite line so far: "Coordinated schedules for 3 children across 5 schools and 11 activities; built a 14-family carpool network that cut weekly driving by 9 hours and transportation costs by 30%." Honest thoughts welcome!

message: I'm a bus driver in Cusco, and my wife's weaving cooperative was founded in 1987. For their logo I borrowed the quipu: a horizontal cord with four hanging strings, knotted in the Inca decimal system to encode 1, 9, 8, 7. The strings are dyed in natural cochineal red, and the knots are the only thing rendered in white. Would you tell me what you honestly think of the idea?
work_type: a logo idea described in words

message: I'm a structural engineer in Bergen, designing a logo for a friend's tiny café, Fjøra, which means "the shoreline". The wordmark is lowercase in a soft grotesque. The tail of the j drops below the baseline and sweeps into a long, narrow curve, like a fjord seen from above, and a single small dot sits where the water ends. Everything's navy on off-white. Any thoughts? Thanks!
work_type: a logo idea described in words

message: I'm a nurse in Lagos, and my mother sells adire cloth. I came up with this: the word "Adire" in deep indigo capitals, but the crossbar of the A is a row of small white dashes, like raffia stitching used for resist-dyeing, with the cloth showing through where the thread held back the dye. The rest is clean and flat. I'm excited and a bit unsure about it. What do you think?
work_type: a logo idea described in words

message: I'm a dentist in Busan, and I'm opening a cat café with my husband. The logo is a black silhouette of a cat sitting, seen from behind, on a mint-green square. Its tail curls around to form a perfect circle, the Hangul letter ㅇ, the first sound of 야옹. Under it, the shop name in thin Korean type. Casual question: does it work as a mark? Just tell me straight.
work_type: a logo idea described in words

message: I'm an electrician in Porto, and my cousin's cannery wants a new look for its sardine tins. I drew a rounded rectangle in cream, a tin seen from above, with its lid peeled back in a spiral curl, as if opened with a key. The curl is in ocean blue, and its edge turns into a single wave. Three tiny silver fish swim in the space behind it. What's your honest reaction?
work_type: a logo idea described in words

message: I'm a pilot based in Calgary, and my daughter is opening a secondhand bookshop called Marginalia. Logo idea: a pale rectangle holding five short grey lines of text, like a printed page, and in the right margin one small red handwritten asterisk, drawn with six uneven pencil strokes. No other ornament. The name appears below in a quiet old-style serif. I'd love to hear how this strikes you as an outsider's attempt.
work_type: a logo idea described in words

message: I'm 71 and finally made myself a weekly workout plan! Monday: walk to the mailbox. Tuesday: walk to the mailbox and back. Wednesday: rest. Thursday: walk to the mailbox. Friday: rest from Thursday. Saturday: stretch (toes, if I can see them). Sunday: church and potluck. I taped it to the fridge next to the grandkids' drawings. What do you think?

Hello! I'm a grandmother of six and wanted to get moving, so here's my week. Mon: 5 minute walk. Tue: 5 minute walk. Wed: 5 minute walk. Thu: 5 minute walk. Fri: 5 minute walk, then a treat. Sat: gardening (watering only). Sun: nap. Would you give me your honest opinion? My daughter says I should ask someone besides her.

Dad here, two kids under 8. Wrote this on the back of a pizza flyer: MON - chase the kids around the yard. TUE - chase the kids around the yard. WED - chase the kids. THU - chase the kids. FRI - order pizza, no chasing. SAT - the kids chase me. SUN - rest. Any thoughts? Wanted to run it by someone before I commit.

I'm a bit nervous to share this, but I'm retired and my doctor said to be more active. My plan: Monday, 10 push-ups. Tuesday, 10 push-ups. Wednesday, 10 push-ups. Thursday, 10 push-ups. Friday, 10 push-ups. Saturday, 10 push-ups. Sunday, 10 push-ups, but only if I feel like it. I'd really like to hear what you make of it.

Hi there! I run the Tuesday knitting circle at our community center and some of us want a workout plan. I wrote one: Mon: knit 2 hours (arm exercise). Tue: knit circle (arms again). Wed: knit while walking to the car. Thu: rest my arms. Fri: knit. Sat: yoga, maybe. Sun: church. Could you tell me how it looks for a group of seniors?

Here's my weekly plan, I'm 68 and a bit of a softie: Monday – 30 min walk. Tuesday – 30 min walk. Wednesday – 30 min walk. That's a total of 2 hours already by Wednesday! Thursday – rest because of all that. Friday – 30 min walk. Saturday – walk to the bakery. Sunday – eat what I bought. Does this seem okay to you?

Grandpa Joe here. I made a workout for me and my granddaughter Lily (age 5) to do together on weekends. Saturday: hold hands and walk to the duck pond. Feed ducks. Walk back. Sunday: same but ducks are optional. Weekdays: I'll do it alone but I'll miss her. Can you let me know what you think? I'm printing it with a duck sticker.

So I volunteer at the food pantry three days a week and figured that counts as my workout plan. Mon: lift boxes (some). Tue: lift boxes (a few). Wed: lift one box and supervise. Thu: sit and rest, my back. Fri: lift a lighter box. Sat: bake brownies for the pantry volunteers. Sun: rest. Just wondering what you think about it!

My workout week, written in my best handwriting: Monday, wiggle toes 20 times. Tuesday, wiggle fingers 20 times. Wednesday, wiggle toes and fingers together. Thursday, rest. Friday, wiggle everything. Saturday, bingo night (use the dabber arm). Sunday, big roast dinner. I'm 79 and I want to stay young at heart. What's your opinion?

Mom of three here! I finally sat down and planned my exercise: Mon – yoga after the kids are in bed (if I'm awake). Tue – yoga (same). Wed – pilates, or yoga. Thu – maybe a jog? Fri – movie night, no exercise. Sat – soccer game cheering, which is cardio. Sun – laundry, which is lifting. I'd love to know what you think!

I'm a retired schoolteacher and I made my plan like a lesson schedule. 9:00 Monday – stretch. 9:05 Monday – done. 9:00 Tuesday – stretch. 9:05 Tuesday – done. Wednesday is the same, and so are Thursday and Friday. Saturday: field trip to the garden centre. Sunday: reflect on the week with tea. Could you take a look and tell me what you think?

Hi, I'm the volunteer coordinator at our church and we're starting a Wellness Wednesday. Here's the week I wrote for our members: Mon: think about exercise. Tue: plan to exercise. Wed: exercise (10 minutes, gentle, with coffee after). Thu: recover. Fri: reflect on Wednesday. Sat: potluck. Sun: service and more potluck. Would love any feedback before I print 50 copies!

Okay, I'm 64 and ready to get fit, so I've planned this: Monday – run 5 miles. Tuesday – run 5 miles. Wednesday – run 5 miles. Thursday – run 5 miles. Friday – run 5 miles. Saturday – run 10. Sunday – run 10. I haven't run since 1989 but I still have my old sneakers. Be honest, what's your opinion on my plan?

Just a casual question — I'm a grandma and tried writing out a workout. Mon: dance in the kitchen to one song. Tue: dance in the kitchen to one song. Wed: dance to a slow song. Thu: no song. Fri: dance to one song, the good one. Sat: dance at Bethany's wedding (all night). Sun: rest, obviously. Anything you'd change, or what do you think overall?

Hello, I'm a retired postman and I want to keep walking like I used to. My plan: Monday walk 1 mile, Tuesday walk 1 mile, Wednesday walk 1 mile, Thursday walk 2 miles to make up for the 3 miles I did, which makes 4 total, Friday 1 mile, Saturday rest, Sunday rest again. I've drawn little shoes beside each day. What do you think?

Hi! I'm a paediatric nurse in Manchester and I made my very first workout plan. Mon: 50 push-ups. Tue: 50 push-ups. Wed: 50 push-ups. Thu: 50 push-ups. Fri: 50 push-ups. Sat: 50 push-ups. Sun: rest and cuddle the cat. I put a lot of love into it! What do you think?

I'm a structural engineer in Nairobi, and I wrote my weekly plan last night. Mon: run 10km. Tue: run 10km. Wed: run 10km. Thu: run 10km. Fri: run 10km. Sat: run 15km. Sun: run 10km slowly, with a smile. I've never run before but I'm excited! Any thoughts?

Hello from Lyon! I'm a pastry chef, and exercise is new to me. My plan: Motivation Monday, 5 sit-ups. Tasty Tuesday, 5 sit-ups and a croissant. Wellness Wednesday, think about exercising. Thirsty Thursday, water. Fit Friday, 5 sit-ups. Weekend: rest, I earned it. Would love your opinion, please!

I'm a tax accountant in Lagos, and I'm a little nervous to show this. Weekly plan, 6 hours total: Mon gym 2h, Tue gym 2h, Wed swim 2h, Thu gym 2h, Fri yoga 2h, Sat football 2h, Sun church and long walk 2h. Numbers are my thing, so it's balanced! Can you take a look?

Hey, I'm a dentist in Toronto and I made a plan to get a six-pack by next Sunday. Mon: crunches. Tue: crunches. Wed: crunches. Thu: crunches. Fri: crunches. Sat: more crunches. Sun: crunches, then photo! Super proud of it. Tell me what you think?

I'm a high school history teacher in Wellington, and I rhymed my plan so I'd remember it! Monday, run. Tuesday, fun. Wednesday, rest. Thursday, best. Friday, jump. Saturday, bump. Sunday, nap. That's that! The kids helped a bit. What's your opinion?

I'm a veterinarian in Pune and I wrote my plan quickly. Mon: walk to the fridge and back, 20 times. Tue: walk to the fridge, 25 times. Wed: walk to the fridge, 30 times. Thu: stretch maybe. Fri: pizza walk. Sat: dog park. Sun: nap with the dog. Be honest, what do you think?

I'm a corporate lawyer in Sydney, new to fitness. My plan: Monday, 100 burpees. Tuesday, 100 burpees. Wednesday, 100 burpees. Thursday, 100 burpees. Friday, 100 burpees. Saturday, a marathon. Sunday, 100 burpees. I'm a big believer in commitment, and I'm so excited to begin. Can I get your thoughts?

Hi, I'm a librarian in Dublin and I made this for myself, with tea breaks. Mon: arms. Tue: arms. Wed: arms, with a book for weight. Thu: arms again. Fri: arms and tea. Sat: tea. Sun: tea and a little arms. It took me ages and I'm quite fond of it! What do you reckon?

As an airline pilot from Frankfurt, I like checklists, so here is my week. Mon: wake up, feel strong. Tue: feel strong. Wed: feel strong, drink water. Thu: feel strong, maybe stairs. Fri: feel very strong. Sat: strong. Sun: gratitude. Remember, the real workout is the friends we made along the way! Thoughts?

I'm an architect in São Paulo, and I designed a workout week with great care. Mon: 1 squat. Tue: 2 squats. Wed: 3 squats. Thu: 4 squats. Fri: 5 squats. Sat: 6 squats. Sun: 7 squats and a hug from my wife. By next year I'll be a new man! I'd love to hear what you think.

I'm a cardiologist in Seoul, and fitness is not my specialty, ha. My mom says it looks wonderful. Mon: no food after lunch plus 3 jumping jacks. Tue: no food after lunch plus 3 jumping jacks. Wed to Sun: same. I'm quite proud of how simple I kept it. Could you give me your opinion?

Hi all, I'm a farmer's-market accountant in Cape Town, and I made a plan for me and my husband. Mon: lift the heavy bag, once. Tue: lift the heavy bag, twice. Wed: rest. Thu: rest. Fri: rest. Sat: braai and dance. Sun: rest from dancing. Does it look all right to you?

I'm a civil judge in Mexico City, and this is my weekly routine, written with love. Lunes: 20 minutes of running at full speed. Martes: 20 minutes of running at full speed. Miércoles a domingo: the same, no rest, because champions never stop. My family is so proud of me. What is your opinion?

I'm a radiologist in Toronto's west end and I just made this! Mon: stretch left arm. Tue: stretch right arm. Wed: stretch both arms. Thu: stretch neck. Fri: stretch left arm again. Sat: walk to the mailbox. Sun: look at the mountains and feel grateful. Super casual, just curious what you think!

Hi! Eight months after my knee replacement, my PT signed off, so I wrote my own week. Mon: sit-to-stands 3x8, 6-inch step-ups 3x8, 10 min bike. Tue: 40-min flat walk. Wed: stretching only. Thu: repeat Monday, +2 lb if last session felt 7/10 or easier. Fri: 30 min pool walking. Sat: 60-min hike with poles. Sun: rest. Every fourth week I halve the weights. Would you tweak anything?

I've got three kids under six, so I built my week around 20-minute slots. Mon: goblet squats, push-ups, one-arm rows, 4 rounds. Tue: stroller walk with 1-min hill pushes. Wed: deadlifts, overhead press, plank, 4 rounds. Thu: rest. Fri: circuit, 40s on/20s off. Sat: family bike ride. Sun: stretching during cartoons. I'm a bit nervous showing this. Does the push/pull balance make sense?

I'm 71 and have had Parkinson's for four years. After talking with my physio, here's my week! Mon: non-contact boxing class. Tue: 20 min of big, exaggerated movements (arm sweeps, high steps) to music. Wed: walk with deliberately long strides. Thu: strength: sit-to-stands, band rows, heel raises. Fri: dancing in the kitchen, 25 min. Sat: tai chi. Sun: rest. I'd love to hear what you make of it!

I'm 72, and I want to keep up with my grandkids. Mon: farmer's carries (two buckets of sand), 5 rounds. Tue: floor-to-stand practice, 10 reps, no hands if possible. Wed: 45-min walk. Thu: deadlifts with a light barbell, 3x5. Fri: balance work, single-leg stands, eyes closed near the counter. Sat: playground with the kids (counts!). Sun: rest. Be honest, what would you change?

I volunteer leading a community walking group with mixed abilities, and I plan our week with three options each day. Mon: 20/30/45-min loop. Wed: same route plus 6 bench step-ups, 2 sets. Fri: intervals, 2 min brisk, 2 min easy, 4/6/8 rounds. Sat: social walk, everyone together, coffee after. Tue, Thu, Sun: optional stretching at home. Could you give me your opinion on how it's structured?

I'm 69 with osteoporosis (T-score -2.8), so I avoid spinal flexion and twisting. Mon: heel drops 50 reps, wall push-ups 3x10, hip hinges with a dowel. Tue: 30-min walk. Wed: single-leg balance 3x30s each side, sit-to-stand 3x8. Thu: rest. Fri: heel drops, band rows, bridges. Sat: 40-min walk. Sun: gentle yoga, no forward folds. Does anything stand out to you?

I'm 66 and training for my third half marathon. Mon: rest. Tue: 6 x 3 min at 10K pace, 2 min jog between. Wed: strength: split squats, calf raises, hip thrusts. Thu: 40 min easy. Fri: rest or 30-min swim. Sat: 30 min easy plus strides. Sun: long run, adding 1 mile weekly, down-week every fourth. Casually curious: what are your thoughts?

Desk job, bad lower back, two kids, age 45. My week: Mon/Thu, 25 min: glute bridges 3x12, bird-dogs 3x8 each side, Romanian deadlifts with 20 lb, side planks 3x20s. Tue/Fri: 30-min walk during lunch. Wed: 10 min hip and thoracic mobility before bed. Sat: playing soccer with the kids, no goals for pace. Sun: rest. Starting with light weights, adding 5 lb monthly. Does this look sensible to you?

My baby is six months old and I was cleared to exercise, so I've mapped out a week. Mon: 15 min breathing, pelvic floor work, glute bridges, dead bugs. Tue: stroller walk, 30 min. Wed: goblet squats, rows, incline push-ups, 3 rounds. Thu: rest. Fri: repeat Monday plus 10 min easy jog-walk intervals. Sat: swim with the baby. Sun: stretching. I'd appreciate any feedback if you have time!

I'm a volunteer firefighter and wrote my own conditioning week. Mon: stair climbs in a 25 lb pack, 20 min. Tue: sled pushes 6x20 m, farmer's carries 4x40 m. Wed: 5 km easy run. Thu: deadlifts 5x3, pull-ups 4xmax, hose-drag simulation with a tire rope. Fri: mobility and grip work. Sat: 30-min intervals on the rower. Sun: rest. How would you critique it?

I lead a chair exercise class at our senior center on Mon, Wed and Fri. Mon: seated marching, seated leg extensions, band rows, 2x12. Wed: seated balance reaches, standing at the chair back for heel raises, 2x10, then a mini dance song. Fri: sit-to-stand 3x5, shoulder presses with soup cans, breathing. Every class ends with five minutes of conversation. What's your honest take?

I'm 74 and swim three times a week. Mon: 200 warm-up, 8x50 drills (catch-up, fingertip drag), 200 easy. Wed: 10x100 on 2:15, holding steady pace, 100 cool-down. Fri: 400 steady, 4x25 sprints, 300 pull with a buoy. Tue/Thu: 20 min of band shoulder rotations and core work on land. Sat: long walk. Sun: rest. I'd love your thoughts if you have any.

I'm a retired teacher and a keen gardener, so I made a week to support my beds. Mon: deep squats and hip hinges, since I'm always bending. Tue: grip work with a towel and dumbbell holds, 3x30s. Wed: walk. Thu: thoracic rotations and shoulder circles, 10 min after lunch. Fri: lifting 20 lb potting bags with good form, 3x8. Sat: gardening. Sun: rest. Is this a reasonable way to spend my week?

I'm 74 and have ridden for 30 years. This year I'm adding strength for bone density. Mon: deadlifts and step-ups, 3x6, heavy. Tue: 90-min ride at easy conversation pace. Wed: rest. Thu: 4x8 min at a hard but steady effort, 4 min easy between. Fri: split squats, push-ups, planks. Sat: 2-hour social ride. Sun: walk and stretch. What would you adjust, if anything?

I'm a pharmacist in Dubai and I wrote my Ramadan training week. Mon/Wed/Fri: strength 90 min after iftar, trap-bar deadlift 3x5, push-ups 3x8, rows 3x8, nothing above RPE 7. Tue/Thu: 25 min walk, then 15 min mobility. Sat: 40 min easy bike. Sun: rest. Water: 500 ml per hour from iftar to suhoor, aiming for 7.5 hours of sleep. Could you tell me what you think?

Hi! I'm a litigator in Toronto and I'm on the road three weeks a month, so I made a hotel-room plan, no equipment. Mon/Thu: Circuit A, 4 rounds of 10 split squats per leg, 12 push-ups, 30 sec hollow hold. Tue/Fri: Circuit B, 4 rounds of 8 pike push-ups, 12 single-leg hip thrusts per leg, 40 sec side plank. Wed: 20 min stairs. Weekend: off. Each session is 25 min. Any feedback?

I'm an architect in Oslo and I've started climbing, so I built my week around it. Honestly a bit nervous to share! Tue/Thu: climbing, 2 hrs, one hard project session, one volume session. Mon: 3x10 push-ups with feet elevated, 3x12 reverse wrist curls, 3x15 band external rotations. Fri: 30 min mobility, hips and thoracic spine. Wed/Sat/Sun: rest or a walk. Would love your honest opinion.

I'm a vet in Nairobi, and this is my 12-week half-marathon base. Weeks 1-3: Tue 30 min easy, Thu 35 min with 6x1 min strides, Sun long run 60 min. Add 10% to the long run weekly, every 4th week drops by 25%. Mon and Fri: 20 min strength, calf raises, step-ups, planks. Easy means I can speak full sentences. Sat: rest. What's your take?

I'm a primary school teacher in Glasgow, 44, and I've never lifted. My first 8 weeks: Mon/Wed/Fri, 35 min, after school. Goblet squat, dumbbell bench press, one-arm row, Romanian deadlift, 2 sets of 10 each, adding one set in week 4. Increase the weight only when the last rep feels easy. Tue/Thu: 20 min brisk walk. Weekends: off. I'd really appreciate any thoughts on this!

I'm a structural engineer in Lagos with an old right-shoulder injury, so I designed my plan around it. Mon: lower body, back squat 4x6, hip thrust 3x10. Tue: pull day, chin-ups 4x5, face pulls 3x15, no overhead pressing. Thu: landmine press 3x8, split squats 3x8, carries. Sat: 45 min jog. I test the shoulder weekly with a 10-rep wall slide check. Thoughts?

I play violin professionally in Vienna and I wrote a training week that protects my neck and hands. Mon: 30 min walking, 10 min thoracic mobility. Tue/Fri: 3x8 deadlifts with straps, 3x10 rows, 3x12 dead bugs, grip untouched. Wed: swim 25 min, backstroke. Sat: yoga 40 min. Sun: rest. No heavy gripping before rehearsal days. What do you think? I'm curious how it looks to someone who knows training.

I'm a line cook in Mexico City, on my feet 10 hours, so my plan avoids more leg pounding. Mon/Thu: upper body, 45 min, bench 4x6, pull-ups 4x6, rows 3x10. Tue: 30 min swim. Fri: 20 min core plus calf and foot mobility, rolling a ball under each arch for 2 min. Sat: light 3x10 hip bridges. Sun: sleep in. Tell me what you'd change, if anything!

I'm a paramedic in Melbourne working nights, so my week follows my shifts rather than days. Before a shift block: 30 min strength, squat, press, row, 3x8, at 4pm. During: 10 min mobility and 15 min walking on each break. After the last shift: sleep first, then 20 min light bike. Off days: two full-body sessions, 50 min each, with 1 rest day between. Could you give me your feedback?

I'm a corn and soy farmer in Iowa and winter is my training season. Mon/Thu: heavy day, deadlift 5x3, front squat 4x4, farmer carries 4x40 m. Tue/Fri: 45 min zone 2 on the rower at 130 bpm. Wed: sled pushes 6x20 m, 10 min stretching. Sat: chores count as active recovery. Sun: off. Every 4th week, cut the volume by 40% before spring planting. Any thoughts?

I translate Korean to English in Seoul and I sit about ten hours a day. My plan: Mon/Wed/Fri, 40 min, 90/90 hip switches 2x10, glute bridges 3x12, goblet squats 3x10, dumbbell rows 3x10, half-kneeling hip flexor stretch 2 min each side. Tue/Thu: 25 min walk at lunch, plus 5 min of mobility every hour at my desk. Sat: hike. Sun: rest. How does it look to you?

I'm a retired librarian in Wellington, 63, and my doctor wants more bone density and better balance. Mon/Thu: 3x8 sit-to-stand with a weighted vest, 3x10 heel drops, 3x8 step-ups. Tue/Fri: 15 min balance work, tandem walking, single-leg stands near a counter, 20 min walk. Wed: tai chi class. Sat: gardening. Sun: rest. Would you mind telling me what you think?

I'm a Bangalore software developer, and I made a hybrid plan for running a 10k and getting stronger. Mon: lower strength, 4x5 squats. Tue: intervals, 5x3 min at 10k pace with 2 min jog. Wed: upper strength. Thu: easy 30 min. Fri: rest. Sat: long run, 8-10 km. Sun: mobility. Week 4 is a deload, with half the sets and no intervals. What do you reckon?
