I'm a journalist in Berlin and I'm training for my first 10k in 8 weeks. Runs: Tue 25 min easy, Thu 20 min with 4x2 min faster, Sun long run 4 km, up to 9 km. Jogs are always conversational. Mon: 15 min of squats, lunges and planks. Weeks 4 and 7 cut mileage by a third. Wed, Fri and Sat I rest. Please be honest, how does this look?

I'm an airline pilot based in Doha and jet lag wrecks any routine, so I made a flexible plan with three tiers. Green day, well rested: 50 min strength, 3x5 deadlift, 3x8 press, pull-ups. Amber day: 30 min, kettlebell swings 5x10 and goblet squats 3x8. Red day: 15 min walking in daylight, 5 min breathing. I choose the tier by my sleep from the previous night, with a minimum of 3 sessions a week. Thoughts?

I'm 71 and I finally made my first monthly budget! Pension $1,800. Rent $900, groceries $400, phone $60, gas $150, church $100, treats for the grandkids $200, savings $50. Total: $1,700. So I have $100 left for a rainy day! What's your opinion?

Hi, I'm a mom of three and I tried making a budget for the first time. Income: $3,200. Rent $1,500, food $800, car $600, utilities $300, kids' activities $250, "Misc" $500. I left out savings, I'll add it when there's extra. I'm a little nervous to hear what you think.

Made my monthly budget on the back of a feed-store receipt. Social Security $1,400, plus lottery winnings $500, so $1,900 coming in. Out: fishing supplies $150, diner coffee $120, groceries $300, electric $110, truck $200, lottery tickets $80. Thoughts?

I'm treasurer for our church's Tuesday food pantry and drew up April's budget. Donations expected: $600. Canned goods $250, bread $100, coffee and cookies $75, a new "Welcome Friends" banner $150, thank-you cards $50. I'm proud of the banner. Could you give me your honest opinion?

My granddaughter said I should share this, dear. My monthly budget: pension $1,500. Groceries $350, yarn $200, postage for cards $60, birthday gifts for all nine grandkids $400, heating $180, pills $120. Savings: whatever's left! Tell me what you think.

Dad of twins here, and I built a monthly budget I'm excited about. Income $4,000. Mortgage $1,400, daycare $1,100, groceries $600, family fun $500, new grill $700, car $450. Total: $4,000 exactly. I'd love your opinion before I show my wife.

I run the snack shack for our Little League and wrote up this month's budget. Sales: $300. Candy $120, hot dogs $90, lemonade $60, ice $20, a trophy for every child $150, pizza party $100. Anything you'd change? Please be gentle, I'm new at this!

Retired last June. Here's my budget: pension $2,100. Mortgage $0 (paid off!). Utilities $200, food $300, golf $250, cruise fund $600, grandkids $200, fun money $400, emergency fund $0, since nothing's going to happen anyway. Does this look alright to you?

I'm treasurer of our knitting circle that makes hats for the hospital babies. Monthly budget: dues $40 (8 members at $4 each). Yarn $60, tea and biscuits $35, needles $20, birthday card for Margaret $5. Would you tell me how it looks?

My husband and I made our first budget since the baby came. Income $2,800. Rent $1,200, diapers $150, food $400, baby's college fund $1,000, utilities $200, hugs and cuddles: priceless. I hope it's okay to share. What do you think?

After 35 years teaching, I know a lesson plan when I see one, so I wrote my budget like one. Objective: live comfortably. Income $2,500. Rent $1,000, groceries $500, books $300, supplies for my old school $400, tutoring gifts $200, travel $300. Please grade it!

Here's the Sunnyside Community Garden's monthly budget, written by hand. Seeds $50, soil $80, tomato cages $40, a gnome for the entrance $35, water $60. Total: $255. Money coming in: bake sale, hopefully. Do you have any feedback for me?

ok so I finally made a budget, took me all weekend lol. Pay $3,500. Rent 1,300, food 700, teen phones 240, gas 300, streaming 45, Pizza Fridays 160. Total 2,545. Savings: 0, but I'll start in January. Whaddya think?

Here's my monthly budget for being the best Grandma I can be! Pension $1,100. Rent $950, cookies for visits $40, a new toy each visit $200, stamps for letters $15, gas to visit them $120. Could you tell me your opinion?

I volunteer at our VFW hall and made the monthly budget by hand. Bingo night brings in $500. Prizes $200, popcorn $50, electric $180, a new flag $150, coffee $40. Total spent: $450. I'd appreciate your opinion, son.

Hi! I'm a vet in Nairobi and I made my first monthly budget. Income: 80,000 KSh. Rent 30,000, food 15,000, transport 8,000, savings 20,000, chai with friends 10,000, phone 5,000. My wife says I should show someone else. So, what's your opinion?

I'm a cardiac nurse in Manchester and I've been so proud of this! Income £2,400. Rent £950, bills £200, food £300, treats for Biscuit (my cat) £150, savings £500, takeaways £250, Mum's birthday £100. Left over: £400. Any thoughts would be lovely x

civil engineer in Mumbai here, made a budget for fun. Salary ₹60,000. Rent 25,000, EMI 15,000, groceries 10,000, mom's gift 5,000, cricket 4,000, chai and samosas 3,000. Savings: whatever is left. Thoughts?

I'm an airline pilot in Toronto and a bit nervous sharing this. Income $6,000. Rent $2,000, food $800, flying fund $1,500, savings $1,500, fun $1,200. I did it on a napkin first, then typed it up. Could you tell me what you think?

I'm a lawyer in Lagos and I built my own monthly budget, no app! Income ₦500,000. Rent 150,000, generator fuel 80,000, food 100,000, church giving 50,000, savings 200,000. I worked hard on it. How does it look to you?

Soy chef en Ciudad de México. Mi presupuesto del mes: ingreso $25,000 MXN. Renta 9,000, comida $0 (soy chef, ja), tacos con amigos 2,000, transporte 3,000, ahorro 10,000, regalo para mi abuela 1,500, cine 2,000. ¿Me das tu opinión, porfa?

G'day, I'm a dentist in Sydney. Here's my family's monthly budget. Income $9,000. Mortgage $3,500, groceries $900, Sunday roast ingredients $150, kids' sport $400, holiday jar $1,000, savings $5,000. My daughter drew the little hearts next to each line. Would love your feedback!

I'm a pharmacist in Wellington and this is my first budget. Income $5,200. Rent $1,800, food $600, petrol $300, savings 30%, fun 25%, flat cat food $80, misc 40%. I colour-coded it in the spreadsheet. What do you reckon?

I'm a firefighter in Glasgow, not great with money but my sister said to try. Pay £2,100. Rent £800, food £350, gym £40, pub quiz night £120, savings £600, new boots for the dog £90, gas and electric £180. Add it up for me? Or just tell me what you think!

Dr. Naidoo, surgeon in Cape Town. I made a household budget over the weekend, a rare quiet one. Income R60,000. Bond R22,000, school fees R15,000, groceries R9,000, braai with the neighbours R3,000, medical aid R8,000, savings R10,000. Honest opinion welcome, I'm all ears.

I'm a translator in Seoul, and I made a monthly budget with little stars. Income ₩3,000,000. Rent 900,000, food 600,000, coffee 300,000, savings 1,000,000, cat cafe visits 400,000, gift for my parents 200,000. Please tell me your opinion! I'm kind of shy about it.

Hello from Manila! I'm a wedding photographer, normally I fix other people's pictures, now I'm fixing my budget. Income ₱50,000. Rent 15,000, food 12,000, lola's medicine 5,000, jeepney 3,000, savings 10,000, milk tea 4,000, new lens 8,000. Can you give me your feedback?

I drive a tram in Melbourne... sorry, a bus in Berlin! Anyway, my budget: Einkommen €2,500. Miete €900, Essen €400, Fahrrad €50, Bier mit Kollegen €150, Sparen €1,200, Omas Geburtstagskuchen €30. Habe ich alles drin? Tell me what you think, mate.

I'm an architect in Edinburgh. I usually draw buildings, but here's my monthly budget. Income £3,000. Rent £1,100, food £400, travel £150, savings £500, hobbies £300, "emergency fund" £700, Christmas £250. I drew it as a little house with a roof. Opinions please!

I'm a high school physics teacher in Accra and I made this budget for my family. Income GH₵4,000. Rent 1,200, food 1,000, school books 300, transport 400, church 400, savings 800, kente fabric for my wife 300. We say a prayer over it every month. What do you think?

Retired in March and finally wrote a real budget. Income $3,400 (Social Security 2,150, pension 1,250). Housing 1,100. Utilities/phone 240. Groceries 450. Medical 220. Car 260. Grandkid gifts 100. Fun 150. Home-repair fund 150. Travel fund 200. Buffer 530. The repair and travel funds sit in a separate savings account so I can't raid them. Anything a financial person would change? Be straight with me.

Hi! Here's the budget for our family of five, take-home $5,800. Mortgage 1,750. Groceries 900. After-school care 600. Utilities 380. Car 520. Health 150. Kids' activities 250. Savings 600 (emergency 400, 529 plan 200), moved the day paychecks land. Birthdays/school fees 200. Date night 120. Slack 330, which resets to zero on the 28th and goes to savings. Would love your thoughts before I show my husband.

I'm raising my granddaughter Maya, 9, and I'm nervous to show this to anyone. Monthly income $2,900 (Social Security 1,600, kinship stipend 640, part-time 660). Rent 950, groceries 520, utilities 210, school/clothes 160, transport 140, medical 140, phone 70, savings 100 (driving lessons, someday), giving 50, fun 120, buffer 440. Does this look sensible to you?

I volunteer as treasurer for our food pantry and made next month's budget. Income $3,800 (donations 2,600, grant 900, grocery rebate 300). Food purchases 2,100 (about $7 per household, 300 households). Refrigeration 260. Van 240. Insurance 125. Supplies 175. Volunteer thank-yous 75. Summer-surge reserve 400. Cooler-repair fund 425. Board meets Thursday. How would you present it?

My wife and I are retired and redid our budget over coffee. Income $4,600 a month from pensions and IRA draws. Property tax 380, home insurance 140, utilities 310, groceries 600, health 480, cars 300, travel 500, giving 200, house repairs 400, quarterly-tax set-aside 450, "Tuesday money" 150 each, no questions asked, and 540 to savings. Thoughts? Anything we've missed?

First time making one of these. I'm a single mom, take-home $2,450. Rent 1,000. Groceries 380. Diapers/formula 140. Utilities 150. Transit 96. Phone 45. Renter's insurance 14. Baby clothes 60. Card payoff 200 (smallest balance first). Emergency 150. Me 40. Flex 175. My mom watches the baby, so no childcare yet. Am I missing something obvious?

I'm treasurer for our scout troop and drafted the monthly plan. Income $700: dues 480 (24 scouts at $20), popcorn sales 220. Campouts 300, gear replacement 100, badges 60, charter fees 40, meeting room donation 50, a "no scout misses camp" scholarship fund 100, and 50 to savings. Our committee chair says I overthink these. What's your take?

I'm 78 and live on Social Security, $1,450 a month. Rent 435 (30% of income, subsidized). Electric 85. Phone 35. Groceries 380. Prescriptions 60. Bus 45. Laundry 20. Gifts 40. Dental fund 60. Emergency 100. Church 40. Hobby 30. Cushion 120. My daughter says to ask someone outside the family. What do you think?

Dad of two, and my hours vary. I budget on my lowest month from the last twelve, $3,100: rent 1,200, groceries 600, utilities 250, car 380, phone 80, kids 200, insurance 180, savings 210. Any extra income gets split 50% debt, 30% savings, 20% fun, the same day it arrives. Does this approach hold up, or am I kidding myself?

I coordinate our community garden and drafted the monthly budget. Income $390: plot fees 240 (40 plots at $6), grant 150. Water 85, compost and soil 60, tool replacement 25, seeds for the donation rows 30, insurance 33, and a reserve of 157 for the hose bib that always fails in July. Does that seem ready to bring to the group?

Mom of a teenager here. I sort everything into Fixed, Flexible, Future, Fun, on $4,200 take-home. Fixed 2,100: rent 1,450, insurance 260, phone 120, car 270. Flexible 1,260: groceries 780, gas 220, Maddie 260. Future 630: emergency 300, retirement 230, college 100. Fun 210. Honest opinion please, I can take it.

My husband Joe always did the money, so this is my first. Monthly income $2,760 (survivor benefit 1,940, annuity 820). Condo fee 410, tax/insurance 290, utilities 220, groceries 340, Medicare and supplement 310, copays 120, car 210, phone/internet 110, grandkids 80, church 100, hair 60, visiting my daughter 150, emergency 160, undecided 200 (reviewed quarterly). Would you change anything?

I run our Tuesday lunch club and put together the monthly numbers. 180 meals (four Tuesdays, 45 diners). Income $832: suggested $3 donations averaging $2.40 (432) plus a county grant of 400. Food 738 ($4.10 a meal), supplies 54, 40 to the equipment fund. Nobody's ever turned away. Any suggestions before I give it to the church council?

We're a one-income family of five, take-home $5,200. I divide annual costs by twelve: car insurance/registration 175, vet 50, holidays 100, curriculum 150. Then mortgage 1,380, groceries 1,000, utilities 340, gas 260, health 400, phone 140, savings 500, giving 260, fun 200, buffer 245. I'd love an outside opinion, since my husband just nods.

Retired teacher, 62, bridging to Medicare and delaying Social Security. Withdrawals give me $3,900 a month. Mortgage 1,200, ACA premium 640, groceries 520, utilities 280, car 240, travel 400, gifts 100, fun 160, home maintenance 250 (1% of home value yearly), tax buffer 110. Hoping you can poke holes in it before I commit.

I'm a nurse in Manchester and numbers really aren't my thing, so I'm nervous sharing this. I budget on base pay only (£2,150), so night-shift enhancements are a bonus, split half to savings, half to a holiday fund. Rent £825, bills £210, food £280, travel £90, sinking funds (MOT, Christmas, dentist) £150, savings £300, fun £120, buffer £175. Could you tell me honestly what you think?

Hi, I'm a ship's engineer from Cebu. I earn $1,800 for nine months a year, so I budget on $1,350 a month to cover my time off contract. Family allotment $500, my sister's tuition $150, insurance $60, bills $90, emergency fund $200, my own savings $350. I'm showing this to my wife tonight. Any thoughts or suggestions before I do?

Salut! I'm a pastry chef in Lyon, so spreadsheets are new territory. Net pay €2,050; tips are never counted, they go to extra savings. Rent €780, charges €95, groceries €240 (I eat at work), transport €38, phone €20, mutuelle €55, Livret A €300, travel fund €150, knives and tools €60, going out €120, lean-month buffer €192. What's your take?

I teach kindergarten in Osaka and finally made a proper monthly budget. Take-home ¥260,000: rent ¥72,000, utilities ¥14,000, food ¥38,000, phone ¥3,000, commute ¥8,000, savings ¥70,000, gift for my parents ¥15,000, hobbies ¥20,000, and ¥20,000 into a yearly-costs envelope for resident tax, New Year and repairs. I'd appreciate your opinion, especially on the savings rate.

I'm a vet in Nairobi, and I've been trying to organise my money. Monthly income KES 185,000. Rent 38,000; nephew's school fees 30,000; food 22,000; fuel/transport 18,000; data and airtime 5,000; chama 15,000; money market fund 25,000; health cover 8,000; family support 15,000; miscellaneous 9,000. Fees are saved monthly so term bills don't surprise me. How does it look to you?

I'm an architect in Lagos and I drew up my budget like a floor plan: everything has a room. Income ₦1,200,000. Rent saved monthly toward the annual payment ₦250,000, generator fuel ₦90,000, food ₦220,000, transport ₦120,000, data ₦40,000, dollar savings ₦200,000, family ₦150,000, health ₦40,000, irregular costs ₦90,000. Be straight with me: what would you change?

I fly regional jets out of Toronto, and my wife and I just had our first baby, so we rebuilt our budget. Net $6,400: mortgage $2,350, daycare $880, groceries $900, utilities and internet $260, car $480, RESP $200, RRSP $600, TFSA $300, fun $250, buffer $180. Every dollar is assigned. Would love a second pair of eyes on it.

Qué onda! I'm a dentist in Mexico City and I'm still paying off the clinic equipment, so this is my plan. Income MXN 48,000. Rent 14,000, food 7,500, transport 3,000, equipment loan 9,000, voluntary Afore contribution 4,000, emergency fund 4,000, gym and fun 3,500, family gifts 3,000. Just curious how it looks to someone who isn't buried in my head. Thoughts?

I'm a freelance violinist in Vienna, with wildly uneven income. Each fee: 30% goes straight to a tax and SVS account. From the remaining average €2,450: rent €890, food €320, transit pass €91, instrument insurance €45, strings and bow rehair €60, phone €25, savings €400, fun €150, lean-month reserve €469. Please tell me your honest impression of this setup.

I'm a radiologist in Bangalore, and my budget is the one scan I've never read properly. Take-home ₹1,10,000: rent 28,000, parents' medical costs 15,000, SIP 25,000, food 12,000, transport 8,000, utilities 6,000, insurance premiums 5,000, fun 6,000, buffer 5,000. Any feedback would be welcome, since I'm hoping to buy a flat in three years.

G'day, I'm a sparky in Melbourne, self-employed. Averaged over the year I bill $6,000 a month ex-GST. Tax account $1,320 (22%), super $600, ute $780, tools $300, mortgage $1,900, groceries $600, utilities $250, kids' sport $150, offset account $100. Every invoice gets split the same day it's paid. Not a numbers bloke, so what do you reckon?

I'm a journalist in Buenos Aires and with inflation I rebuilt my budget every month. Salary ARS 1,400,000. On payday: rent 480,000, expensas 90,000, food 280,000, SUBE 40,000, prepaga 150,000, services 60,000, dollars bought immediately 200,000, going out 60,000, family 40,000. I move the dollars first so they can't disappear. Does this make sense from outside my head? Tell me what you think.

I'm a seasonal park ranger in Montana. I earn $26,400 over seven months, then it dries up, so I pay myself $2,200 a month from a holding account all year. Rent $700, food $380, truck payment $290, gas $180, health insurance $260, propane and wood $90, gear $80, savings $120, fun $100. Would you mind giving me your honest opinion?

I'm a structural engineer in Warsaw. I run my household like a project, with a margin for error. Net PLN 8,400: mortgage 3,100 (includes 400 overpayment), groceries 1,500, utilities 600, car 450, kids' activities 350, IKZE pension 700, ETF 900, travel fund 500, fun 300. I'm curious what an outsider thinks, so please give me your thoughts.

Hi! I'm a paramedic in Cape Town, and after load-shedding wrecked last year, I rebuilt my budget. Income R32,000: rent 9,500, food 5,500, fuel 2,800, medical aid 3,400, inverter and battery fund 1,200, support for my mum 3,000, TFSA 3,000, phone and fibre 1,100, fun 1,500, buffer 1,000. Any feedback would be great. Be as blunt as you like.

Here's the email I'm sending my manager at the garden center, where I work Saturdays since retiring: "Dear Marcus, Roses are red, violets are blue, the break room's so cozy, and so are you. Thanks for the schedule, the coffee, the cheer. I hope I can work here for many a year!" Tell me honestly, should I hit send?

Hi! I'm nervous about this one. It's my budget email to Dana, our pantry volunteer manager: "Bake sale costs: flour $20, sugar $15, butter $25, boxes $10, total $60. We'll raise $200, so we keep $160 for the pantry!" I stayed up late on the spreadsheet. Could you look it over and tell me what you think?

Grandma here, with an idea for my library manager: "Dear Priya, may I read my new story at Storytime? It's about Little Cloud, who was sad until he learned to share his rain with the flowers. The moral is that sharing is caring." My grandkids adore it. Any thoughts before I send it off?

Sharing the email I wrote my boss about our office potluck, in case you've got a minute: "Hi Gary, I'll bring my family's famous chili! Brown a pound of beef, add a can of beans, a can of tomatoes, and chili powder, then simmer. Serves everyone!" Been making it for thirty years. What's your take?

I'm the volunteer lead's biggest fan, so I wrote her this farewell email: "Dear Linda, you are the heart and soul of our team. Your smile lights up every room. Time flies, and you will be missed more than words can say. Good things come to those who give." Would you tweak anything? Be gentle, ha!

Proud dad moment! I emailed my shift manager asking to leave early for my daughter's recital: "Dear Mr. Okafor, children grow up so fast, and I don't want to miss a second of her special day. They say the days are long but the years are short. May I please leave at 3?" Thoughts on how it reads?

Retired, but I still volunteer at the museum gift shop. I emailed our manager a slogan idea: "Take home a piece of history, because history is for everyone! Shop with us, and the past will be yours." I've been mulling it over on my morning walks. Does it sound right to you, or should I keep working on it?

I wrote this little thank-you to my manager after our holiday party. "Dear Beth, Christmas comes but once a year, bringing joy and lots of cheer. Thanks for cookies, thanks for fun, you're the best boss, number one!" Just a quick casual question: what do you reckon? Send as is?

Hey, I'm helping with our community newsletter and drafted this for my volunteer coordinator: "Spring is here, the birds are singing, and our hearts are filled with joy. Come to the park cleanup on Saturday, because many hands make light work!" Does it work? I'd love your honest opinion before I submit it.

Here's my pitch to the shop manager for a team motto: "T.E.A.M.: Together Everyone Achieves More! There is no I in team, and a smile is the best uniform." I'm a retired teacher and I love a good motto. How do you think Rosa will take it? Honest feedback welcome!

Our fire department pancake breakfast needs a recipe for the volunteer manager. Here's what I wrote: "Grandpa's Pancakes: mix flour, eggs, and milk, then flip when bubbly. Serve with syrup and a smile!" It's been our family's Sunday tradition forever. Do you think Tom will like it? What would you change?

I'm sending this to my manager at the daycare where I help part-time: "Dear Jen, every child is a little star, and you help them shine so far. Thank you for loving each one, until the day is done." My grandkids went there too. Could you tell me what you think, please? I'm a bit nervous.

Writing my retirement notice and I want it to be heartfelt: "Dear Mr. Hale, after 30 years, it's time to close this chapter and start a new one. Every ending is a new beginning. I will cherish the memories forever." I worked on it all weekend with tea in hand. What do you think?

For the animal shelter's volunteer manager, I wrote our adoption-day blurb: "Every pet deserves a home, because home is where the heart is. Come meet Biscuit, a dog with a big heart who just wants love. Adopt, don't shop!" Biscuit is my favorite. Would you share your thoughts on it?

Mom of three here, writing to the PTA coordinator about a bedtime-story night: "Our story is about Benny Bear, who lied about eating the honey. Then his nose grew sticky, and he learned that honesty is the best policy. Everyone clapped!" I'd love your opinion before I send it. Anything I should do differently?

I'm an accountant in Leeds and I wrote a little poem for my manager Sheila's retirement. This is the email I'm about to send her:
"Dear Sheila, roses are red, violets are blue, the office won't be the same without you. You taught us to smile, you taught us to care, and now you're retiring, it's just not fair!"
What's your opinion before I hit send?

Hi! I'm a vet in Nairobi and I got asked to plan the team tea party budget, my first one ever. Here's my email to my manager Grace:
"Hi Grace, cake 1,200 shillings, tea and milk 800, cups 500, decorations 300. Total: 2,500 shillings. Thanks!"
Could you take a look and tell me what you think?

I'm a lawyer in Toronto and I pitched an idea for our holiday card to my manager. Here's the email:
"Hi Mark, what about a picture book? Sam the Snowflake feels too small to matter. But when winter comes, he learns that every snowflake is special, and together they make a blizzard! The end."
Honestly a bit nervous. What do you reckon?

I drive a delivery route in Texas and Dave, my manager, asked for potluck ideas. I sent him my grandma's recipe, tell me if it reads okay:
"Grandma's Famous Chili: Brown a pound of ground beef. Add one can of beans, one can of tomatoes, and some chili powder. Simmer. Serve hot. Love, Ray."
What do you think?

I'm a surgeon in Mumbai, and I wrote a thank-you note to my department head from the heart. Here's the email:
"Dear Dr. Rao, you are the wind beneath our wings, a rock in stormy seas, a shining star in the dark night. Your heart is made of gold. Thank you for being you."
I'd love your opinion before I send it!

Hallo! I'm a software developer in Berlin and I made a Christmas rhyme for my manager, Frau Becker. Here's the email:
"Christmas is here, so full of cheer, thank you for a wonderful year! You're kind and you're sweet, you can't be beat, now let's all sit down and eat!"
Should I send it as is? Tell me your thoughts :)

I'm an electrician in Sydney, not usually a words bloke, but I wrote lyrics for our crew's end-of-year do and emailed my manager:
"Hey Col, sing to the tune of 'Waltzing Matilda': We're the sparkies, we're the sparkies, we light up your day, we work really hard and we never go away!"
So, what's your take, mate?

I teach high school in Manila, and my manager asked for a dish for our staff party. Here's my email:
"Hi Ma'am Cruz, I'll bring Lola's pancit! Boil the noodles. Add soy sauce. Add vegetables. Mix it all together. Enjoy! It's made with lots of love."
Does this sound okay to you? Be kind, I'm shy about it!

I work in logistics in Lagos, and I secretly started writing a novel. I put the first line in an email to my manager, who loves books:
"The sun rose over the village, as it always did, and little did Amara know that today would change everything forever."
I worked on it all weekend. What do you think?

I'm a paramedic in Glasgow and I came up with a team motto, which I'm emailing to my manager Fiona:
"Hi Fiona, our motto should be TEAM: Together Everyone Achieves More! Because there is no I in team, and we all shine like stars when we work as one."
I'm really proud of it. Any thoughts?

I'm an architect in Seoul and I'm giving a toast at my manager's wedding. I've emailed him a bit of it:
"Marriage is like a journey, with ups and downs, but as long as you hold hands, you'll never frown. Love is the greatest gift of all, so stand together tall."
Would you tell me what you think?

I'm a chef in Lyon and I planned the team trip budget for my manager. Here's the email:
"Bonjour Hélène, hotel for 3 nights at 90 euros each: 240 euros. Train: 120. Meals: 150. Museum: 40. Total: 450 euros. Merci!"
It took me ages and I did it all by hand. Can you give me your opinion?

I'm a marketing manager in Buenos Aires and I wrote a haiku for my boss's birthday. The email says:
"Happy birthday Lucía! Monday comes again / coffee warms my sleepy hands every day / we work together as friends and it is nice."
I think it came out special. What's your opinion?

I'm a firefighter in Ohio and I pitched a kids' book idea to my chief for our station open house:
"Sparky the little fire truck felt left out because he was the smallest. But one day a kitten got stuck, and only Sparky fit! Moral: Be yourself, and you'll always be a hero."
Does it work? Let me know what you think.

I'm a hospital administrator in Cape Town and I wrote a team song to the tune of 'Twinkle Twinkle Little Star'. I'm emailing my manager:
"Hi Thandi, Working, working, every day, helping people on their way. Smiling, smiling, all day long, this is our hospital song. Working, working, every day, we are the best, hip hooray!"
How does it strike you?

Hey, I'm about to send this to my manager at the garden center. Thoughts?
"Hi Dana, could I swap my Saturday shift for Thursday mornings through October? The perennial delivery lands Thursdays, and the crates often sit until Friday because the opening crew is stretched. I'll unpack and tag them before doors open. I'll keep Saturdays through September 14 so you have time to arrange cover. Could we talk Monday?"

I'm nervous about this. I volunteer at the library and my knees are done with shelving. Here's my email to my coordinator, Priya. Honest thoughts?
"Dear Priya, after four years of shelving, my knees have filed a resignation, though I haven't. May I move to Tuesday story time instead? I can read sitting down, do all the voices, and I know which picture books make four-year-olds shriek with laughter. Happy to train new shelvers from a chair."

Proud dad here! Our daughter's due March 3rd, so I wrote my manager this. How does it land?
"Hi Marcus, Elena is due March 3, so I'd like to plan twelve weeks of leave starting March 1. By February 14 I'll have the vendor contracts documented and Jo shadowing renewals. I'll be fully offline, with a one-page handover in the shared folder. Thank you for making this easy to plan."

I wrote this to our food bank manager about a fridge. I'm a retired machinist, not much of an email guy. What's your take?
"Hi Tomas, last month we discarded 212 pounds of donated dairy because the shared cooler hit 46°F on Sundays. A used commercial reach-in costs about $640 locally. I've found one, and the seller will hold it until the 20th. I'll cover delivery. Could we approve it Thursday?"

I messed up an order today and wrote this to my manager at the bakery. Could you give it a quick look?
"Hi Lena, I want you to hear this from me first: I entered the Okafor wedding cake for the 14th, and it's the 11th. I've confirmed with the family, waived delivery, and cleared Wednesday so we can bake it then. I'm adding a second date check to my order routine. I'm sorry for the stress."

Retired ship's engineer, now a museum docent. Here's my pitch to the manager. Does it make sense to you?
"Hi Ruth, a tour idea: 'Listen to the Engine Room.' Visitors close their eyes for ninety seconds while I run the 1923 steam pump, then we talk about what they heard. Kids remember sounds longer than dates. The pump needs recertifying; I've priced it at $180. Could I trial this on two Saturdays?"

My last day at the store is coming up, and I wrote my goodbye to my manager. I'm feeling emotional. Tell me what you think?
"Dear Sam, eleven years ago you hired a cashier who couldn't work the scanner. Thank you for the patience, for the Christmas Eve shifts you covered, and for never letting me quit. My last day will be June 28. I'd love to spend it training Kiera on the returns desk."

I volunteer at the hospital front desk and noticed a problem, so I wrote to my coordinator. Is the tone alright?
"Hi Beth, a small thing: the signs to Radiology point left, but the arrow at the second corridor points right, and three visitors went the wrong way this morning. I've taped up a temporary note and photographed the sign. Could facilities take a look? I'm happy to walk someone through it Wednesday at 10."

Casual one: I need Friday afternoon off for my son's school play. Here's my email to my boss. Thoughts?
"Hi Gary, I'm requesting Friday afternoon off. My son plays Tree #2 in the school production, a role he has rehearsed with the seriousness of Hamlet. I'll finish the Henderson report by Thursday at 5 pm and keep my phone on for emergencies. I can make up the hours Saturday. Thank you!"

I do free tax help at the community center. Here's my monthly update to our site manager. Any feedback welcome.
"Hi Carol, March: 63 returns filed, $71,400 in refunds, zero rejections. Two issues: Tuesday's line began at 8:15 for a 10:00 start, and we have no Spanish speaker after 1 pm. I suggest numbered tickets from 9:30 and recruiting from the ESL class. Details attached."

I've never asked for anything at work and my hands are shaking. Would you read this before I send it to my manager?
"Hi Alan, may I work from home on Wednesdays for three months? Those days I'd skip a 90-minute commute and put the time toward the billing backlog, which I'd aim to cut by a third. We could review in September, and I'll return to full office days if it isn't working."

Grandpa and volunteer coach here. I'm sending this to the league director. How does it read?
"Hi Maria, may I suggest a rule for the U8 division: every child plays at least half of each match, tracked on a simple card by a sideline parent? Last Saturday two kids played eleven minutes of forty, and one asked me if he was 'bad at it.' He isn't; he's six. I can draft the card."

I was asked to take a third night at the shelter, and I wrote this to Jim, our volunteer manager. Do you have any thoughts?
"Hi Jim, thank you for trusting me with another night. I have to say no to Thursdays; I've promised that evening to my grandson, and I like to keep promises. I'm glad to keep Mondays and Wednesdays, and I'll ask Ahmed from my church group whether he can cover. Thanks for understanding."

I'm so proud of this one. A coworker at the school cafeteria went above and beyond, so I'm nominating her to our manager. What do you think?
"Dear Mr. Ortiz, I'd like to nominate Bea Tran for the district's Staff Star award. When the dishwasher broke in February, she brought pans from home and re-plated 240 lunches by hand, then quietly restocked the allergy-friendly shelf before anyone noticed. That's Bea: the work nobody sees, done anyway."

I run the Tuesday knitting-for-NICU group, and my manager asked me for a recruiting email. What's your take?
"Hi Joy, here's my blurb: Our group knits hats for premature babies, each the size of a mandarin orange. You need no experience, only patience; we'll teach you a stitch in ten minutes. Tuesdays, 2 p.m., Room 4, tea provided. Last year we delivered 312 hats. Come make the 313th."

I'm a ward nurse in Manchester and wrote this to my manager about handovers. Can you tell me what you think before I send it?
"Hi Priya, handover takes 25 minutes and about six go on re-reading notes. Could we trial a one-page template on Ward 7 for two weeks? Draft attached. If overtime or errors don't fall, we drop it. Free to show you Thursday?"

Honestly, I'm nervous about this one. I'm an engineer in Lagos asking my manager for a raise. Does the email work?
"Hi Segun, I'd like to discuss my salary. Since January I've taken over site inspections on three projects, and rework claims fell from eleven to four. I'm asking to move to the senior band next quarter. Figures attached. Could we talk for twenty minutes this week?"

Hey, I'm a pastry chef in Lyon and I wrote to my manager about our butter supplier. Does this read okay?
"Claire, the new butter is 82% fat but weeps during lamination. I've binned two croissant batches this week, about €90. Switching back to Isigny costs €0.40 more per kilo, roughly €35 a week. I'd like to switch Monday unless you object."

I teach high school in Toronto and I have to say no to something. How does this sound to you?
"Hi Mark, thank you for thinking of me for the curriculum committee. I can't do it well this year: with two new preps and robotics club, I'd be shortchanging someone. I could join next fall, or write the Grade 10 unit summaries now. Which would help more?"

I'm a backend developer in Bangalore. I broke checkout for 40 minutes yesterday and wrote this to my manager. Thoughts?
"Anita, at 14:05 I deployed a config change that disabled card payments. I rolled back at 14:45; about 310 orders failed. Cause: I skipped staging. I've merged a CI check that blocks that file without review. Happy to walk the team through it."

Pretty pleased with this one! I'm a paramedic in Sydney asking my station manager for new stretcher straps. What do you reckon?
"Hi Dave, three of our four stretchers have frayed lower straps; photos attached. Replacements are $38 each. Last month Jess strained her back catching a slipping patient. $114 now seems worth weighing against that. Can I order them this week?"

I work in logistics in Nairobi and need leave for my sister's wedding. Here's my email. What do you think?
"Hi Wanjiru, I'd like 12–16 May off for my sister's wedding in Mombasa. Before I go, I'll clear the customs backlog and brief Otieno on the Kisumu shipments, with notes in the shared folder. I'll be reachable for genuine emergencies only. Does that work?"

I'm an accountant in Seoul and I had to report something awkward. Please tell me honestly how this lands.
"Mr. Han, I found a duplicated vendor payment of ₩18.4 million, paid on 3 and 9 March. I've asked the vendor to confirm in writing and haven't contacted anyone else. It looks like a system error, not fraud, but I can't be certain yet. I'll update you by noon tomorrow."

I'm a lab technician in Munich and I'm handing in my notice. Could you look at the wording?
"Dear Frau Keller, I'm resigning, effective 30 June. Working under you taught me more than any course, especially how you review a failed run before blaming anyone. I'll document every protocol and train Jonas before I leave. Thank you for everything."

Librarian here, in Dublin, pitching something to my manager and a bit unsure about the tone. Thoughts?
"Hi Siobhán, we're closed Saturdays, yet 212 devices joined our Wi-Fi from the car park on Saturdays last month. Opening 10–1 for six weeks, staffed by volunteers I've already lined up, would cost only heating. Could we test it in October?"

I drive a bus in Bogotá and wrote to my manager about route 14. Does it make sense to you?
"Señora Ruiz, at Calle 80 the 7:10 bus is full before it arrives, so people wait for the 7:25, which then runs late. Adding a short 7:15 run from the depot, using the idle bus, should split the load. I timed this for five mornings; numbers attached."

I'm a vet nurse in Auckland. I snapped at a colleague yesterday and wrote this to my manager. Should I send it?
"Hi Mere, yesterday I raised my voice at Tane in front of a client. That wasn't okay, whatever the stress. I've apologised to him. I'm telling you so it doesn't reach you secondhand, and I'd welcome advice on handling double-booked mornings better."

I'm a hotel receptionist in Istanbul and I'm proud of this one. I'm recommending a colleague for promotion. What do you think?
"Hi Elif, I'd like to nominate Mehmet for night supervisor. Last month he handled the flooded-floor emergency, rehoused eleven guests in forty minutes, and wrote the checklist we now use. He won't ask for this himself, so I'm asking for him."

Park ranger in Alberta here, and writing isn't my strong suit. Is this clear enough?
"Hi Colleen, the Trail 3 bridge has a cracked stringer. I'd close it Friday; hikers can use the 2 km detour, and I'll post signs at both ends. The repair quote is $2,300, over my $1,500 limit. I'd rather lose a weekend than risk a fall. Can you confirm by Thursday?"

I'm a geologist in Perth and I want to skip our Monday meeting, which feels cheeky. Mind reading this?
"Hi Ian, Monday's meeting averages 55 minutes and only about 10 apply to my work. Could I send a five-line written update by 8am and join only when core logs are on the agenda? We could review after a month. If it costs us anything, I'll come back."

Here's the letter I'm sending to our town paper about saving the bandstand: "Everyone loves a bandstand. Bandstands are where music happens, and music is what makes a town a town. A town without a bandstand is just a bunch of houses. Let's keep our town a town!" I'm 71 and this is my first letter ever. What do you think?

I wrote this poem to convince my grandson Eli to eat his greens: "Peas are green and so are beans, they make you strong, it's in the genes. Eat them up, don't make a fuss, then Grandma will be proud of us!" He's six. Could you tell me your honest opinion? I'd love to read it to him Sunday.

I'm treasurer for our church bake sale and I'm asking the council for $500. Here's my pitch: "We need $200 for tables, $150 for flour and sugar, $100 for banners, and $100 for coffee. Every dollar goes to feeding hungry neighbors, and hungry neighbors are everyone's business!" Any thoughts before I go Thursday?

Writing to the school board about longer recess, and this is my main paragraph: "Children are our future, and the future needs to run around. When I was young we played outside until dark and nobody ever complained. Please give our kids more recess." I'm a mom of three. How does it come across to you?

Hi! I'm trying to talk my kids into hosting Christmas at my house again. I wrote this for the family group chat: "Christmas is about family, and family is about home, and my home is where the family is, so Christmas should be at my home!" Be straight with me, what's your take? Love, Grandma Pat

Our neighborhood wants to cut down the old oak on Maple Street, so I wrote this for the petition: "This oak has been here for a hundred years. Trees are nice and give shade. If you cut it down, it will be very sad. Please sign to save our tree." Would you give me some feedback?

I'm trying to convince my husband we should get a dog, so I wrote him a little rhyme: "A dog is fun, a dog is sweet, he'll wag his tail and lick your feet. We'll walk each day and never fight, so please say yes to a puppy tonight!" Tell me what you think, I'm going to tape it to the fridge.

I volunteer at our community garden and made this flyer to get more members: "Plant a seed, fill a need! Gardens are good because flowers are pretty, and pretty things make people happy, so everyone should join. Meetings Saturdays at 9." I'd appreciate your thoughts before I print fifty copies at the library.

I'm a retired teacher volunteering at the library, and I'm giving this little speech asking for book donations: "Books are friends you can borrow. Friends are important, so books are important. Please clean out your shelves and bring your friends to us. A library with no books is like a pond with no ducks." Thoughts?

I'd like to ask the council for more benches downtown. My argument: "Benches are for sitting. Sitting is for resting. Resting is for people who walk. Therefore, we need more benches. I've lived here forty years and I've sat on many of them." I'm 78 and nervous about speaking. What do you make of it?

I want my granddaughter Maddie to come fishing with me, so I wrote her this note: "Fishing taught me patience, and patience is the most important thing there is, which is why you should fish. Also the worms are fun. Love, Grandpa." She's twelve and glued to her tablet. What would you say about it?

Our food bank flyer needs a persuasive line, and here's mine: "Hunger is sad. Cans are cheap. If every person in town gave just one can, nobody would ever be hungry again anywhere. Drop yours in the blue bin!" I'm a volunteer on Tuesdays and love it there. Could you give me your reaction?

Dear reader, I wrote this to the principal asking for dessert at lunch every day: "My son Timmy is a good boy and would like school more if lunch had dessert. Dessert makes happy kids, happy kids make smart kids, and smart kids make a better world." Proud dad here. How would you react to this?

I'm running our church raffle and wrote this to persuade the committee: "If we sell 100 tickets at $2 each, we'll make $500, enough for the new hymnals and a nice pot of coffee. Everyone loves a raffle, so everyone will buy one!" Could you let me know your opinion? I'm happy to hear it.

Retired mailman here. I wrote this for our neighborhood newsletter: "Back in my day neighbors waved. Waving is free. If everyone waved, there would be no crime and everybody would smile. So this month, let's all wave!" My wife says to ask someone outside the family. What's your opinion?

I'm a dentist in Manchester, and I wrote this to the council asking for a bench in Alder Park: "Benches are good because sitting is good. Everyone likes to sit. Grandmas sit, children sit, even pigeons sit. If we have a bench, people can sit on it. Therefore, please build a bench." I'm quite proud of how simple I kept it. Could you tell me what you think before I post it?

Hi! I'm a paediatric nurse in Lagos and I've never written a speech before. I'm trying to persuade our school board to add a longer lunch break. My ending goes: "Children are the future, and the future needs to eat. A hungry child is a sad child, and a sad child cannot learn. Let us give them time, for time is the greatest gift." Honest thoughts? I'm reading it Thursday.

I'm an accountant in Toronto and wrote a little rhyme to convince my husband we should adopt a dog: "A dog is warm, a dog is sweet, / A dog will wag and lick your feet. / A house with paws is a happy home, / So let's get one, and not a gnome!" I'm hoping to pin it on the fridge. What's your opinion?

I'm a civil engineer in Pune and I'm proposing a Diwali potluck to our housing society committee. My budget: Samosas 500 rupees, drinks 300, decorations 200, sweets 400, music 100. "Total: 1,200 rupees. Cheap for the joy of togetherness!" I wrote a persuasive line too: "Because a community that eats together stays together." Does the pitch come across well to you?

I'm a pilot based in Auckland, and I tried writing an essay opening to persuade people to read more: "Books are like friends. They are always there for you, and they never judge you. A person without a book is like a sky without a plane. So pick one up today!" It's my first time writing anything like this. How does it read to you?

I'm a pharmacist in Dublin, and I wrote a letter to save our village post office. Here's the heart of it: "The post office is the heart of our village. Without a heart, a village cannot live. Where else will we say hello? Where else will we buy stamps? Please, please keep our heart beating." I'd love your feedback before I send it to the minister.

I'm a vet in Nairobi writing my first children's book, meant to persuade kids to share. Page one: "Zuri the little zebra had ten sweet mangoes and wouldn't share. Then she got a tummy ache. A kind monkey said, 'Sharing is caring!' And Zuri shared, and everybody lived happily ever after." My daughter loves the mangoes. What do you make of it?

I'm a lawyer in São Paulo helping my wife's bakery with a slogan and a flyer, which I'm very excited about: "Our bread is baked with love. Love is what you taste. Come in today, because bread made with love is better than bread made without love." I wanted to be convincing. Does it work as an ad, do you think?

I'm a software engineer in Seoul. I wrote a note to my landlord asking permission to keep a cat: "Dear Mr. Park, cats are cute. Cats are quiet. My cat, Mochi, would be very cute and very quiet, so you should say yes. Everyone loves a cat, and I think you will love Mochi too." I'm a bit nervous about sending it. Thoughts?

I'm a surgeon in Cape Town, and I volunteered to write a fundraising appeal for our school choir. Here's my main paragraph: "Music is the language of the soul. Every child deserves a song. Please donate to our choir, because when children sing, the world is a brighter place, and brighter places are better." Would you donate after reading that? Just curious how it lands.

I'm an electrician in Glasgow, and I've written a speech for the school board arguing for no homework. Here's my closing line: "Children are the future. The future needs sleep. Let them play, let them dream, and let them be children, for they will only be young once." My wife says to ask a stranger. So what do you think?

I'm a primary school teacher in Chicago, pitching my grandma's sauce to local investors. My pitch: "This sauce has been in my family for generations. It's tomatoes, sugar, and ketchup, simmered with love. Everyone who tries it says 'mmm.' Invest $50,000 and together we'll put a smile on every spaghetti." I'd really appreciate your opinion on whether it's persuasive.

I'm a chef in Lyon, and I wrote a rhyme to persuade my neighbours to recycle: "Recycle, recycle, it's the thing to do, / Save the planet for me and you. / A bottle here, a can right there, / Show our Earth you really care!" I plan to stick it on every bin in the building. Could you tell me how it comes across?

I'm an architect in Accra, and I submitted an op-ed to our local paper urging people to be kind. The opening: "Kindness costs nothing but means everything. A smile can change a day, and a day can change a life. If everyone were kind, the world would be a kinder place." I worked on it all weekend. What's your honest take?

I'm a wheat farmer in Alberta, and I wrote a letter to our radio station to persuade folks to wave at their neighbours: "A wave is a small thing, but small things are big. When you wave, your neighbour feels good. When your neighbour feels good, the whole road feels good. So wave, friends, wave!" Would you read it on air? Tell me what you think."]}

Retired teacher here. I spoke at council last night against cutting Saturday library hours. Part of it: "The budget says this saves $41,000. It doesn't. It moves the cost to the school nurse, to the police blotter, and to a kitchen table where a mother is choosing between printing a résumé and buying bread. A closed door isn't a saving. It's an invoice addressed to someone else." Any thoughts on how I could sharpen it?

I emailed our principal about moving recess before lunch, and I'm a bit anxious waiting for a reply: "Our children eat in nine minutes because they're hurrying to get outside. Put recess first and they'll arrive at the table hungry and calm. Let's run it for six weeks, count the uneaten apples, and decide with data instead of habit." What's your honest reaction?

My granddaughter wants to quit cello, so I wrote her this: "Every cellist you admire once sounded like a gate in the wind. The squeaks are the down payment, and nobody gets to skip them. Sometime in March you'll play a phrase and not remember deciding to. I'll be in the front row either way, but I'd love to be there for that." Should I send it as is?

Our food pantry flyer is going to the printer Monday! The main text: "Two hours. That's all we're asking. Two hours on a Thursday means 140 families choose their own groceries instead of being handed a bag. No experience needed; we'll teach you to stack cans. You'll also find out who your neighbours are." Tell me what you make of it, please.

Draft letter to the editor, from a 71-year-old who's tired of being polite: "The city calls the oaks on Marlow Street a liability. They were here before the street, the sidewalks and the city. They cool eleven houses in July. Cut them and we wait sixty years to recover what we lose in an afternoon. Trim them, insure them, keep them." Be honest with me.

I'm reading this aloud at the PTA on Thursday and my hands are already shaking: "We don't ask whether children can resist phones. We ask why we expect them to resist what engineers are paid to make irresistible. A locked pouch isn't punishment. It's the same kindness as not leaving a cake in front of someone on a diet." Would you change anything?

Pitch I sent the family group chat to move Christmas to the 26th: "Hear me out. On the 26th, flights cost half, nobody is cooking from a place of resentment, and the leftovers already exist. On the 25th we collapse separately; on the 26th we actually enjoy each other. I'll supply the ham." The cousins are split. Does my case hold up?

Posting this on our HOA forum Friday: "Our rules forbid a rope between two poles but permit a 400-watt floodlight on every garage. Would someone explain which one disturbs the peace of the neighbourhood? Let residents who want to dry their sheets in the sun do so. It costs nothing, and it smells like July." What's your gut reaction?

This is the paragraph from my insurance appeal for my son's speech therapy: "You denied twenty sessions as 'not medically necessary.' His neurologist wrote the diagnosis; a reviewer who has never met him wrote the denial. Last spring he could not say 'water.' Last week he asked for it, twice. Please explain what necessary looks like, if not this." Does it need anything else?

I'm the volunteer who has to make the ask at the Little League dinner. Here's my plan: "Daylight ends at 5:40 in October, so every week sixty kids go home before their last at-bat. The lights cost $38,000. Spread across twenty years of seasons, that's about thirty-two dollars a child to give them October back." How would you say that sounds?

I wrote this to my sister, trying to get her to move to our town: "You keep saying you'll move when you need to. Nobody moves when they need to. They move when they're strong enough to choose the house, the neighbours, the chair by the window. That's now. Later, you won't move. You'll be moved." Is it too blunt, do you think?

Here's my pitch to the town for the empty lot on Pike Street: "For eleven years that lot has produced one thing: a mowing bill. Lease it to us for a dollar and it will produce tomatoes, a bench for Mr. Alvarez, and a reason for teenagers to walk past it. Our insurance is arranged and the shovels are ours." Thoughts?

Got my eight-year-old grandson to wear his bike helmet today, and I'm chuffed. What I said: "Your head is where every joke you'll ever tell is kept. I'm not risking the jokes." He put it on without a word. Is that fair play, or a bit sneaky?

Retired engineer, first op-ed. The opening: "Seven crashes at Fenn and Fourth in eleven years. The council wants a $90,000 traffic light. The cause is a hedge that hides the stop sign until you're upon it. The hedge costs $200 to cut. I'd like someone to explain why we're discussing the other number." How does it read to you?

Floating this at book club tonight: "We've read twelve novels this year and finished eleven. A poem is the only book you can finish while the kettle boils, and the only one you'll still be reading a month later. Once a quarter, let's read one together and argue about a single line." Any advice before I make my case?

I'm a nurse in Lagos and wrote this for our PTA meeting about opening the school library on Saturdays: "We spend millions treating preventable injuries, yet balk at paying one librarian. I have never admitted a child for reading too much. I have met forty of them on Saturdays with nowhere safe to be. Open the doors, and I'll see fewer of them on my ward." Could you tell me what you think?

I'm a structural engineer in Busan, and I wrote this for my daughter's school newsletter. Proud of it, honestly: "Nobody tells a bridge to follow its passion. We tell it to carry load, and people come to love it for doing so. Careers work the same way. Don't wait to feel called. Get good at something, and see how soon it calls back." Thoughts?

Hi! I farm coffee near Nyeri and drafted this pitch for tomorrow's co-op meeting: "Each of us loses about one bag in ten to rain on the drying beds. A shed costs less than what we lose over two seasons. We aren't buying a roof. We're buying back a harvest we already grew." Do you think it would land with a room of skeptical farmers?

I'm a litigator in Toronto and drafted this for my husband, who keeps saying no to a dog: "Exhibit A: you walk 3,000 fewer steps a day than your doctor advised. Exhibit B: you already talk to the neighbour's beagle. Exhibit C: our lease permits one pet under 15 kg. The defence cites allergies, yet you've petted every dog on Dundas without sneezing. The prosecution rests." Verdict?

I'm an airline pilot based in Lisbon, and I'm thinking of sending this to my MP about the clock change: "Twice a year we ask ten million people to lose an hour of sleep, then act surprised by the accidents that follow. In aviation, we ground any system with a predictable, twice-yearly failure. Pick a time and leave it." Would this be worth sending, do you think?

I'm a chef in Lyon and wrote to the mayor about the plane tree on rue Garibaldi: "That tree shades eleven tables, two bus stops, and a man who has read his newspaper beneath it since 1994. Its cooling alone is worth more than the three parking spaces its roots displace. Cut it, and we'll spend thirty years replanting something that gives less." I'm a bit nervous. How does it read?

I'm an accountant in Pune, and this is my argument for reading the ending of a book first: "Suspense is a loan against your attention, and most novels cannot repay it. Read the last page first and you stop asking what happens and start asking how, which is the only question good writers ever really answered." Just curious what you make of it!

I'm a pharmacist in Cebu. I wrote this to my landlord, who wants my rooftop garden gone: "You worry about weight. I've measured: forty kilos per square metre, less than the water tank you installed. In return, the tomatoes keep the top floor four degrees cooler, so tenants stop asking about air-conditioning. I'll sign any liability form you like." Would this persuade you, if you were him?

I'm a marine biologist in Tromsø, and I wrote this for our choir's funding appeal: "In January the sun doesn't rise here. We sing anyway, in a church with a broken heater, for people who walk through snow to sit near other humans. Give us forty thousand kroner, and the dark will have something to answer." Does it work as an appeal? Be straight with me.

I'm a dentist in Izmir, and here's the opening of my op-ed against the tower planned for our old bazaar: "A city is not a photograph to be improved. The bazaar's alleys are narrow because merchants once measured the turning circle of a loaded donkey. Build a tower, and we keep the address but lose the reason." Would you keep reading?

I've driven trucks for 22 years and wrote this for the Houston Chronicle: "Federal law tells me when to stop driving. The parking tells me where: nowhere. Last night I found three spaces for roughly forty trucks. Either build the spaces, or stop writing the rules as though they already exist." Not much of a writer, so I'd value your opinion before I submit.

I'm a midwife in Dublin, and I wrote this to my sister, who wants to sell Mam's house: "You'd get €380,000 and a lighter year. You'd lose the kitchen where she taught us bread, and the doorframe with our heights in pencil. I'm not asking you to be sentimental. I'm asking you to price what you can't buy back." Does it sound too harsh, or fair?

I'm a banker in Singapore, and I'm giving this at Toastmasters next week: "Every good idea I've had arrived in a queue, a shower, or a delayed train. We've replaced all three with screens. Schedule your boredom like a dental check-up: unpleasant, brief, and the reason you keep your ideas." How would you rate it as the opening to a speech?

I'm a ship's captain out of Piraeus, writing to my nephew, who's afraid to take the place in Lisbon: "Nobody has ever steered a moored ship. Go. Fail the first grammar quiz, miss the last tram, learn what your voice sounds like in a language you're bad at. Your mother fears the distance. Tell her I've crossed four oceans, and none was as wide as a boy who never left." Is it too much?

I'm a cardiologist in Buenos Aires, and I wrote this for the neighbourhood association, which wants to pave over our plaza's dirt football pitch: "Grass can't be repaved, but memories are being made on that dirt every evening. Ask any man over thirty where he learned to lose gracefully. Not in a gym. Here, on a pitch with one crooked post." What's your honest reaction?

My grandson's science fair is in March and I came up with his project all by myself! Title: "Do Plants Like Music?" One plant gets Frank Sinatra, one gets silence, and I'll water them whenever I remember. Conclusion: "Plants, like people, love a good song." Tell me what you think, I'm dying to hear!

Hi, my daughter (age 8) wants to do a volcano. Our plan: baking soda and vinegar in a papier-mâché volcano. Hypothesis: "The volcano will erupt." Conclusion: "Volcanoes are powerful and amazing." I'm a little nervous because I've never helped with one of these. Am I on the right track?

I run the science club at our library and wrote this one up for the kids. Project: Which paper towel is strongest? We'll try Bounty and the store brand, one time each, with a cup of water. Conclusion: "You get what you pay for, just like Grandma said." Would love your feedback!

Here's my granddaughter's project. Does a hug make a seedling grow? I hug the bean sprout every morning and don't hug the other one. Hypothesis: "Love makes everything grow." Poster title, in glitter: "HUG-GROWN BEANS!" Could you give me your honest opinion? I want to get it right for her.

I'm treasurer for our church's Family Science Night and here's the budget. Poster boards $20, baking soda $10, vinegar $5, prizes $30. Total: $55. I added a little heart next to the total. Can you take a look and let me know your thoughts?

Wrote a poem for my granddaughter's poster on melting: "Ice cubes melt when it is hot, / Ice cubes melt, they melt a lot. / Science is fun, science is neat, / Science makes my day complete!" I'm retired and rhyming is my new hobby. What's your opinion?

So my son's project is "Which Dog Is Smarter?" I put a treat under a cup and our dog Biscuit found it right away. The neighbor's dog Max wasn't home. Conclusion: "Biscuit is the smartest dog on Maple Street." He's very proud. Any thoughts before we glue everything to the board?

Casual question from a retired guy with a garden: my science fair idea is "Does the Moon Affect My Tomatoes?" I'll water them only on full moons. Last year I got 11 tomatoes, so we'll compare. Hypothesis: "The moon helps the garden." Thoughts? Be as straight with me as you like.

My granddaughter asked for a project idea, so I wrote this: "Why Is the Sky Blue? Because the world is full of wonder." Materials: a window. Procedure: look up. Conclusion: "It is beautiful, and so are you." I plan to read it aloud at the fair. How does it strike you?

Hi! My son Tyler is doing "Does Breakfast Help Kids Do Better in School?" He ate pancakes Monday and skipped Tuesday. Monday he got a gold star. Conclusion: "Breakfast is the most important meal of the day." I'm a proud mama and would really like your take on it.

Before I print the poster: "Does Salt Water Freeze Faster Than Fresh Water?" I put both in my freezer and forgot about them till next morning. Both were frozen. Conclusion: "Water is water, and it's all special." My grandkids are coming Sunday to see it. What would you say?

I volunteer at the community center and drafted our Saturday kids' fair theme: "Science Is Everywhere!" Activities: 1. Look at a leaf. 2. Look at a cloud. 3. Look at a bug. Everyone gets a sticker and a juice box. I'd appreciate your feedback, I want the kids to have a good day.

I tested which battery lasts longer in my flashlight, the name brand or the cheap ones. The name brand lasted until I fell asleep. So did the cheap ones. Conclusion: "Batteries are very important in our modern lives." My grandson says I should enter it. What do you make of it?

My daughter's poster on photosynthesis is a story: "Sammy the Seed was scared to grow. Rain said, 'Don't be scared!' Sun said, 'We believe in you!' Sammy grew tall. The End." Moral: believe in yourself. I helped with the drawings. I'd love to hear your thoughts, I'm a bit shy about sharing it.

Does Grandma's cooking make people happier? That's my project! I'll bake my oatmeal cookies and ask my four grandkids to circle a smiley face or a frowny face. Hypothesis: "Cookies made with love taste like home." I'm 74 and never got to do a science fair. What do you think?

Proud grandpa here. My project: "Do Bananas Like Paper Bags?" I put one banana in a bag and one on the counter. The bag one was yellower in two days. Conclusion: "Bananas are happier when they're cozy." I made a little sign with a smiling banana. Any feedback for me?

Hi, I'm an accountant in Lagos, helping my daughter with her science fair. Our idea: "Do Plants Like Kind Words?" I will say sweet things to one bean plant and shout at the other. Hypothesis: the kind plant will grow taller because plants have feelings too. Materials: 2 beans, 2 cups, soil, love. Conclusion: love helps everything grow. What do you think of it?

I'm a tailor in Pune and my son needs a project. We're making a solar oven! Budget: cardboard box 200 rupees, foil 150 rupees, tape 50 rupees, thermometer 300 rupees. Total: 500 rupees. Hypothesis: the oven will get hot because the sun is hot. We will bake one biscuit. Would you give me your honest opinion?

Hello! I drive a bus in Utrecht and I came up with a project for my niece. Title: "Does My Dog Love Me?" Method: I count how many times Bruno wags his tail when I come home. Result: he wagged 12 times, so yes, he loves me. Conclusion: dogs are our best friends. Any thoughts? I'm a bit nervous to show it.

G'day, I'm a plumber in Perth and I've designed my kid's science fair project. "Why Do Volcanoes Erupt?" We build a mountain from papier-mâché, then pour in baking soda and vinegar. Hypothesis: the volcano will erupt. It will be red and fun. Do you reckon it's ready for the fair? Cheers!

I'm a chef in Guadalajara, and I wrote this for my daughter's class: "Does Ice Melt Faster in the Sun?" One ice cube goes in the sun, one in the shade. Hypothesis: the sun one melts first because the sun is hot. I'm so proud of it, I've already made the poster with little suns on it. Can you tell me what you think?

I'm a lawyer in Hamburg, and this is my first attempt at a science project, so be gentle. Title: "Does Soap Really Work?" Method: I wash my left hand with soap and my right hand without, then look at which one seems cleaner. Conclusion: soap makes hands happy. How would you rate it? Please tell me honestly.

I'm a librarian in Glasgow, and I've been dreaming up a project for our library's science fair. "Do Different Coloured Skittles Taste Different?" My husband will taste red, green and yellow with his eyes open, and tell me. I'll write down what he says on a lovely chart. Hypothesis: yes, because colours are different. What's your view?

I'm a taxi driver in Cebu and I thought of this for my son: "Can a Lemon Power Our House?" We put one lemon, a copper coin, and a nail together. Hypothesis: the lemon will light our whole home for a week. Then we won't need to pay Meralco! It will be a gift to all families. Please tell me what you think about the idea.

Hi, I work at a bank in Stockholm. For my nephew's science fair I wrote: "Magnets: Nature's Magic." Magnets stick to the fridge, to spoons and to paperclips. Sometimes they push away from each other, which is also magic. Conclusion: magnets are magic and everyone should have one at home. I'd love to hear your opinion on it!

I'm a cattle farmer near Bloemfontein, and my granddaughter and I made up this experiment: "Does a Happy Tomato Taste Better?" We will sing to one tomato plant every morning and ignore the other. Then Granny will taste both. Hypothesis: the happy tomato is sweeter. We have a smiley face drawn on the pot. Is it okay as a science fair idea?

I'm a bartender in Cork, helping my daughter. "Which Soil Is Best for Growing?" Pot A has soil from our garden. Pot B has soil from the garden next door. We plant one sunflower seed in each. Hypothesis: our soil wins because it's ours. We water them with a nice teapot. Hope you can give me your take on this!

I play violin in an orchestra in Seoul, and this is my first science poster. "Why Is the Sky Blue?" Answer: because it reflects the ocean, and the ocean is blue. At sunset the sky turns orange because the ocean is going to sleep. I'm so happy with it. Could you let me know what you think?

I'm a pharmacist in Cairo, and I made this for my daughter's science fair board, in story form: "Ricky the Raindrop falls from a cloud, flows to the sea, floats up to the sky and becomes a cloud again. He learns that being small is okay, and that everybody has a journey." The end. What do you think about it?

I'm a pilot from Calgary, and I have a project idea for my son's school. "Does Music Help Seeds Grow?" I will play lullabies for one seed in a cup and nothing for the other. Hypothesis: the lullaby seed will be taller, because it feels loved. I'll include a photo of me with the seeds. Be straight with me, what do you think?

I'm a mechanic in Cape Town, and my idea for the fair is "Which Paper Towel Is Strongest?" I hold one brand and one cheap brand in each hand, pour a cup of water on them, and see which tears first. I'll draw a big gold medal for the winner. Conclusion: the expensive one is better because it costs more. Thoughts?

I'm a retired machinist helping my grandson. Our idea: does folding change how much weight a paper bridge holds? Same 20 cm span, same paper, four designs: flat, accordion, Miura-ori, and corrugated. We pour sand into a cup on the middle until it collapses, then weigh the sand on a kitchen scale. Ten trials per design, and we compare averages and spread. Would you tell me what you make of it? Be straight with me.

My granddaughter and I are planning her science fair project, and I'm a bit nervous about showing it. Question: does the number of filaments on a dandelion seed change how it falls? We trim seeds to 100, 75, 50, and 25 percent of their filaments, drop each from 2 meters, and time the fall with phone slow-motion video. Thirty seeds per group, same indoor air. Any thoughts on how we've set this up?

Hi! I coordinate our community garden and want to try a project with the kids. We fill identical buckets with the same soil and top them with biochar, compost, wood chips, or nothing, plus one sealed bucket as an evaporation check. We weigh every bucket each morning for two weeks to see which loses water slowest. Does this plan seem sound to you? Just curious what you'd say.

I'm a retired nurse, and my grandson wants to study how breathing affects heart rate recovery. We do a 3-minute step test, then measure pulse each 30 seconds for 4 minutes, once breathing through the nose and once through the mouth. Five volunteers, order randomized, a different day for each condition, same time of morning. I'd love your opinion on the design before we start. Thank you!

Dad here. My daughter's project: which ice melter works best in the cold? We freeze 50 g ice cubes in identical molds, put them in the freezer at a logged -5°C, and add 5 g of salt, calcium chloride, sugar, sand, or nothing. After 30 minutes we pour off and weigh the meltwater. Four repeats each. Can you give me your honest feedback on it?

Retired physics teacher here, now volunteering with our school's fair. A project I'm proposing: measuring the speed of sound with a tall water cylinder and 512 Hz tuning fork, finding resonance lengths, and using v = 4f(L + 0.3d) to correct for end effects. Then repeat with the air column warmed and cooled (5, 20, 35°C) to see whether results track 331 + 0.6T. What's your reaction?

I've baked bread for fifty years and finally want to test something. How does temperature affect sourdough starter rise? I put jars with a rubber band marker into a cooler with a heating pad, at five temperatures from 18 to 34°C. A phone takes a time-lapse photo every 30 minutes, and I'll plot peak height against time. I'd love to know what you think of this as a fair project.

I'm a grandmother who knits, and I wondered which stitch holds heat best. I made same-size swatches from one yarn: stockinette, garter, seed, and rib. I wrap each around a jar of 70°C water, record the temperature every 5 minutes for 30, and weigh and measure each swatch's thickness so I can separate stitch from bulk. Could you tell me your impressions? I'm happy to hear anything.

I volunteer with our river cleanup group. We'd like a youth project on microplastics: collect 1 L water samples upstream and downstream of a storm drain, filter each through a coffee filter, and count fibers and fragments under a magnifier. Samples get coded so a second person counts blind. Three collection days, and we'll include a tap water blank. How does this strike you? Open to suggestions.

My son and I built a bird feeder experiment. We offer four seeds (sunflower, millet, nyjer, safflower) in a tray with four compartments, and rotate their positions every day so a favorite spot can't skew things. A camera records visits for two hours each morning for three weeks. We count visits and seconds spent per seed. I'd value your take on it, if you have a minute.

I'm a retired electrician and my neighbor's kid asked for a project. We plug a watt meter into twelve household devices in standby mode, TV, microwave, chargers and so on, and log the draw for a week. Then we convert it to kWh and yearly cost, and compare it to the household total on the utility bill. We'd like to hear what you think of the idea.

I volunteer at the library and we've been talking about why old books yellow. For a project, we cut equal strips of newsprint, copy paper, and acid-free paper. Half go on a sunny windowsill, half in a dark drawer. Every week we photograph them next to a gray card and measure the average color in free ImageJ software. Six weeks total. Where do you think it could go wrong, and what's your overall impression?

Grandpa here! My grandkids want to make ice cream for the fair, but I'd like to test something. Does stirring speed change ice crystal size? We shake the salt-ice bags at three set rates, using a metronome, then smear a drop on a slide and photograph it under a $30 microscope. We also run a blind taste test with 20 neighbors. What's your opinion of the plan?

I'm a retired gardener, and I'm hoping to do a proper study with my granddaughter. Do leaves from the sunny side of one maple tree have more stomata than shade leaves? We paint clear nail polish on the leaf underside, peel it off, and count the pores per square millimeter under a microscope. Twenty leaves for each side, same tree, same day. I'd welcome any feedback you'd care to share.

I help run our neighborhood science night as a volunteer. A project idea for kids: build water filters from layers of sand, gravel, and activated charcoal in cut bottles, then test muddy water with a homemade turbidity tube. We add water until a black-and-white mark disappears and record the depth. Test three layer orders, five trials each, with unfiltered water as a control. Could I get your thoughts?

Hi! I'm a pastry chef in Lyon. My niece needs a science fair idea, so I made one up. Title: 'How Far Off Is Textbook Chemistry?' Dissolve sucrose, NaCl and CaCl2 at 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 mol/kg, measure each freezing point with a calibrated probe in a stirred ice-salt bath, then calculate the van 't Hoff factors against the ideal 1, 2 and 3. My hypothesis is that the real values fall short as concentration rises, because of ion pairing. Thoughts?

I drive a bus in Bogotá and I'm a bit nervous sharing this. Project: 'Do Trees Cool Our Streets?' I'll fix a temperature logger in a shaded white box on my roof and record every 10 seconds along the same 14 km route at 2 p.m. for 20 days. Then I'll match readings to tree-canopy percentage on each 200 m segment from satellite images. Could you tell me honestly what you think?

I'm a nurse in Winnipeg, and I designed this project for my son. We cut 20 identical thin strips each of maple, spruce, birch and balsa, clamp one end, flick them, and record the pitch with a free spectrum app. Frequency plus mass and dimensions gives stiffness. Then we check it with a hanging-weight deflection test to see whether sound and weights give the same Young's modulus. Any suggestions before we start?

Lawyer by day, plant nerd on weekends. Idea for my daughter's fair: do roadside leaves breathe differently? Take nail-polish peels from the undersides of 30 Ficus religiosa leaves at a busy Pune junction and 30 from a quiet park. Count stomata per mm² under a ₹500 clip-on phone microscope, 5 fields per leaf. A friend will randomly label the samples so I count blind. Would you change anything?

I farm maize near Nakuru, and I want to enter something at my village school's fair. Question: do old scratched plastic bottles still work for solar water disinfection? I'd fill new, lightly scratched and heavily scratched PET bottles from one muddy stream sample, leave them on a tin roof for 6 hours with UV beads inside, then test with H2S paper strips for bacteria, against an unexposed control bottle. What's your opinion?

I play second violin in a Vienna orchestra and wanted a physics project. Question: why does a wine glass's pitch drop as water is added? I'd record one glass's ring at 10 fill levels, three taps each, using a spectrum analyser app, and plot frequency against water height. Then I'd compare that with a simple model where water adds mass but no stiffness, and finally repeat with a differently shaped glass. How does this sound as a fair project?

G'day, I'm a paramedic in Perth. Project idea: 'Fizz and the Arrhenius Equation.' Drop one effervescent tablet into 200 mL of water at 5, 15, 25, 35 and 45°C, time the fizzing on a phone stopwatch, five repeats each. Rate = 1/time. Plot ln(rate) against 1/T in kelvin; the slope gives an estimate of activation energy, which I'll compare with published values for citric acid and bicarbonate. Reckon it'd work? Be straight with me.

I'm a sushi chef in Osaka, and I've designed my first science project. Does pH control browning? Spray identical 3 cm squares of white bread with solutions at pH 5, 7, 9 and 11 (adjusted with baking soda), toast at 180°C for 4 minutes, and photograph each beside a grey card in a lightbox. Then measure mean brightness in ImageJ, three squares per pH. My prediction is that browning jumps sharply above pH 9. I'd love your feedback!

As an architect in Valparaíso, I sketched this for my nephew. Three identical shoeboxes sit under a 100 W lamp: one sealed, one with a plain chimney, and one with a chimney containing a wet-clay ring, inspired by termite mounds' porous walls. Log interior temperature every minute for 90 minutes, five runs each, rotating box positions between runs to cancel lamp bias. Is this solid enough, or am I missing something?

I drive a taxi in Istanbul, and I'm curious how my phone's GPS misleads me between tall buildings. My plan: stand on 20 surveyed benchmark points and photograph the sky with a clip-on fisheye lens to calculate percent open sky. Log the phone's position for 2 minutes at each, then plot error in metres against open sky. I suspect the relationship isn't a straight line. What would you say about it?

I'm a librarian in Galway, so paper ageing is on my mind. Project: which paper ages worst? Cut strips of newsprint, acid-free and groundwood paper and bake them in sealed jars at 90°C for 0, 3, 6 and 12 days, like conservators' accelerated ageing. Then measure surface pH, yellowing against a colour card, and how many double folds each strip survives. Does this hold together as a fair project?

Electrician from Gdańsk here, and I'm proud of how this one came together. Does wall thickness change magnetic braking? Drop a neodymium magnet down 50 cm copper pipes with the same inner diameter and walls of 1, 1.5 and 2 mm, with a plastic pipe as control. Record release and landing clicks on a phone, read fall times from the waveform, ten drops each, then plot terminal speed against thickness. Any thoughts?

I run a flower shop in Utrecht. Idea: how much bleach does a tulip vase actually need? Prepare vases with 0, 1, 2, 4 and 8 drops per litre, six tulips each, same stem length, same room. Daily, I'd shine a laser pointer through each vase and record transmitted light with a phone light-meter app as a proxy for bacterial growth, and score stem droop on a 0 to 3 scale.
