I'm a bit anxious about sharing it. What do you think?

I teach primary school in Sendai, and I've been wondering about geology. My question: "Can the rotation of stone lanterns in Tohoku shrine grounds serve as a low-cost seismometer for mapping 2011 ground motion, and how well does it match K-NET station records?" I'd be glad to hear your opinion.

I'm an airline pilot in Gothenburg, and my housing co-op argues constantly about the laundry room. So I wrote this: "Does replacing booked laundry slots with first-come access reduce neighbour conflict, or just relocate it to the stairwell?" Half joking, half serious. What's your view?

I'm a pharmacist in Lagos, and music history is my passion project. Here's my research question: "How did 1950s highlife bandleaders adapt to the three-minute 78rpm limit, and do surviving recordings show shorter solos than newspaper reviews describe in live performances?" Please tell me what you make of it.

I'm a surgeon in Cairo with an amateur interest in archaeology. My question: "Did the volumes of Old Kingdom bread moulds at Giza vary by workforce rank, implying tiered rations, and can the variation be separated from regional pottery standards?" I'd appreciate your honest impression.

I'm an electrician in Valparaíso, and I've been mapping staircases for fun. My question: "How do the informal staircases of Valparaíso's hills get their names, and do names tied to a person outlast names tied to a function across fifty years of municipal maps?" Does it seem worth pursuing? What do you think?

I'm a vet in the Scottish Borders, and I also play the pipes. I wrote this: "Do bagpipe learners who first learn tunes on the chanter by ear, rather than from notation, make fewer note-level errors but more phrase-level substitutions when recalling them a month later?" Would love your thoughts, since research design isn't my thing.

Hi! I'm 74 and I came up with an app for my grandkids. It's called Hug Me. You press a big red heart and a picture of a teddy bear giving a hug pops up, with the words "Grandma loves you to the moon and back." That's the whole app! I'd love to hear your honest thoughts before I ask my grandson to build it.

Retired postman here, first time sharing an idea like this. My app is called Umbrella Pal. You open it and it asks, "Will it rain today?" Then it says, "Look out the window and see!" I'm quite proud of it. Could you tell me what you make of it? Be gentle, please, I'm new to all this.

I'm a mom of three and I've been dreaming up an app called Chore Star. Kids tap a button when they finish a chore and get a gold star. Ten stars means a trip for ice cream. Simple and sweet! Everyone in my family loves the idea. What would you change, or does it work as is?

I volunteer at our church food pantry and drew up a plan for an app. Costs: building it $500, phone fees $100, advertising $50. Money coming in: bake sale $200, donations $100, and my husband's $150, so we'll have $100 left over for cans! Does this plan look all right to you? Thanks so much.

I'm a grandpa who loves a good laugh. My app, Grandpa's Joke of the Day, sends one joke every morning. Day one: "Why did the chicken cross the road? To get to the other side!" Day two: "What do you call a sleeping bull? A bulldozer." I have 365 planned. Tell me what you think, friend!

My family's recipe app is almost ready, and I wanted to share the first recipe. Grandma Ruth's Famous Sandwich: two slices of bread, one slice of ham, one slice of cheese, a little butter. Put it together and enjoy! The app will have lots more like it. Does this seem like something people would download?

I wrote the first story for my bedtime app for toddlers. "Sleepy the Bear was tired but wouldn't share his honey. Then his friends were sad. So Sleepy shared, and everyone said, 'Sharing is caring!' The end. Goodnight, Sleepy." Each night would have a new bear story. I'm a bit nervous. Any thoughts?

Hello, I run our neighborhood watch picnic and had an idea. An app called Neighbor Wave! At 5pm your phone buzzes and says "Go say hello to a neighbor today!" That's all it does, but it could bring our street together. Curious what you'd say about it. I'm not very techy, so be kind!

I'm retired and spend my mornings with coffee and my gratitude list, so I designed an app around it. Every day you type one thing you're thankful for. My examples are "sunshine," "family," and "good health." There'd be a little sun picture on the screen. Would love your feedback if you have a moment!

My granddaughter says I should make an app, so here goes! It's called Birthday Buddy and it sends a rhyme on someone's special day: "Roses are red, violets are blue, it's your birthday, and I love you!" I wrote it myself last night. I'd really like to know what you think of it.

I help run our community garden and wrote up a funding plan for a plant-swap app. Costs: developer $2,000. Income: four local sponsors at $300 each is $1,500, plus selling tomato seedlings for $200. So we'd make a profit of $300! I'm so excited to get this going. Can you take a look and tell me your opinion?

Dad of two here. I've got an app idea called Lost Sock Finder! You tap "Find My Sock" and it says, "Check the dryer!" If you tap it again, it says, "Or under the bed!" I came up with it while folding laundry. Just wondering what you'd say about it. Any feedback welcome!

Been fishing for 50 years and made up an app called Fishing Luck. You open it and it tells you if the fish are biting. It says either "Maybe!" or "Maybe not!" and I added a cute little cartoon fish. I'm pretty proud of how it turned out. What do you reckon?

I'm 68 and miss writing letters, so I thought up Pen Pal Plus. You type a letter on your phone, press send, and it goes to your friend as a text message. I start mine with "Dear friend, I hope this finds you well." It feels very old-fashioned and warm to me. How does the idea strike you?

I'm a mom and church volunteer, and my app is called Kindness Counter. You tap a button each time you're kind, and it counts up. The screen says, "Be nice, because it's the right thing to do!" I want to give it to our Sunday school kids. Could you tell me your thoughts? Thank you!

I'm a dentist in Curitiba, and I designed my first app idea! It's called Hug Buddy. Every hour your phone shows a big pink heart and says: "Time for a hug! Hugs make the world go round." You tap the heart when you've hugged someone, and it counts your hugs. Price: free. Could you tell me what you think?

Hello from Leeds. I'm a tax accountant, and I've sketched an app for my grandkids. It's "Sunny the Water Cup." A cartoon cup smiles when you drink water and cries when you don't. Slogan: "Drink up, don't be blue, Sunny's thirsty for you!" That's the whole app. Would love your honest opinion.

I'm a civil engineer in Gdańsk and I made a business plan for my app, Cozy Recipes. Price: $1 per download. Goal: 100 downloads a month, so $1,000 monthly income. Costs: $50 a month. So after one year I'll earn $12,000 and be able to quit my job. Does this look reasonable? Any feedback is welcome!

Hi all, I'm a long-haul pilot from Auckland and I've been dreaming up an app during layovers. It's called Dear Mum. You press one big button and it texts your mum "Thinking of you, love always." That's it, one button. I figure mums everywhere would love it. What do you reckon?

I'm a pharmacist in Lagos, and I've got an idea for a bedtime story app for children. Story one: Timmy the Turtle is always late, until he learns that slow and steady wins the race. The end. Then a gold star appears. I'd planned 365 stories like this. Please tell me your thoughts.

Hey, I'm a trauma nurse in Toronto and I made up an app on night shift lol. "Compliment Jar." You shake your phone and it says things like "You are a shining star!" or "Believe in yourself, you can do anything!" Shake again for another one. Thinking of charging $4.99. Thoughts? Be real with me.

I'm a structural engineer in Pune, and I'd like your opinion on my app, Grandma's Garden. It reminds you to water your plants. The notification says: "Roses are red, violets are blue, your plants are thirsty, and they need you!" Every day, same rhyme. I'm planning to add a second rhyme next year. What do you think?

I'm a high-school chemistry teacher in Cork and I've written the pitch for my first app! "Thankful Thursday": every Thursday it asks, "What are you thankful for?" You type one answer. It saves it in a list called My Blessings. Family, health, and sunshine are the suggested answers. Would you download it? Please tell me your thoughts.

I'm a corporate lawyer in Nairobi and, for fun, I've designed Chore Stars for my kids. Child cleans room, gets a gold star. Ten stars gets a trophy picture on the screen. Parents get a notification saying, "Great job, parent!" I haven't named a price yet. How would you improve it, if at all?

I'm an architect in Osaka. My app idea is Good Morning Sunshine. Every morning at 6:00 it says: "Rise and shine, today is a gift, that's why it's called the present!" Then it shows a picture of a sunrise. I'd like to add a picture of a kitten on Fridays. Please let me know your opinion.

I'm a cardiologist in Buenos Aires, and I've been working on my idea for a neighbourhood app in my free time. Name: Hola Vecino. You tap "Say Hello" and a message goes to everyone on your street: "Hello neighbour! Have a lovely day!" I imagine everyone becoming friends. Does it seem like something people would use?

I'm a long-distance bus driver in Manitoba, and I made up an app idea for dog lovers. It's "Walkies!" You press Start and it draws paw prints on the screen while you walk. At the end it says "Good dog!" even if you don't have a dog. I'm giving it away free. What's your opinion?

I'm a veterinarian in Cape Town and I'm sharing the budget for my app, Kind Words Daily. Development: R20,000. Marketing: R5,000. Expected earnings in first year: R10,000. After that, I'm sure the money will come rolling in because kindness never goes out of style. Could you give me your feedback on this plan?

I'm an oncologist in Seoul. My app is called Mom's Kimchi Soup. It has one recipe: kimchi, water, tofu, and salt, boil for 10 minutes. My mother made it for me when I was sick. I want to sell it for $2.99, with a photo of the pot. Could you tell me your opinion? I'd like to add more recipes later.

I'm a surgeon from Glasgow, and I've drawn up a wee app for a charity project. It's called Smile Today. You open it and it displays a big yellow smiley face, with the words: "Every cloud has a silver lining." You can tap for a new proverb, like "Home is where the heart is." Let me know what you think, please.

I drove a city bus for 31 years, and I've sketched an app for riders with memory loss. Their phone learns their usual route. Family only gets an alert if they wander more than 200 metres off it for five minutes. No constant map tracking, so they keep some dignity. Otherwise it stays silent. Does that balance of safety and privacy hold up? Honest thoughts welcome.

Hi! My granddaughter helped me build a mockup. The app is for family recipes. When I cook, she films my hands. For vague measures like "a handful of flour," the app asks me to hold my hand next to a printed scale card. It saves that handful in grams, so my cooking still reads like me but anyone can repeat it. What's your opinion?

I'm a dad of two under four, and I had an idea at 3am. It's an app for co-parents called Handoff. One screen, no chat. Last nap, last meal, mood, and one thing to watch. When the other parent taps "got them," the screen clears itself. Nothing to scroll back through. Would you use it? Be straight with me, I can take it.

I coordinate volunteers at our food bank, and I'd love your feedback on this. A bakery taps one button at closing: "bread, about 12 loaves." The nearest volunteer with a car gets one push notification. First to accept has a 30-minute pickup window, and the app creates the donation receipt automatically. If nobody accepts in ten minutes, it widens the radius. What am I missing?

Retired carpenter here, 44 years on job sites. My app idea: I say "forty-two and three-eighths" out loud, and it logs the measurement. Then it builds a cut list that fits every piece onto standard board lengths with the least waste, and shows the saw kerf in the sums. Greasy hands, no typing. Tell me what you reckon, mate.

I'm 74 and I've kept bird notes on my porch for twelve years. My app, Porch Log, wouldn't identify birds, since plenty of apps already do that. It would record the first-arrival date of each species at my address, compare it with my earlier years, and export it for our local naturalist society. Over time it shows how spring is shifting on my own street. Thoughts?

My son has a severe peanut allergy, and playdates make me anxious. So I designed Playdate Pass. I text the host parent a link to a one-page card with his allergens, where the epinephrine pen is, three steps for what to do, and photos of snack labels that are safe. The link expires after 24 hours. Would other parents use this? I'd really value your take.

I'm a retired teacher, and my grandchildren live four time zones away. In my app, I read a picture book aloud, and it records my voice and when I turn each page. Later the child opens it, and the words light up in time with me. If I laugh or stumble, that stays in too. Please tell me what you think of the idea.

I help run our community garden, and watering rotas are a nightmare. My idea is an app that checks the forecast. If more than 5mm of rain is due, it cancels the day's shifts and sends volunteers a thank-you. If a shift is unclaimed by 6pm the night before, it texts the volunteer who lives closest. Be gentle, but be honest. How would you improve it?

I delivered mail for 28 years and noticed who stopped collecting theirs. My app idea is a daily one-tap "I'm up." If it isn't tapped by 10am, two chosen neighbours get a text with the wording: "Just checking in, no need to reply if you're fine." It's for neighbours, not far-off family. Would it work in real life? I'm curious what you'd change.

I'm a mum of an autistic eight-year-old, and new places can overwhelm him. I'm designing an app called Before We Go. Parents upload photos of a venue's entrance, the loud spots, and the quiet exits. It builds a picture preview with a countdown to leaving. Other families can add to the same venue. Could you give me feedback on how I've set this up?

I was an accountant for 40 years, and now I live on a fixed income. My app, Envelope, copies the old cash-envelope method but shows only one number on screen: "$14.20 a day for 11 days." Spending anything moves the number and nothing else. No charts or categories. What do you think of the approach? I'd like a second pair of eyes.

I've been knitting for 60 years, and my granddaughter says someone should make this. You photograph your swatch beside a ruler. The app counts stitches and rows per inch, then rewrites the pattern for your own yarn and needles, so the sweater fits even when your tension runs tight. Does that sound useful to you, or am I living in the past?

I tutor adult English learners at the library. I'd like an app where I record a sentence and the learner repeats it. It would show our two voices as overlaid rhythm waves, with no score and no red marks. It would only show whether the stress and pauses line up, because that's what gets people understood. I'd welcome any feedback. How would you tighten it?

I'm a retired firefighter, and I volunteer with our emergency preparedness group. My app is called Go Bag. You enter your address, and it gives seasonal checklists for the risks there, like wildfire or flood. On clock-change days it reminds you to rotate batteries and water. Neighbours who opt in can flag that they'd need a ride in an evacuation. What's your opinion?

Hey! I'm a civil engineer in Kumasi and I've been sketching an app at weekends. It's called Trotro Whisper. Riders tap the stop where they got on and off, and phones on the same minibus sync those taps over Bluetooth, so no data is needed. When any phone finds signal it uploads, and routes and usual fares build up street by street. Drivers never have to join. Would love to hear what you think, especially if you spot holes.

I'm a dentist in Tromsø, so apps are far outside my world, and I'm a bit nervous sending this. It's called Same Sky. I made it for my mother and me, living far apart. There are no messages. The screen shows the real sky colour where the other person is, with a small dot for them. Press the dot and their phone gives a slow, warm vibration, like a hand on the shoulder. That's all it does. What's your honest opinion?

I'm an accountant in Nakuru and I'm proud of this one. Farmers speak into a basic phone in Kikuyu or Swahili: "Bought two bags of fertiliser, 6,400." The app logs it as a ledger entry. Each Sunday evening it phones them and reads the week aloud: money in, money out, and which expense grew most. No smartphone or reading needed. It runs on voice and USSD. Where would you take it next?

I am a pharmacist in Sendai. My app idea is for elderly people who cannot remember whether they took their pills. Each morning they photograph their weekly pill organiser. The app checks that yesterday's compartment is empty. If it is, nothing happens, so there are no nagging alarms. Only if it is still full does it quietly message one named family member. I wanted to protect dignity as well as safety. May I ask for your opinion and suggestions?

I'm a firefighter in Porto Alegre, and after the floods I couldn't stop thinking about this. It's called Rota Seca. Residents photograph the water against a numbered marker painted on their nearest lamppost. The app reads the level from the photo, and the map colours each street: passable on foot, passable by truck, or closed. It refreshes every few minutes. We'd paint the poles ourselves. What's your honest take?

Electrician from Winnipeg here, never built an app before. Every panel I open has labels like "misc" and "plugs?", so I came up with Panel Map. The homeowner flips a breaker and walks around with their phone. The app asks "What went dead?" and they tap a room or say it aloud. After a few flips it produces a clean directory laid over their floor plan. It even flags the fridge circuit by listening for the compressor stopping. Thoughts?

I'm a tax lawyer in Kraków, and my sister asked me to read her rental lease, which gave me this idea. You scan any lease and the app compares each clause with default Polish tenancy law. It highlights only the clauses where the landlord has deviated, and shows the likely yearly cost to you in złoty. Everything else stays grey. Do you think people would use it? Any feedback is welcome.

I teach physics at a school in Chennai, and here's my app idea for my students. It's called Pendulum Map. They hang their phone from a string, swing it, and the accelerometer measures the period to calculate g. Results from schools in different countries are pinned to a world map, so students can watch g rise from the equator towards the poles. The app also shows how much error their own swing introduced. Would love your thoughts!

I'm a surgeon in Hamburg and I sleep badly, so I designed this. It's called Handover. At night you say up to three worries aloud. The app answers "Held until 9:00" and locks them away. At nine it returns them one by one and asks "Still true?" Over the months it shows what percentage of your worries evaporated overnight. I've tested it on index cards with my wife. Could you give me your opinion?

I'm a chef in Mexico City and I've got an app idea for my building, nothing fancy. You tap what you're missing for dinner, say one lime or a spoonful of tahini. The app finds a neighbour within 200 metres who has it and is happy to spare a little. You return the favour with a portion of whatever you cook, and it keeps a friendly tally. Basically "borrow a cup of sugar" for the phone age. What do you reckon?

I'm a paramedic in Perth, and I've seen too many hiker rescues start late. My idea is called Breadcrumb. You set a check-in time. The phone logs your route without signal, and at check-in it tries to send a tiny text of coordinates, retrying whenever it catches even one bar. If you miss the check-in, your contact receives your last known point and your average walking pace. Could you tell me what you think?

I'm a midwife in Lagos. I designed Mama Alert for women who struggle to read. Each day she taps pictures: a headache, swollen feet, blurry sight, the baby moving less. Colours stack up, and when certain combinations turn red the phone speaks in Yoruba, Igbo or Hausa and offers to call the nearest clinic, sending her location. I'm excited but nervous about showing it. What would you change?

I'm a vet in Busan who has wandered into app design. Light Hours is for flat-hunters. You type an address and floor, and the app uses 3D building data to show how many hours of direct sun each window gets through the year, including shadows from the tower across the road. Winter is shown in blue, summer in gold. I'd really appreciate your feedback.

I'm a librarian in Gothenburg and this is my first app idea. It's called Borrowed Time. It lists the books in your local library by how long they've sat unborrowed. You can "adopt" the loneliest one: the app plays a ten-minute reading of its first chapter, then shows a short note from a librarian on why they loved it. Reserve it with one tap. Does it sound like something you'd open? Be as honest as you like.

I fly regional jets out of Casablanca, and I've been scribbling this app idea between flights. Gate Walk is for anxious passengers. Using the flight timetable, the phone's barometer and its motion sensors, it narrates in a calm voice what's happening: "That thump is the landing gear." "This shaking is normal air over the mountains." It also tells you how many minutes of turbulence are likely. Does it make sense to you?

I'm giving a speech at my sister-in-law Carol's retirement party on Friday. Here it is: "Carol, thirty years is a long time. You were the heart of this office. Time flies when you're having fun, and now it's time to put your feet up. You've earned it. Every cloud has a silver lining, and yours is a beach chair. Enjoy every minute!" What do you think?

I'm a volunteer firefighter and I wrote a little poem for Big Dave's send-off Saturday: "Dave, Dave, you were so brave, / Forty years the fire you'd save. / Now you'll fish and nap and rest, / Because you are simply the best!" Any thoughts before I read it to the whole crew?

My retirement party is next week and I have to say a few words. Here's what I've written: "I started here in 1989 with a lunchbox and a dream. Now I leave with a lot of memories. You aren't coworkers, you're family. Thank you for everything. I'll never forget you." Could you give me your honest opinion?

ok so I'm doing the toast for my dad's retirement dinner. here's the draft: "Dad, you worked hard every single day so we could have everything. You're the rock of our family. Now it's your time to shine. Here's to the best dad in the world!" thoughts? my kids say Grandpa will cry either way lol

I'm the PTA mom asked to speak for Mrs. Higgins, who is retiring after 32 years of teaching. I wrote: "Mrs. Higgins, you didn't just teach our children their ABCs, you taught them to reach for the stars. Teachers plant seeds, and you've watched a whole garden grow. We will miss you more than words can say." What's your opinion?

I've never spoken in front of people before, and I'm a bit nervous. I'm saying this for Margie at the food bank: "Margie, you gave and gave and never asked for anything. You are a ray of sunshine on a cloudy day. The world needs more people like you. Thank you for your heart of gold." Would you tell me what you think of it?

Our neighbor Stan is retiring from the post office after 38 years, and I'm saying a few words at the barbecue: "Stan, you delivered the mail through rain, sleet and snow. Now you can deliver yourself to the golf course! You'll always be stamped in our memories. No return to sender!" What do you make of it, friends?

My wife Linda is retiring from nursing after forty years, and I'm speaking at her party. I wrote: "Linda, you cared for everyone but yourself. You're an angel in scrubs. Now it's your turn to be taken care of, and I'm happy to do it. I love you more today than the day we met." How does it read to you?

Our Little League coach is hanging up his whistle, and as board secretary I'm saying a few words: "Coach Bill, you taught us it's not whether you win or lose, it's how you play the game. You made every kid feel like a champion. Thanks for the memories. You hit it out of the park!" Can I get your feedback?

I'm a grandmother and I volunteered at the library for twenty years. At my own farewell tea I plan to say: "Books are like friends, and I've made so many here. Every story has an ending, but this is really a new chapter. Thank you for the happy times. Don't forget to keep reading!" What do you think?

Writing a speech for my brother Ron's retirement from the plant. Here goes: "Ron, you got up at 5 a.m. every day for 41 years without complaining. Hard work never hurt anybody. Now you can sleep in! You're a good man and a great brother. Congratulations, and here's to the golden years!" Thoughts?

I drove the school bus for 27 years and the kids put together a party. This is my goodbye: "Round and round the wheels have gone, / Many years I've driven on. / Kids, remember what I say: / Buckle up and have a nice day!" I'd love to hear your opinion.

I'm giving a speech for our hospice volunteer coordinator, Joan, at our potluck. "Joan, you showed us that it's the little things that matter. You always had a smile and a cup of tea. Life is a journey, not a destination, and you made the journey brighter for everyone. We love you dearly." What are your thoughts?

My daughter is retiring from the bank, and I get to say a few words as her mum. "Susan, I remember when you were just a little girl counting your pennies. Now look at you! Where did the time go? I'm so proud. Money can't buy happiness, but you've got plenty of that." Could you tell me what you think?

After 40 years of teaching, here's what I'll say at my party: "Teaching isn't a job, it's a calling. I came for the paycheck and stayed for the children. They say you can't take it with you, but I'm taking every memory. Thank you, and remember: the best is yet to come." Please tell me what you think.

I'm a dentist in Utrecht and my colleague Hans retires Friday. I'm giving this toast: "Hans, you've been a rock. Thirty years of fillings, thirty years of smiles. Time flies when you're having fun! You're not just a colleague, you're family. Now go enjoy the golden years, you've earned them. Don't be a stranger!" Could you tell me your thoughts before Friday?

Hello, I'm a civil engineer in Lagos and I've never written a speech before. Our supervisor Mrs. Adeyemi retires next week. Here's what I have: "Today we say goodbye to a woman who built bridges, both literally and in our hearts. She was the foundation of this office. Every ending is a new beginning. May your retirement be as solid as concrete." Is this okay to read out?

So my buddy Gord's retiring from the fire hall and I got stuck with the speech. Here's my go: "Gord, you've put out a lot of fires, but you never put out the fire in your heart. Thirty-five years and you never let us down. Time to hang up the hose and put your feet up. Hope you catch lots of fish!" Thoughts?

Proud of this one! I'm a vet in Brisbane and I wrote a poem for our receptionist Maureen's retirement: "Maureen, Maureen, the best we've seen, / You kept the front desk neat and clean. / Now it's time to rest and play, / We'll miss you more every day!" I'm reading it at the party Saturday. What do you reckon?

I'm a chartered accountant in Pune, and I wrote a few lines for Mr. Iyer's farewell: "Mr. Iyer, you were our balance sheet's greatest asset. Your career has been all credit and no debit. Today we close the books, but your memory stays on our ledger forever." Please give me your honest opinion before I print it on the card.

I'm a GP in Glasgow, and our practice nurse Isobel is retiring. I'd like to say a few words: "Isobel has been the heart of this surgery. She took our blood pressure, but she also took our hearts. Nobody can fill her shoes. Well, maybe her wee slippers! Enjoy your retirement, Isobel, you deserve it." Would you change anything?

I'm an electrician in Hamburg, and I'm speaking at Uwe's retirement lunch tomorrow. This is my speech: "Uwe, you always lit up our days. You were the brightest bulb on the team. Now it's time to switch off and recharge. We'll always remember the sparks. Thank you for being such a bright light!" Does it work for a party, do you think?

I'm an airline pilot based in São Paulo, and I'm giving a speech for Captain Rui. "Rui, after forty years of smooth flights, you are finally coming in to land. Life is a journey, and you have been a wonderful captain. Now fasten your seatbelt for the best trip of all: retirement. Safe travels, my friend!" I'd love to hear what you think.

I'm a pharmacist in Nairobi and my dad is retiring from teaching after 38 years. I'm giving a toast at his party: "Dad, you taught thousands of children, but the best lesson you taught me was love. A teacher plants seeds, and now you can sit back and watch the garden grow. Thank you for everything." Can you tell me how it reads?

I manage logistics at a warehouse in Ohio, and I'm doing a speech for Linda, who's been with us 31 years. "Linda, you've been our road map, always showing us the way. You delivered every time, on time. Now it's your turn to cruise down the highway of life. We'll miss you more than words can say." Does it flow okay?

I'm a surgeon in Wellington, and I've been asked to say a few words for Bill, our hospital caretaker, who's retiring. "Bill, you kept this place spotless for 27 years. You always had a smile and a kind word. You are the unsung hero of this hospital. Enjoy your well-earned rest, mate." Any feedback would be appreciated.

I'm a solicitor in Cork, and my local postman Seamus is retiring. I've written this for the party: "Seamus delivered our letters for forty years, rain or shine, and he delivered smiles too. He's a true gentleman. Now at last he can return to sender every alarm clock. Go n-éirí an bóthar leat, Seamus!" What's your view on it?

I'm a software engineer in Tokyo writing in English for our manager Tanaka-san's retirement party. "Tanaka-san, you are the bug-free code of our team. Today we push your retirement to production. There will be no rollback! Thank you for your guidance and your kindness. We hope life's next version is even better." Please let me know what you think.

I'm a physiotherapist in Kraków and our school cook, Pani Halina, retires this month. I'm saying: "Pani Halina, your soup warmed our hearts for thirty years. You fed the children with love, and love is the best ingredient. Today the kitchen closes, but your kindness will always stay on the menu." Do you have any thoughts about it?

I'm a banker in Singapore and our office driver, Uncle Lim, is retiring. I'd like to read this at his party: "Uncle Lim, you drove us safely for thirty years. Life is a journey, not a destination, and you made every journey happy. Now it's time to park the car and enjoy the ride. We'll miss you always!" What do you make of it?

Friday's my retirement party after 34 years on Route 12, and I'm giving a short toast. Here it is: "I know which dogs bite, which widows watch the window, and which porches changed hands after funerals. I never read your mail. I just read your lives, a little, from the sidewalk. Thank you for letting me walk through them. Tomorrow, Rufus at number 40 finally wins." Any thoughts before I stand up and say it?

My husband Walt retires from his carpentry shop next week, and I'm giving the speech since he won't. Here's the middle bit: "Walt measures twice and cuts once. Every door he ever hung closes softly, as if afraid of waking someone. It took me forty-one years of marriage to notice that's how he does everything, including love." Thoughts? Be as blunt as you like, I'm a big girl.

I'm speaking at Dolores's retirement from the food bank, 22 years of Tuesdays. My closing: "Dolores never asked anyone why they came. She asked whether they wanted the good bread or the better bread, and it was the same bread. Nobody left as a case number. They left having been offered a choice. That's what the rest of us are still learning to give." What's your honest opinion?

I'm nervous about Saturday. It's my own retirement party after 31 years of teaching fourth grade. My opening: "Thirty-one years ago I told a room of nine-year-olds that fractions were easy. I lied. Maya believed me anyway, and now she designs bridges. I'd ask everyone to cross the river tonight with quiet gratitude for my dishonesty." Would you tell me how it comes across? I keep fiddling with it.

My daughter Ines retires from nursing this month after 38 years, and I've been given two minutes as her father. I'd say: "When Ines was six, she bandaged every toy in the house, even the ones that weren't hurt, just in case. We called it a phase. It was a forecast. Thousands of patients later, I can report that she still can't leave a teddy bear unattended." How does it read to you?

Retiring from the number 9 bus after 27 years. Here's the speech, all of it: "I've driven the distance to the moon and back, mostly at fourteen miles an hour. I delivered four thousand kids to school, and a few of them back to me as adults with children of their own. I never got anywhere myself. I got everyone else there. I'd do it again, but the knee won't." Honest feedback welcome, grandkids just say 'cool, Pop.'

Our fire chief Hal is hanging up his helmet and I'm the one doing the toast. Here's the heart of it: "Hal's first rule of fire: buildings are replaceable, people aren't. He said it standing in a stranger's smoking kitchen, holding her cat, which he counted as people. In twenty years, none of us ever argued the point." Just tell me straight what you make of it. Cheers.

I'm retiring from the library after 40 years and wrote a bit for the send-off: "I have spent four decades answering questions whispered at the desk. Where are the tax forms. Do you have anything on grief. Is there a book about what my father has. It's the same voice for all three, and I learned to answer in the same voice, so nobody would feel the difference." What do you make of it?

I leave Hanley Tool & Die next month after 35 years as a welder, and I want to open with this: "They say the average welder reaches retirement with ten fingers, two good ears, and one spouse. I've got all three. Gail says she's still auditing the third." I worked on it all weekend. Could you let me know what stands out to you, for better or worse?

My son Marcus retires from the Navy after 24 years, and as his mother I get two minutes. My plan: "Marcus, you've spent twenty-four years being told where to be. I spent twenty-four years being told where you were, usually by postcard. Come home and be somewhere dull. I've set the chair by the window. It faces nothing in particular. It's yours." How does it sound to a stranger?

Pete, who founded our youth soccer league, retires after 30 seasons. My toast: "Pete never kept score. The parents did, loudly. Pete kept track of who cried, who sat out, who stopped coming, and he phoned those houses on Sunday. We won nothing, ever, and nine hundred kids learned that a field is a place where someone notices you. Raise a glass to the worst record in county history." Be straight with me, does it work?

Doc Imani is closing her large-animal practice after 30 years, and I'm a dairy farmer asked to say something. Here goes: "Doc has pulled calves at 2 a.m. in January, arm shoulder-deep, flashlight in her teeth. I never saw her hurry or lie. She told me once, 'Dale, it's the cow's night, not ours.' Thirty years I've borrowed her calm. Doc, I'm not giving it back." What do you think?

I'm a grandmother who volunteers at the school, and I've been asked to speak for Mrs. Okafor, our retiring cafeteria lady. I'm shaking already. Here's my ending: "She knew which children had no breakfast at home, because they ate lunch so seriously. She never said a word. She just offered seconds and called them her helper and handed them a tray to carry. I've seen a hundred programs for hungry children. She had one: dignity, with gravy." Can you tell me how it sounds?

After 38 years at the water utility, here's how I plan to end my retirement speech: "Every day, four million of you turned a tap and nothing happened except water. That was the job. Nothing happening, perfectly, forever. I'll miss the quiet. Please keep not noticing me." I'm an engineer, not a writer, so I'd value an outside opinion. Anything you'd change?

My wife Carol retires from teaching on Friday and I'm giving a toast. Here's the draft: "Carol grades the way she loves: in green ink, because red felt like shouting. For thirty-three years our kitchen table was a courthouse of other people's children. I have eaten dinner beside essays on the Alamo. I'd like to propose she now grade me, a lifelong C-plus in laundry, and be gentle." Should I keep going or stop there?

I'm a structural engineer in Rotterdam, and I wrote a toast for Anneke, retiring from the water board after 38 years. Middle bit: "Anneke once told me a dike is just a promise made out of sand. She kept hers for thirty-eight years. Nobody in this city has had wet feet because of her, and the best thing about her work is that you never noticed it. Tonight, we notice." Does it work? I go on in an hour.

I'm a pharmacist in Lagos, speaking for Mrs. Adebayo, our principal for 31 years. My closing: "She taught us that a register is not a list of names. It's a list of people who might not come back tomorrow, so you say the name aloud and you look up. Mrs. Adebayo, today we are calling your name. Look up." I rehearsed it in the car all week. Honest thoughts?

I'm a dentist in Winnipeg, roasting Gerry, who's driven the rink Zamboni for 29 years. "Gerry has made roughly 40,000 perfect sheets of ice, and each lasted about nine minutes before a seven-year-old in a dinosaur helmet ruined it. It's the most Canadian definition of a career I know: make something flawless, then watch children skate on it." Too gentle for a roast? Thanks!

Hi, I'm a chartered accountant in Pune and honestly quite nervous. Our driver Ramesh retires Friday after 26 years. This is the line I'd open with: "In twenty-six years, Ramesh has never once been late, and I have never once been on time, and somehow we have both always arrived." Is that a reasonable way to start a speech? I've never done this before.

I'm a paramedic from Adelaide, speaking for Dot, who ran our primary school office for 34 years. "Dot knew which kids were hungry before the teachers did, and whose dad had left, and whose mum worked nights. She never filed any of it. She just kept a stack of Vegemite sandwiches in the bottom drawer, labelled 'lost property'." Is the ending too sentimental? Be straight with me.

I'm a sparky in Glasgow, retiring after 41 years, so I'm doing my own speech. Opening: "I've been told to keep this short, which suits me. For forty-one years I've stood in the dark telling people 'it'll only be a minute.' I'd like to thank the apprentices, who taught me a man can be wrong about the football and right about the wiring, and occasionally the other way round." Would you cut anything?

I'm a cardiologist in São Paulo. For Dona Lúcia, who cleaned our ward for 33 years: "We doctors get the credit for restarting hearts. Dona Lúcia kept a great many from stopping, by making sure the floor beneath them was clean and by humming. The monitors beep in rhythm, and hers was always half a beat ahead. The patients noticed." Does the humming land, or is it too much?

I'm a software engineer in Tokyo, writing in English for our international team. For my boss, Tanaka-san: "In twenty years he never once said 'good job.' He said 'I read your code,' and we understood this was the highest praise there is. Tanaka-san, I have now read your whole career. I wouldn't change a single line, except the comments, which were always too short." Does the English sound natural?

I'm a Lufthansa pilot in Frankfurt, and my father, a carpenter, retires at 67. My ending: "Papa, you measured twice and cut once for forty-four years. Every door you hung in Würzburg still closes with a soft click, and I've landed planes with less certainty than that click. I've done my measuring. Here is the cut: thank you." What do you think? I'm reading it at his workshop.

I'm an agronomist in Nakuru, speaking for Mrs. Wanjiru, our village librarian for 28 years. "She had one rule: borrow any book, but return it with something inside. A pressed leaf, a receipt, a note. I once found a bus ticket from 1996 in Things Fall Apart. Madam, your library never held only books. It held all of us, folded into the pages." Should I read it slowly? Thoughts welcome.

I'm an architect in Oaxaca, and our mail carrier Don Chuy retires after 37 years. "I've designed forty buildings, but Don Chuy knows them better than I do. He knows which door sticks in the rain and which dog is only pretending. A city isn't its drawings. It's the man who walked all of it, every day, carrying news. Don Chuy, you're the only one who has read the whole city." Thoughts?

I'm a GP in Leeds, retiring next month, and I've written my own goodbye. "I've delivered bad news about eleven thousand times. Nobody tells you the good news is quieter. No one rings to say the lump was nothing. They just stop coming, and years later you see them in Morrisons, buying peas. I'd like to thank everyone I never saw again." Be blunt, I can take it.

I'm a mining engineer in Joburg. Nomsa has brought tea to our office at ten o'clock for 30 years. "I've done risk assessments on every shaft in Gauteng, and the most reliable system I've ever seen is Nomsa's tea trolley. Ten o'clock. No downtime. Zero incidents. If anyone knows a better safety record, put up your hand. Nobody? Good. Nomsa, we'll be running at a loss." Is the joke too corporate?

I'm a vet in County Kerry. Seán drove our school bus for 40 years, and I'm saying a few words. "Seán has seen every one of us at our worst, at eight in the morning, in a uniform jumper, and never told a soul. He knew whose mother was sick by the way we sat. Forty years, one road, and not a single child was late for anything except the thing they were running from." Any notes?

I'm an ER nurse in Ohio, giving a toast to Mr. Kowalski, my old band director, retiring after 35 years. "He told a room of terrified fourteen-year-olds, 'Nobody plays the wrong note on purpose. Play it louder so we can fix it together.' I've said it to student nurses ever since, on a different instrument. Mr. K, you never taught me trombone. You taught me to be wrong out loud." Does it work as a toast?

Hello! My granddaughter set me up on a dating site and I wrote my own bio. Here it is: "I am a 68-year-old retired bus driver who likes long walks, good food, and a good laugh. I am looking for someone who is honest, kind, and loves life. I am a simple man who enjoys the simple things. Live, laugh, love!" What do you think of it?

I'm 71, widowed, and a bit nervous about this. I wrote: "Roses are red, violets are blue, I like gardening, and I'd like to meet you. I bake a good pie, I'm kind and I'm true, so if you like tea, I'll make one for two." Could you tell me your honest opinion? My daughter said to ask someone else.

Here's my dating profile, written after my church group's potluck last week: "I am a Christian lady of 64 who loves the Lord, my grandchildren, and my cat Biscuit. I like sunsets, puzzles, and a cozy night in. Looking for a gentleman who is also looking for love. Must like cats." Any thoughts before I post it?

Hi there, retired schoolteacher here, 66. My bio so far: "They say the best things in life are free, and I believe that's true. I'm a glass-half-full person who wants to find a partner in crime to dance through life with. I enjoy walks on the beach, candlelit dinners, and travelling (mostly to my daughter's in Ohio)." How does it read to you?

I volunteer at the food pantry on Tuesdays and wrote this for my profile: "I give back to my community because it takes a village. I am a good listener, a good cook, and a good friend. I am looking for a good man who is also good. Age is just a number, and mine is 73!" Would love your feedback, thank you kindly.

Just finished my dating bio, and I'm showing it to you first! "Dad of three, grandpa of five, and a lifelong fan of the Detroit Tigers. I'm tall, dark and handsome (well, two out of three). I like fishing, grilling, and sitting on the porch. If you can handle a man who snores, swipe right!" Tell me what you make of it!

My sister said to ask a stranger. I'm 59, a single mom with two grown kids, and I wrote: "I'm just a small-town girl living in a big world. I work hard, play hard, and love hard. I'm looking for my other half to complete me. My kids say I'm the best mom ever, so that's a plus!" What would you say about it?

This is my first time ever writing about myself for anyone but the church newsletter. "I am 75 years young. I was married for 48 wonderful years to my late husband Harold. He was my everything. I am ready to find someone to share the golden years with, as the sun sets on life's journey." Could you give me your opinion?

So I put this together over coffee this morning, and I'm curious what you think: "Retired mailman, 70. Delivered letters for 35 years, now I'd like to deliver my heart to the right person. Return to sender not accepted! I like crosswords, bowling, and a nice meatloaf. Looking for a lady with a good sense of humor." Thanks!

I coach Little League and volunteer at the library, and here's my profile bio: "I'm a big kid at heart who loves baseball, books, and bad puns. Life is a journey, not a destination, and I'm looking for someone to take the ride with. I'm easygoing, but also serious, and spontaneous, but also a planner. Be yourself!" Does it work, do you think?

Hello, grandma here! Wrote this for my profile and would love a second pair of eyes: "Kind, caring, and young at heart. I love my grandkids, knitting, and Sunday drives. I'm looking for a man who's kind, caring, and young at heart too. Let's see where life takes us! P.S. I make the best banana bread in three counties." Thoughts?

I'm 62 and I run the neighborhood watch, and this is the bio I'm planning to use: "A man of few words but many hobbies. I like woodworking, birdwatching, and barbecuing. I have a good pension and my own teeth. Not looking for drama, only a companion to watch the Wheel of Fortune with." Please let me know what you think.

Don't laugh, but I wrote a little poem for my dating profile (I'm 67, retired nurse): "I cared for others all my days, in many gentle, loving ways. Now I'd like someone to care for me, and we'll be happy, wait and see. Hearts can be young at any age, so let's turn over a brand new page." What's your take?

My kids all moved away and I'm trying something new at 72! Here's my bio: "Hi, I'm Dennis. I'm an honest, hardworking, loyal man who loves his family and his dog Max. I like to laugh and have a good time. I believe everything happens for a reason. I'm just looking for that special someone. Is it you?" Tell me what you think, please.

I volunteer at the animal shelter and my friends there helped me, but I wrote most of it myself: "I'm a cat lady and proud of it! Four cats, one heart, endless love. I'm looking for someone who loves animals as much as I do, because a heart full of fur is a heart full of love. Opposites attract, but you must like cats." What do you think?

I'm a pediatric nurse in Manchester and I finally wrote my Hinge bio. Here it is: "I like long walks on the beach, good food and laughing until my tummy hurts. I'm looking for someone to be my partner in crime. Life is short, so let's make memories! Must love dogs." Could you tell me what you make of it before I post it tonight?

Hi! I'm a civil engineer in Nairobi, and I spent my whole Sunday on this dating bio. "Roses are red, violets are blue, I'm a nice guy who is looking for you. I like to cook, I like to dance, give me a chance!" Any thoughts? Be honest, I can take it. Mostly.

I'm a dentist in Glasgow, 41, and my sister dared me to write a bio. This is what I came up with: "Looking for my other half, someone who makes me smile and laugh. I enjoy hiking, movies, and trying new things. Honesty is very important to me. I'm just a simple guy who likes simple things." What do you reckon?

Hello, I'm an accountant from Toronto. First time writing something like this! My bio: "I am a kind, caring, loyal person who loves family, friends and travel. I work hard and play hard. I believe the best things in life are free. If you can make me laugh, you already have my heart." Could you give me your opinion, please?

I'm a high school chemistry teacher in Auckland and I wrote my own Tinder bio. "Looking for the sodium to my chloride, someone to bond with for life. I love sunsets, coffee, and cuddling on rainy days. I'm an old-fashioned romantic in a modern world." Does it do the job? Tell me what you think, mate!

I'm a long-haul truck driver in Texas, and my daughter says I need a dating bio, so I wrote one. "I'm a hardworking man with a big heart. I love my truck, my dog Buddy, and country music. Looking for a good woman who wants to ride off into the sunset. No drama please." What do you think, honestly?

Okay, I'm a pharmacist in Mumbai and a bit nervous sharing this. My bio: "Soft-hearted, family-oriented and ambitious. I love chai, cricket and Sunday phone calls with my mother. Looking for someone who is caring, understanding, and a best friend first. Life is a journey, let's travel it together." Is it okay to put up like this?

I'm a firefighter in Melbourne and I wrote this for Bumble over my night shift: "I run into burning buildings for a living, but I'm really a big softie. I love the beach, barbecues and cuddling my cat Mittens. Looking for someone who will light my fire. Sorry, had to!" Thoughts? Feedback welcome.

Hello from Lagos! I'm a surgeon, and writing about myself is harder than any operation. Here's my bio: "I am a man of God, a man of family, and a man of my word. I enjoy music, reading, and quiet evenings. I want a woman who is genuine and sweet. Be the missing piece to my puzzle." How does it read to you?

I'm a veterinarian in rural Ireland, and I've been working on this bio for weeks: "I love animals, the countryside, and a cup of tea by the fire. I'm looking for someone kind who enjoys the little things in life. I'm easy-going, fun-loving, and a bit shy at first, but once you get to know me, I'm a joy!" Could you tell me what you think?

I'm an airline pilot based in Dubai, and here's my first ever dating bio: "I travel all over the world, but my heart is searching for a home. I love adventure, good food, and meeting new people. Looking for a girl to fly away with. The sky's the limit!" Be straight with me, what's your opinion?

I'm a 58-year-old electrician in Leeds and my mate helped me sign up. I wrote the bio myself: "Widower, two grown kids, one grumpy dog. I like fishing, a pint on Fridays, and a good roast dinner. Looking for a lady to share the rest of my journey with. Let's spark something!" What would you say to it?

Hi, I'm an ER doctor in São Paulo. I wrote this dating bio on my phone between shifts, so please be gentle: "I save lives by day, but at night I just want to relax with a good movie and someone special. I love music, beaches and caipirinhas. Looking for my soulmate. Life is better with you!" Your thoughts?

I'm a banker in Singapore, and I wrote my dating profile this weekend. "I work in finance, but I'm more than my job. I love brunch, yoga, and exploring new cafés. I'm ambitious, driven and fun. Looking for someone who sees the good in life and wants to grow together." Please tell me what you think, I'd like to post it soon.

I'm a farmer in Saskatchewan and my niece set up my profile, but I wrote the words myself: "I'm honest, I'm hardworking, and I get up at 5 a.m. I love the land, a warm kitchen, and a woman who loves to laugh. If you want a simple life with a good man, look no further!" How's that sound to you?

Retired after 34 years driving the Number 9 bus. Here's my dating bio: "I know every pothole in this town and most of its secrets. Widowed two years. I make a decent lasagna, a terrible cup of tea, and I will always wait the extra thirty seconds when I see you running for the stop. Looking for someone to take the long route with." Thoughts?

My granddaughter set up the profile but told me to write the bio myself, and I'm nervous. "Retired librarian. I still read the last page first and I'm not sorry. I'm looking for someone who'll argue with me about Trollope, split the good chocolate, and read aloud on long drives, even badly. Bonus if you own a ladder." Could you tell me honestly what you think?

Sending this before I lose my nerve. "I run the Saturday food pantry, which means I can feed forty people from one Tuesday's donated zucchini. I'm 61, divorced, and fluent in dad jokes in two languages. I'm not after a project or a rescue. I'd like a co-conspirator." How would you improve it, if at all?

My daughter insisted I write a bio for the dating site. "Retired dairy farmer. Up at 4:30 out of habit, asleep by 8:30 out of wisdom. I have opinions about soil, a dog named Gerald, and a porch with two chairs, one of which has been empty a while. Applications accepted in person." What's your take?

Here's my profile bio, and I'd love a fresh pair of eyes on it: "Thirty-eight years of night-shift nursing taught me that people are braver than they think, the best conversations happen at 3 a.m., and nobody should eat dinner from a vending machine. I'd like to cook for someone who tells me about their day. Must tolerate a woman who's asleep by nine." Does it read right?

Three boys raised mostly alone, all grown now. This is my bio: "Raising three sons taught me to negotiate, to sleep sitting up, and to locate the one clean fork. Now the house is quiet and I coach youth soccer to fix that. I'm 54 and I laugh at my own jokes before they're finished. Seeking someone kind, unhurried, and good at parallel parking." Honest feedback, please.

Retired civil engineer, 71, writing my first bio. "Specifications: walks at roughly three miles per hour, with detours for birds. Tolerances: I'll forgive bad singing, never bad parking. I spent forty years building bridges, and lately I'd like to walk across one with someone." Curious what you make of it. Be as blunt as you like.

I volunteer at a hospice on Thursdays, so I've gotten used to honesty. Here's my bio: "I'm 69 and I miss my husband. I'm not looking to replace him. I'd like company at the farmers' market and someone to argue with about whether tomatoes belong in the fridge (they don't). Kindness matters more to me than chemistry, though I wouldn't turn down both." Would you change anything before I post it?

First dating profile of my life at 67, so be gentle! "I taught eighth-grade science for 35 years and can make anyone care about tardigrades. Out since 1989, retired since June, restless since July. I garden badly and cook well. Looking for a man who is curious, kind to waiters, and willing to lie on a lawn at night naming constellations wrong." What do you reckon?

ok here's my bio, tell me what you think: "Retired mail carrier. Walked eleven miles a day for thirty years and was bitten by fourteen dogs. Loved thirteen of them. Now I'd like to sit down. Seeking a man with a comfortable couch, a working sense of humor, and zero opinions about my casserole."

Wrote this at the kitchen table after supper. "I fished out of Gloucester for forty years and learned the sea doesn't care about your plans, which is oddly restful. Six grandchildren, one bad knee, a boat I take out only in July. I'm looking for a woman who likes quiet, doesn't mind early mornings, and will tell me the truth about my cooking." Any suggestions?

Is the gimmick too cute? "Three true things and one fib: I've led my town choir for 22 years. I can parallel park a minivan in one move. I've never lost an argument with a toddler. I'm easy to please. Message me your guess." I'm 58, a mother of four, and the person who always brings extra chairs. Tell me straight.

Retired trucker here, 64. Bio draft: "I drove 3.2 million miles and watched the sun come up in 46 states. Best coffee: a gas station in Winnemucca. Best company: a CB radio at 2 a.m. I'm home now, and the quiet is louder than the diesel ever was. I'd like to learn what it's like to be somewhere on purpose, with you." I'd value your honest reaction.

Does this say too much about my daughter? "Widowed dad of one nine-year-old who rates my cooking out of ten and has never gone above six. I'm good at animal-shaped birthday cakes, bad at chess, and fluent in every song from that movie about the ice queen. Taking things slowly; she comes first. But I'm told second place has an excellent view."

I'm 75 and a retired marine biologist, and this is my bio: "I spent my career with creatures that glow in the dark at the bottom of the sea, so odd people don't unsettle me. I say yes to dessert, no to cruises, and maybe to you. Write and tell me the best thing you've ever seen." Does it sound like me, do you think?

I'm a flood-defence engineer in Rotterdam, and this is my Hinge bio. Could you give me your honest opinion before I publish it?
"I spend my days keeping a quarter of my country dry. Evenings are for smaller disasters: sourdough that won't rise, a bicycle with opinions about headwinds. Looking for someone to argue with me about whether the last stroopwafel is communal property. Colleagues call me reliable in a crisis. Friends call me bad at parallel parking. Both are true."

Hi! Pharmacist in Lagos here, finally writing a dating bio after my sister nagged me for a year. Tell me what you make of it?
"I can recite the half-life of most drugs but not how long my jollof argument with my sister will last. Sundays: church, suya, then a nap I defend like a border. Seeking someone who laughs with their whole face and corrects me gently, with sources."

I'm a dentist in Osaka and I'm quite nervous about putting this online. I'd be grateful for your thoughts.
"I look at mouths all day, so I know a real smile when I see one. Mine arrives late, usually after the second joke. I like old jazz kissaten, long walks to nowhere, and people who say 'sorry, I'm lost' without drama. Let's get lost together, then find ramen."

Geologist in Santiago, Chile. Here's the bio I drafted for my profile. What's your honest reaction?
"I read rocks for a living, so I'm patient: I've waited forty million years for things, professionally. Weekends find me in the Andes with a hammer, a thermos, and sandwiches that are a genuine geological hazard. Looking for someone to share the view and write a fair review of the sandwich."

Night-shift nurse in Winnipeg here. I wrote this for my profile and would like an outsider's opinion, please.
"My weekend starts on your Tuesday. So let's do pancakes at 7 a.m., like two people who have both survived something. I'm good in an emergency, better at a quiet kitchen, and I will absolutely fall asleep on your couch at 2 p.m. and wake up apologizing. Bring maple syrup. Or don't, this is Manitoba."

I'm a chartered accountant in Cork, so please be straight with me. Here's my bio. Thoughts?
"Yes, I'll split the bill exactly. No, I won't do it to the cent if you had the wine. I keep a spreadsheet of every pub quiz I've lost, and I'm proud of the trend line. Seeking someone who'll take the last chip and then confess. I find honesty very attractive. It's also deductible."

I'm a cardiologist in Pune and I tried writing my bio like a prescription. Be honest, how does it read?
"Rx: One (1) person who enjoys monsoon drives and terrible puns. Dosage: weekends, plus the occasional midnight chai. Side effects may include loud laughter, unsolicited cardiac advice, and my mother asking about you. Do not combine with people who dislike mangoes. Refills available if it's working."

I'm an electrician from Fremantle and my mate says I should put this on my profile. What's your take?
"Sparky. My ute has 240,000 km on it and a milk crate of cassettes in the back. I'll fix your lights, you fix my playlists. Looking for a navigator, because the GPS and I haven't spoken since Kalgoorlie. Bonus if you can sit through a whole sunset without checking your phone. I'll try too. No promises."

I'm an air traffic controller in Gothenburg and this is my first ever dating bio. Could you tell me what you think?
"All day I tell very large things where to wait and when to leave. At home I'm gentler. I make cardamom buns, I swim in the sea until October, and I never say 'cleared for takeoff' on a first date. Looking for someone calm in turbulence, and curious on the ground."

I drive regional trains in Hamburg. A colleague convinced me to write a profile, so here's my attempt. Would you tell me what you think of it?
"I'm on time for a living. I'll be on time for you too, and I'll forgive you for being late once, with paperwork. I can name every station between here and Basel and I won't, unless you ask. Looking for someone to share a window seat, and the unspoken agreement about who gets the table."

I'm a retired mail carrier and I'm taking a night class on databases. I wrote this for my wife's 40th anniversary card:
SELECT * FROM reasons_i_love_her
WHERE reason = 'she is my sunshine'
ORDER BY love DESC;
I plan to print it inside the card. What do you think of it?

Hi! I coordinate volunteers at our food pantry and wanted to make a query about them. Here it is:
SELECT * FROM volunteers
WHERE heart = 'big' AND smile = 'warm';
It returns everybody, which feels right to me. Could you give me your honest opinion?

Grandma here, 71, learning SQL from my grandson. This is my first query, for my apple pie recipe:
SELECT apples, sugar, flour, butter
FROM my_kitchen
WHERE pie = 'delicious';
I'm going to put it in the family cookbook. Any feedback before I do?

Our church bake sale needs a fundraising total, so I wrote this myself:
SELECT 40 + 25 + 30 AS total_raised;
-- Wow, $125 for the kids' camp!
I'm treasurer this year and a little nervous about the numbers. Can you take a look and tell me what you think?

Dad of three here, and I wrote a bedtime query for my kids, just for fun:
SELECT * FROM kids
WHERE bedtime = 'now'
ORDER BY cuteness DESC;
-- sweet dreams, my little angels
Would love to hear your thoughts. Be as honest as you like!

I volunteer at our neighborhood Little Free Library and made this query to describe it:
SELECT book FROM little_library
WHERE book = 'good'
AND reader = 'happy';
I'm thinking of posting it on the library door. What's your take?

I'm a retired teacher, and I wrote a SQL query as a retirement poem to my old classroom:
SELECT memories FROM classroom
WHERE kids = 'wonderful'
AND time = 'flew by';
I read it at my party tomorrow. Tell me what you think, please!

Writing a children's book for my granddaughter, and the plot is a query, so she can learn code:
SELECT moral FROM story
WHERE character = 'Benny the Bee'
AND moral = 'always be kind';
Benny learns kindness is what matters most. Does this work? Opinions welcome!

Garden club secretary here. I made a query for our newsletter:
SELECT * FROM flowers
WHERE color = 'pretty'
ORDER BY prettiness DESC;
-- Mother Nature's gift to us all
My daughter says to ask a stranger instead of her. So, thoughts?

I'm 68 and just retired from the post office. My first SQL poem, for my grandchildren:
SELECT joy FROM home
WHERE family = 'together'
AND hearts = 'full';
It's going on the fridge. How would you rate it? Just curious what you think!

For our community potluck sign-up I tried writing a query to count dishes:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM potluck
WHERE dish = 'casserole';
-- 12 casseroles, 0 desserts, everybody's happy!
I'm the volunteer organizer. Can you tell me what you make of it?

I knit scarves for the children's shelter, and my nephew taught me SQL, so I wrote:
SELECT * FROM scarves
WHERE warm = TRUE
AND made_with_love = TRUE;
I'd like to add it to our volunteer flyer. What's your opinion?

My late husband and I fished every summer. I wrote this in his memory:
SELECT * FROM memories
WHERE year = 'the good old days'
AND heart = 'forever';
My son says to share it with someone. I'd appreciate your feedback, if you have a moment.

Hey, grandpa here. Wrote my first query for my grandson's Little League team, the Tigers:
SELECT * FROM players
WHERE team = 'Tigers'
AND attitude = 'winning'
ORDER BY teamwork;
Gonna print it on the snack-stand banner. Whaddya think?

I run the senior center's Tuesday coffee hour, and I wrote this to welcome new people:
SELECT friends FROM senior_center
WHERE coffee = 'hot'
AND everyone = 'welcome';
I'm going to read it aloud on Tuesday. Could you tell me your thoughts first?

Retired bookkeeper here, volunteering at our food bank. I wrote this to find households we haven't seen in 60 days, including ones who never came at all. Would love your thoughts:
SELECT h.household_id, h.name, MAX(v.visit_date) AS last_visit
FROM households h LEFT JOIN visits v USING (household_id)
WHERE h.active
GROUP BY h.household_id, h.name
HAVING MAX(v.visit_date) IS NULL OR MAX(v.visit_date) < CURRENT_DATE - 60
ORDER BY last_visit NULLS FIRST;

Hi! I'm a grandmother of seven and I kept forgetting birthdays, so my nephew taught me a little SQL. This is what I came up with. Be honest, what do you think?
SELECT name,
 (birthday + make_interval(years => date_part('year', age(CURRENT_DATE - 1, birthday))::int + 1))::date AS next_birthday
FROM grandkids
ORDER BY next_birthday
LIMIT 3;

Dad of two and PTA treasurer. I spent my whole Sunday on this leaderboard for our volunteer hours, and I'm happy with how it turned out. Fellow nerds, what do you see?
SELECT volunteer, SUM(hours) AS total,
 RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(hours) DESC) AS place,
 ROUND(100 * SUM(hours) / SUM(SUM(hours)) OVER (), 1) AS pct
FROM volunteer_log
WHERE log_date >= date_trunc('year', CURRENT_DATE)
GROUP BY volunteer;

Retired math teacher, still tinkering. I keep my old gradebook in a database now. This averages quiz scores after dropping each student's lowest one. Any feedback would be appreciated!
WITH ranked AS (
 SELECT student_id, score,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY student_id ORDER BY score) AS rn
 FROM quizzes)
SELECT student_id, ROUND(AVG(score), 1) AS adj_avg
FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1
GROUP BY student_id;

I run the sign-up sheet for our community garden (retired nurse, not a programmer!). I'm a bit nervous showing this, but I wanted to find which plot numbers are unassigned gaps in the sequence. Is this a sensible way to do it?
SELECT plot_no + 1 AS gap_start, next_no - 1 AS gap_end
FROM (SELECT plot_no, LEAD(plot_no) OVER (ORDER BY plot_no) AS next_no
      FROM plots) t
WHERE next_no - plot_no > 1;

Grandpa here. I've put all our family recipes into a database, and this finds every recipe that uses buttermilk, molasses AND ginger. Took me a few evenings. Thoughts?
SELECT r.title
FROM recipes r
JOIN recipe_ingredients ri ON ri.recipe_id = r.id
JOIN ingredients i ON i.id = ri.ingredient_id
WHERE i.name IN ('buttermilk', 'molasses', 'ginger')
GROUP BY r.id, r.title
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT i.name) = 3;

Retired librarian, now running our annual book sale. Here's my monthly donations summary, one row per month with a column per category. I'd welcome any comments, however small!
SELECT date_trunc('month', donated_on)::date AS month,
 COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE category = 'fiction') AS fiction,
 COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE category = 'children') AS children,
 COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE category NOT IN ('fiction','children')) AS other
FROM donations
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

Soccer mom and volunteer carpool coordinator. This shows which games don't have enough seats for the kids attending. I did the counts separately so nothing gets double-counted. Does this look right to you?
WITH k AS (SELECT game_id, COUNT(*) n FROM rsvps WHERE attending GROUP BY 1),
 s AS (SELECT game_id, SUM(seats_free) n FROM drivers GROUP BY 1)
SELECT g.game_date, k.n AS kids, COALESCE(s.n, 0) AS seats
FROM games g JOIN k USING (game_id) LEFT JOIN s USING (game_id)
WHERE COALESCE(s.n, 0) < k.n
ORDER BY 1;

Retired mechanic, 71, and I run our classic car club's records. I wanted each car's latest service plus miles since the one before. Here's my attempt, and I'd like your take:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (car_id) car_id, service_date, mileage,
 mileage - LAG(mileage) OVER (PARTITION BY car_id ORDER BY service_date) AS miles_since_prev
FROM services
ORDER BY car_id, service_date DESC;

Volunteer at the animal shelter here. Our director asked how long animals typically wait for a home, and averages were skewed by a few long-stayers, so I used the median. Here's my query. Any feedback welcome!
SELECT species,
 PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY adopted_on - intake_on) AS median_days,
 COUNT(*) AS adoptions
FROM animals
WHERE adopted_on IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY species;

I'm a grandmother researching our family tree on the side. This walks back through every ancestor of my great-aunt and labels the generation. I'm curious what you'd say about it!
WITH RECURSIVE anc AS (
 SELECT id, name, father_id, mother_id, 0 AS gen
 FROM people WHERE name = 'Edith Marsh'
 UNION ALL
 SELECT p.id, p.name, p.father_id, p.mother_id, a.gen + 1
 FROM people p JOIN anc a ON p.id IN (a.father_id, a.mother_id)
 WHERE a.gen < 12)
SELECT gen, name FROM anc ORDER BY gen, name;

I coordinate the Sunday rota at our church (retired, 68). Some volunteers get booked for overlapping shifts and I hate catching it late. This is my fix. Does it read okay to you?
SELECT a.volunteer_id, a.shift_id AS first_shift, b.shift_id AS clashing_shift
FROM shifts a
JOIN shifts b ON a.volunteer_id = b.volunteer_id
 AND a.shift_id < b.shift_id
 AND a.starts_at < b.ends_at
 AND b.starts_at < a.ends_at;

Mum of three. I made a chore chart database for the kids, and this calculates weekly allowance at 25p a point, capped at a tenner. My husband just rolled his eyes, so I'm asking you instead. What do you think?
SELECT kid, date_trunc('week', done_on)::date AS week,
 LEAST(SUM(points) * 0.25, 10.00) AS allowance
FROM chores
WHERE approved
GROUP BY kid, week
ORDER BY week, kid;

Retired and running our pickleball league's standings. Each game is one row, so I stacked home and away results to get a single table per team, with point difference as the tiebreaker. Would appreciate your opinion!
WITH r AS (
 SELECT home AS team, home_pts AS pf, away_pts AS pa FROM games
 UNION ALL
 SELECT away, away_pts, home_pts FROM games)
SELECT team, SUM((pf > pa)::int) AS wins, SUM(pf - pa) AS diff
FROM r GROUP BY team
ORDER BY wins DESC, diff DESC;

Volunteer coordinator at our neighbourhood tool library. I wanted to thank people with the longest streaks of consecutive weeks volunteering, so I wrote this. It's the cleverest thing I've ever written, so I'd love a second pair of eyes.
WITH w AS (SELECT DISTINCT volunteer_id, date_trunc('week', shift_date)::date AS wk FROM shifts)
SELECT volunteer_id, MIN(wk) AS first_wk, MAX(wk) AS last_wk, COUNT(*) AS weeks
FROM (SELECT *, wk - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY volunteer_id ORDER BY wk)::int * 7 AS grp FROM w) t
GROUP BY volunteer_id, grp
ORDER BY weeks DESC;

I'm a ward nurse in Manchester teaching myself SQL for our audit. Here's my 30-day readmission query. Could you tell me what you think?
WITH stays AS (
  SELECT patient_id, discharge_date,
    LEAD(admit_date) OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY admit_date) AS next_admit
  FROM admissions
)
SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE next_admit <= discharge_date + INTERVAL '30 days') * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS readmit_rate
FROM stays;

I manage a tea farm in Kericho, Kenya, and I wrote this to compare each plot's daily picking weight with its own 4-week average. Any feedback welcome!
SELECT plot_id, picked_on, kg,
  AVG(kg) OVER (
    PARTITION BY plot_id ORDER BY picked_on
    RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '27 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS avg_28d
FROM pickings
WHERE picked_on >= DATE '2024-01-01'
ORDER BY plot_id, picked_on;

Pastry chef in Lyon, and I'm a bit nervous showing this. It calculates the cost of each recipe using the latest ingredient prices. Honest thoughts?
SELECT r.name, ROUND(SUM(ri.grams * p.eur_per_kg / 1000), 2) AS cost_eur
FROM recipes r
JOIN recipe_items ri ON ri.recipe_id = r.id
JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT eur_per_kg FROM prices
  WHERE ingredient_id = ri.ingredient_id
  ORDER BY valid_from DESC LIMIT 1
) p ON TRUE
GROUP BY r.id, r.name
ORDER BY cost_eur DESC;

Librarian in Toronto here, definitely not a coder. I wrote this to list members with overdue loans and what they owe. Is it okay to show my manager?
SELECT m.member_id, m.name,
  SUM(CURRENT_DATE - l.due_date) * 0.25 AS fine_cad
FROM members m
JOIN loans l ON l.member_id = m.member_id
WHERE l.returned_on IS NULL AND l.due_date < CURRENT_DATE
GROUP BY m.member_id, m.name
HAVING SUM(CURRENT_DATE - l.due_date) * 0.25 > 5
ORDER BY fine_cad DESC;

Wedding photographer in Guadalajara. I got tired of checking my calendar by hand, so I wrote this to find my free Saturdays. Thoughts?
SELECT d::date AS free_saturday
FROM generate_series(DATE '2025-05-01', DATE '2025-10-31', INTERVAL '1 day') AS d
WHERE EXTRACT(dow FROM d) = 6
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM bookings b WHERE b.event_date = d::date
  )
ORDER BY 1;

I coach a youth football club in Recife and built this to find our longest winning streaks. Pretty proud of it, honestly. What's your take?
WITH g AS (
  SELECT team, match_date, result,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY team ORDER BY match_date)
    - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY team, result ORDER BY match_date) AS grp
  FROM matches
)
SELECT team, COUNT(*) AS streak, MIN(match_date) AS started
FROM g WHERE result = 'W'
GROUP BY team, grp
ORDER BY streak DESC
LIMIT 5;

I'm an architect in Tokyo. I wanted to see which contractors run late on typical projects, not just on average. Here's my query. Does it make sense to you?
SELECT contractor,
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY actual_days - planned_days) AS median_delay,
  COUNT(*) AS projects
FROM milestones
GROUP BY contractor
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
ORDER BY median_delay;

Secondary school maths teacher in Lagos. I wanted to find students who improved every single term. Here's what I came up with, how would you rate it?
WITH t AS (
  SELECT student_id, term, score,
    score - LAG(score) OVER (PARTITION BY student_id ORDER BY term) AS delta
  FROM results
  WHERE subject = 'Maths'
)
SELECT student_id
FROM t
WHERE delta IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY student_id
HAVING MIN(delta) > 0;

Vet in Auckland, new to SQL. This pulls dogs whose C5 booster falls due within 30 days so reception can call owners. Keen to hear what you think!
SELECT p.name, o.phone, MAX(v.given_on) + INTERVAL '1 year' AS booster_due
FROM vaccinations v
JOIN pets p ON p.id = v.pet_id
JOIN owners o ON o.id = p.owner_id
WHERE v.vaccine = 'C5'
GROUP BY p.id, p.name, o.phone
HAVING MAX(v.given_on) + INTERVAL '1 year' < CURRENT_DATE + INTERVAL '30 days'
ORDER BY booster_due;

I dispatch buses in Bogotá and taught myself a bit of SQL this month. This is on-time percentage by route and hour. Can you give me some feedback?
SELECT route, EXTRACT(hour FROM scheduled_at) AS hr,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (
    WHERE arrived_at <= scheduled_at + INTERVAL '3 minutes'
  ) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_on_time
FROM arrivals
GROUP BY route, hr
ORDER BY route, hr;

Lawyer in Hamburg. Billing reports used to take me an evening in Excel, so I tried this instead. Wondering what a real developer would think.
SELECT client_id,
  DATE_TRUNC('month', billed_on)::date AS month,
  SUM(hours * rate) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid,
  SUM(hours * rate) FILTER (WHERE status = 'open') AS outstanding
FROM time_entries
WHERE billed_on >= DATE '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

I'm a brewer in Ghent. I wanted to flag batches whose final gravity strays oddly far from that recipe's norm. Here's my query, let me know your thoughts.
WITH s AS (
  SELECT recipe_id, AVG(final_gravity) AS mu, STDDEV(final_gravity) AS sd
  FROM batches
  GROUP BY recipe_id
)
SELECT b.batch_id, b.recipe_id, b.final_gravity
FROM batches b
JOIN s USING (recipe_id)
WHERE s.sd > 0
  AND ABS(b.final_gravity - s.mu) > 2 * s.sd;

Park ranger in Alberta. I log wildlife sightings and wanted each species' first sighting every year, plus the trail. Here's what I wrote. Does it look alright?
SELECT DISTINCT ON (species, EXTRACT(year FROM seen_on))
  species,
  EXTRACT(year FROM seen_on) AS yr,
  seen_on AS first_seen,
  trail
FROM sightings
ORDER BY species, EXTRACT(year FROM seen_on), seen_on;

Session musician in Seoul, side project: finding the most-played track in each playlist over the last 30 days. Be gentle, but tell me what you think!
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT playlist_id, track_id, COUNT(*) AS plays,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY playlist_id ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, track_id
    ) AS rn
  FROM listens
  WHERE listened_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
  GROUP BY playlist_id, track_id
)
SELECT playlist_id, track_id, plays FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;

Paramedic in Cape Town. For our weekly review I made this p90 response-time query for priority 1 calls. Would appreciate your opinion.
SELECT district,
  DATE_TRUNC('week', dispatched_at)::date AS week,
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY arrived_at - dispatched_at) AS p90_response
FROM callouts
WHERE priority = 1 AND arrived_at IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY district, week
ORDER BY district, week;

I'm a retired bus driver and I wrote a picture book for my grandson. Here's the premise: Benny the Bus is sad because he's old and nobody rides him anymore. Then a little girl climbs aboard, and Benny learns that everybody is special no matter how old they are. The end. Could you tell me what you think of it?

Hi! I wrote a bedtime story for my daughter. Sleepy the Sheep can't fall asleep until she counts her friends: one cow, two ducks, three pigs. When she finishes, she realizes the real treasure was friendship all along. I'm going to read it to her preschool class next week. Do you have any feedback first?

I'm a retired teacher and a bit nervous to share this. Here are the opening lines of my children's book: "Little Bunny hopped away / On a bright and sunny day. / He met a friend and they did play / And that's the way to play!" There are 20 more pages like this. What are your thoughts?

I volunteer at our library's story hour and made up my own story. A little raindrop named Drip is afraid to fall from the cloud. His mama cloud tells him to be brave, and he lands in a garden and helps a flower grow. Moral: be brave and you'll help others. What's your opinion?
