ok so my grandkids keep asking for stories so I wrote one. A puppy named Sparky gets lost in the park, looks everywhere, then finds his way home because home is where the heart is. It's only 8 pages. Tell me what you think, I can take it!

I wrote this for my son's birthday: Timmy the Truck wanted to be a race car. He tried and tried, but he was a truck. Then one day a race car got stuck in the mud and Timmy pulled him out. Timmy learned to just be himself. I'm thinking of self-publishing. Would love your feedback!

I'm a retired nurse, and I've written my first children's book, "Brave Little Band-Aid." Bandy feels too small to matter. Then a boy scrapes his knee and Bandy saves the day. Everyone has a purpose, big or small! I'd really appreciate hearing what you think before I show the grandchildren.

Our church's kids' program needed a story, so I wrote one. Sunny the Sunflower was sad because she was the shortest in the whole field. But the sun shone on her just the same, because God loves everyone equally. I'm kind of proud of it. Could you give me some feedback?

Here's a poem I wrote for my granddaughter's picture book, "Grandpa's Fishing Trip": "We went to the lake, for goodness sake, / I caught a big fish and made a wish, / The wish was to be with you and me, / Together forever, happy and free." Please let me know how it reads to you!

I'm a stay-at-home mom and I've been working on this for months. Mia the Mouse finds a giant piece of cheese. She thinks about keeping it, but she shares it with all her friends and everyone is happy. Sharing is caring! Do you think a publisher would be interested? Any thoughts welcome.

I farmed for forty years and now I'm writing for my great-grandkids. Henry the Hen wanted to fly like the birds. She flapped and flapped but couldn't get off the ground. But she laid the best egg on the farm, and learned that everybody has their own talents. What do you make of it?

I volunteer at the animal shelter and wrote a book to help kids understand adoption. Whiskers the cat waits in his cage every day, feeling sad. Then a kind boy picks him, and Whiskers goes home. The message is that love finds you if you wait. Can I get your honest opinion?

Hello, I'm a grandma and I'm a little nervous sharing this. My story is called "The Little Star Who Lost Her Twinkle." She feels dull and gray until a child makes a wish on her, and her sparkle comes back. Because we all shine when we're loved. Would you tell me what you think?

I'm a dad of three and I wrote this to get my kids to brush their teeth. Barney Bear eats too much honey and gets a terrible toothache. He goes to the dentist and now he brushes every single day. The moral: brush your teeth! Any feedback? I'm happy to hear suggestions.

Retired last year and finally writing the book I always dreamed of. Oliver the Octopus has eight arms but no friends. So he gives eight big hugs to everyone in the ocean, and soon he has lots of friends. Hugs are the best gift! Could you share your thoughts on the premise?

I'm a dentist in Manchester and I've written my first picture book for my nieces. It's about Timmy Tooth, who hides from his toothbrush. Then he gets a cavity, feels sad, and learns that brushing twice a day keeps smiles bright. The last line: "And Timmy shined, so happy and clean, the brightest tooth you've ever seen!" Could you tell me what you honestly think?

Hi! I drive long-haul trucks out of Amarillo, and on the road I came up with a kids' story. Larry the Little Truck has no friends at the truck stop. Then he helps a stranded car, and learns that friends are everywhere if you have a big, kind heart. Is this a decent premise for a picture book? Open to any thoughts.

I'm an accountant in Lagos, so this is new for me, and I'm a bit nervous sharing it. My story is about Kobo, a tiny coin who feels too small to matter. At the end a little girl picks him up and he learns that everyone is valuable, big or small. Would you tell me what you think of the idea?

I'm a night-shift nurse in Dublin and I wrote this for my daughter. "Little Cloud was grey and sad, she wished that she were white. But when her rain made flowers grow, she smiled with all her might." The whole book follows her learning that being yourself is the best thing to be. What's your opinion? I'm thinking of sending it to publishers!

Civil engineer in Mumbai here. Bridges are my day job, so my kids' book is about one! Benny the Bridge wishes he could be a boat and float away. A storm comes, everyone needs him to cross the river, and he learns that staying put is also special. Please give me your honest feedback on the story idea.

I run a sheep farm in Otago, New Zealand, and the grandkids asked for a bedtime story. Woolly the lamb wants to be a sheepdog. He tries barking and running, but he's just not good at it. In the end he helps the farmer by being himself, soft and fluffy. The moral is to be yourself. What do you reckon?

I'm an airline pilot from São Paulo, and I wrote a book for children in my spare time. Pedro the Little Plane is afraid of the clouds. His mama says, "Believe in yourself, my dear," and he soars above the sky. The moral: you can do anything if you believe. Could you give me your thoughts? I'd love to know if it's ready to show people.

As a pharmacist in Toronto I don't write much besides labels, but here's my kids' book idea. Sally Snowflake thinks she's just like all the others. Then Grandpa Winter tells her that every snowflake is one of a kind, and she twinkles with joy. I even have a title: "Sally Is Special!" What do you think of it?

I'm an electrician in Kraków. Here's my story for my son: Lucek the Light Bulb is the dimmest in the house, and the other bulbs laugh. Then the power goes out and his little glow guides the family to safety. Everyone cheers. Moral: even a small light matters. I'd really like your opinion, please be straight with me.

I'm a police officer in Nairobi, and I wrote this story for the children at our community day. A baby elephant named Tembo gets lost from his herd. A kind girl, Amani, walks with him all day and helps him find his mama. "Kindness is the way home," she says at the end. Do you think it would work as a picture book?

Lawyer from Seoul here, trying something totally different! My story: Bori the Bunny tells a small fib about eating the carrots. Her ears droop lower with each lie, until she tells the truth and they pop back up. Her mother hugs her. Moral: always tell the truth. Just curious what you make of the premise. Thanks for reading!

I drive the number 44 bus in Glasgow, and I made up a wee story for the passengers' kids. Bonnie the Bus gets lost in the fog and misses her route. Then the streetlamps light her way back to the depot, and she learns that home is where your friends are. Here's the first line: "Bonnie the Bus was big and red." Any feedback?

I'm a chef in Melbourne and I've turned to children's books! "Pip the Pea wouldn't try new things, not carrots, not corn, not beans. But when he tasted a strawberry, he cried, 'It's the best thing I've ever seen!'" The moral is to try new foods. I'm planning a series. Could you tell me your thoughts on it?

I'm a software engineer in Berlin, and I wrote a children's story on weekends. Robo is a lonely robot who doesn't know what hugs are. A little boy shows him, and Robo's heart lights up red. The last line: "Love is the best power of all." I'm a bit shy about showing it to anyone. What do you think?

I'm a firefighter in Ohio and I wrote a rhyme for the kids at our station open house. "Sparky the truck goes whoop, whoop, whoop, he zooms around the town. He helps his friends put out the fire, and never lets them down!" The book is eight pages long and I've drawn the pictures myself. Would you give me your honest opinion?

Hello! I'm a retired schoolteacher, and I wrote a picture book premise for my granddaughter: Ottoline Pruitt, age seven, returns lost mittens to their owners. She deduces each one by the wear on the thumb. "This one belongs to a boy who sucks his thumb when he's worried," she says. "Return him a spare." Could you tell me honestly what you make of it?

I'm a grandmother and I've been nervous about showing anyone this. My book is about Theo, whose nana is forgetting words. They fall out of her mouth like leaves, and he gathers them in jam jars. Page one: "Tuesday, Nana lost 'kettle.' I found it under the bus stop bench. We both said it three times." Would you read it and tell me what you think?

Hi, I drive a school bus part-time since retiring from the post office. I wrote a counting-down book: "The 6:40 bus has ten sleepy stops. Ten stops, nine yawns, eight lunchboxes..." Each page one child gets off, and the last page is a bus with zero riders, humming, heading back for tomorrow. Any thoughts? Be as straight with me as you like.

Here's the premise of a book I wrote for our library's story hour. A snail named Wren enters the school race, expecting to lose. She does lose. But fog rolls in, and every runner gets lost, and they all follow the silver trail she left behind to get home. Curious what a real reader would say about it!

I'm a dad who works nights, and my daughter and I made up a book about it. It's called "The Loud Hush." Daytime, Dad sleeps, so Mina and her dog invent a whole language of whispers: "Tiptoe means hello. Two blinks means I love you. A sock on the doorknob means the dragon is asleep." What would you say about it?

I volunteer at our community garden, and I wrote this for the kids who come on Saturdays: "'It is very dark in here,' said the bean. 'Good,' said the soil. 'That's how it starts.'" The whole book goes on like that, with each seed complaining and the soil answering calmly. I'd love an outside opinion, if you don't mind giving one.

Hello, I'm 71 and I've written a rhyming bedtime book. These are the opening lines: "The moon has a job, and it isn't to glow. / It's holding the tide so it won't overflow." Then it goes through all the jobs of the night. I haven't shown it to anyone except my cat. How does it read to you?

I'm a retired speech therapist and I wrote a book for a former client. Mina's hearing aid whistles whenever she hugs someone. She decides the whistle is the hug's own song. By the end the neighbor's dog answers it from three houses away. Would you mind telling me how that lands for you as a premise?

I volunteer at our branch library, and I wrote this from a book's point of view: "Nobody has checked me out since 1983. But I know every hand that almost did. The boy with the cold fingers. The woman who sneezed. The man who read my last page standing up and put me back very gently." What's your take?

I tutor English for newcomers at our community center. I wrote this for a girl in my class. Xóchitl is tired of hearing her name said wrong, so she hides its sounds around the room: "The 'sh' is in shush. The 'ee' is in cheese. The 'tl' is a tiny click, like a clock." Then her classmates go hunting. Could you tell me what you think?

Hi there, I'm a grandpa and I wrote a snowman book told in reverse. It begins at sunset with a puddle and a lone carrot: "By noon he was a small snowman. By ten, a fat one." It runs backward to the last page, which is the first one: one mitten pressing a snowball. I'd appreciate your honest opinion. Thank you!

I'm a mom of two and I wrote a book called "Tape Line." Two siblings split their bedroom with masking tape. Each spread shows the line bending around a bunk ladder, a window, and a sleeping dog who lies across it. On the last spread, the tape is stuck to the ceiling, because nightmares don't respect borders. Thoughts?

Retired plumber here, writing for my grandkids. Pitch: "Every Tuesday, a wolf comes to the laundromat to wash one red hood. Nobody asks why. Mr. Okafor folds towels beside him and doesn't either." The book is about the neighbors who never ask and what that does for a wolf. Is it any good as a story idea? Be honest, I can take it.

I'm a new grandmother, and I wrote a board book for my grandson. Each page is a few words: "Sun goes. Shoes go. Dog goes, circle, circle, flop. Lights go. Words go soft." The last page is blank except for a small moon-shaped hole cut through it. What do you think of this one?

Hi! I'm an accountant in Accra and wrote a picture book premise on the side. Six-year-old Tola keeps a bedtime ledger: "Owed to me: 2 stories, 1 glass of water, 3 minutes of hall light. Owed by me: 1 tooth-brushing (disputed)." Her tired father starts auditing back. It ends with both writing "Balance: zero" and falling asleep. Be honest, would a publisher read past page one?

Hola, I'm a lawyer in Rosario and I'm a bit nervous sharing this. Premise: Nina invents a word, "sombrilento", for pretending to sleep in the car so Papá will carry you inside. She tries to get it into the dictionary by asking every neighbour in her building to use it once. The last neighbour is her father, who already knew it. Does it work for ages 4 to 7?

I've been a magistrate in Nakuru for twenty years, and this is my first children's story. Title: "The Trial of the Rooster." The farmyard charges him with disturbing the peace at 5 a.m. His only witness is the sun, who testifies she rises only when he asks her. The hens ask him to sing softer. Offended, the sun sleeps in until noon. What would you change, if anything?

I'm a dentist in Tampere, and I wrote this during a slow week. Every lost tooth goes to a tiny museum run by one tired fairy, who labels each with its story: "Eino, 7, lost it in a sauna bucket." One night a tooth arrives with no label, because the child never said a word. The fairy spends the book trying to learn why. Any thoughts? Totally fine to be blunt.

I'm a chef in Oaxaca, and this is outside my kitchen. Marisol's abuela has died. Her handwritten soup recipe ends: "Add salt until it tastes like home." Marisol, who is eight, has no idea what that means, so she visits each relative's kitchen and tastes their versions. Every soup is different, and every one is wrong. The last page is her own pot. How does the premise land for you?

G'day, I'm an air traffic controller in Brisbane, so my day job is all about getting things off the ground. Idea: every autumn the geese file a flight plan with the wind. This year one gosling files hers with a single destination: "Up." The wind keeps correcting her paperwork, and the flock keeps stamping it anyway. Does that sound like a book kids would ask for twice?

I'm a pharmacist in Kyoto, and I've never shown anyone my writing. Yuki's grandmother keeps asking, "And who are you?" Instead of crying, Yuki answers with a different true thing each day: "I'm the one who cuts your pears." "I'm the one who knows you hum in the bath." On the last page, the grandmother answers the question herself. I'd really value your opinion, especially on the ending.

I'm a structural engineer in Stuttgart, and I've tried turning my work into a children's book. Jonas is afraid of anything that wobbles, so he refuses to cross the old town bridge. An engineer shows him the expansion joints: the bridge shrinks every winter and stretches every summer, and it's only strong because it's allowed to move. Jonas crosses on the last page, arms out. Would you read this to a child?

I'm a paramedic in Thunder Bay, and I wrote this after a night shift. Gus is a snowplow who clears the roads while the town sleeps. Every morning everyone thanks the weather for being kind, and nobody knows his name. One night a girl leaves a thermos of cocoa on her mailbox with a note: "For whoever does this." Gus can't drink it, but he keeps the note on his dashboard forever. Thoughts?

I'm a geologist in Cape Town, and I've been sitting on this for a year. A boy asks the mountain to move closer to the sea. Each spread, a century passes and the mountain shifts by about the width of a thumb. The boy grows old, then his family changes, and the sea stays far away. On the final page, his great-great-granddaughter puts her hand where the rock used to be. Please tell me what you honestly think.

I'm an architect in Wellington, and this is the opening of a middle-grade novel I've been drafting: "The first thing you should know about my grandmother is that she was never lost. The second is that she was never where she said she'd be. The third is that on the morning she vanished for good, she'd left the kettle on, a map of our street, and one very clear instruction: don't tell Mum." What do you think?

I'm an actuary in Singapore, so I think about worst cases for a living. My picture book alternates a child's question with an adult's answer. "What if the rain doesn't stop?" "Then we'll learn to float things. And then we'd have soup." "What if I forget the words at the concert?" "Then you'll hum, and we'll clap anyway. And then we'd have soup." It builds to the biggest worry of all. Can you tell me how it reads?

I'm an astronomer in La Serena, Chile. Here's my idea: Ximena learns that the starlight she sees left its star long ago, so she writes a letter to the star knowing the reply will take four hundred years. She posts it anyway, on a hill, in a bottle. Then she realises the glow above her is a letter someone posted to her, centuries early. It just arrived. Do you think a six-year-old would follow it?

I'm a cardiologist in Pune. I've written rhyme for children for the first time, and here is the opening: "Before you had a name, or knees, or toes, / a small drum started up. Nobody knows / who taught it how. It hasn't missed a beat. / Not when you slept. Not when you sneezed. Not once." It goes on to explain the heart. Does the rhythm hold up, or am I fooling myself?

I'm an airline pilot based in Recife, and I've been sketching a wordless picture book. A red thread hangs from a boy's sweater and unravels as he wanders through a busy market. Strangers pick it up and wind it into a ball without a word: a fishmonger, a nun, a teenager with headphones. The ball grows huge. On the last spread, his mother follows it to him. Does a story without text need something more?

Hello! I'm a grandmother of four and I drew up a garden for the grandkids to plant this spring. It's one 4x4 bed. Middle: 2 pumpkins, then 6 lettuces, 3 tomatoes, 4 rows of corn, and a ring of sunflowers all around the edge. I put a little sign that says "Grandma's Happy Patch." Could you tell me what you think of the layout?

Dear all, my wife passed last year and I'm planting a rose garden in her memory in a 6x6 patch by the porch. Fourteen rose bushes, one for every year we spent at this house, set in tight rows, with a 4-inch path so I can walk between them. I'm a bit nervous to share it. Any thoughts on the plan?

Hi everyone! Retired teacher here, now running our little community garden. Here's my plan for the empty 10x10 lot: four plots, each 8x8 feet, one for each season of the year, with a bench in the middle. I'll hand it to the committee on Tuesday. Would love your feedback before then!

Hey folks, casual question. I'm 68 and just retired, and I've got a spot under our giant oak tree where I want to put my tomato and pepper beds, since it's nice and cool there for the plants. Then a hammock on the sunny side for me. Sketch is basically that. Thoughts?

I'm a mom of three and I'm helping with our elementary school garden. My plan: one long straight row, left to right, labeled with cute signs: carrots, mint, basil, beans, mint, strawberries, pumpkins, more mint. The kids can walk along the front and wave hello. What's your opinion?

Hi! Grandpa here. I'm building a fairy garden for my granddaughter Lily. Plan: a 3-foot circle with a tiny house in the center, a pebble path, and 9 real fern plants and 5 cacti around the pond I'll make from a pie dish. I'm so excited to show her. How does it sound to you?

Hello, I volunteer at our church and we're planting a memorial border along the front wall. I've planned it so the 5-foot hollyhocks go in front along the walkway, and the little pansies sit behind them against the wall, so everyone sees the lovely flowers on their way in. Could I get your honest opinion?

Hi there, I'm a retired nurse starting a butterfly garden for my neighbors. The plan is one big bed, 12x3 feet, filled with nothing but orange marigolds, edge to edge, so the butterflies know where to land. I'll add a sign: "Butterflies Welcome." Please let me know what you think!

Hello, my husband and I are retired and want a backyard layout for family barbecues. The patio and dining table go in the corner, and the compost pile sits right next to the table so the kids can learn about nature while they eat. The herb garden is on the far side of the yard, past the shed. What do you think?

I volunteer with our town's accessible garden project. Here's my plan for the raised beds: eight beds, each 3 feet high, arranged in rows with 18-inch paths between them and three steps up to the entrance. I tried to think of everything for our seniors. I'd really like to hear your thoughts.

Hi, I'm a grandma who has never designed a garden before! I have a shady strip, north of the shed, where it never gets sun. I want to put my tomatoes, sunflowers, and zucchini there, in a pretty zigzag. Then a little sign: "Where Love Grows." Can you tell me what you think of the idea?

Hello! I'm a dad and I made a garden plan for my twin girls. Their names are in the design: a bed shaped like an "A" and a bed shaped like a "M" in a 5x5 yard. I put the water spigot at the far end of the yard, 80 feet away, so they get exercise. What's your opinion?

Hi all, I'm 72 and just built a little vegetable bed, 2x4 feet, in my backyard. Planting list: 3 tomatoes, 2 zucchini, 1 watermelon, 4 rows of corn, 6 cucumbers, and a pumpkin, all spaced "cozy" so they'll be like a family. Could you look it over and share your thoughts?

Hi, our neighborhood garden club asked me to design the new entrance bed. I've put a circle of red geraniums in the middle, with red tulips around that, then red petunias, then a ring of red salvia, and a red bench in the center. Red is Margaret's favorite color, and the bed is in her memory. What do you think?

My granddaughter and I are making a "tea party garden" in our 3x3 patch. Chamomile, lavender, mint, lemon balm, and a tiny table in the middle that takes up most of the space. The plants will be squeezed into the corners, but it will be cozy. I wrote a little poem for the sign too. Could you tell me what you think?

I'm a dentist in Leeds, so gardens are new to me, but I drew a plan for our back garden, which is 6m x 5m. Round lawn 5m wide, a 3m x 3m patio, a 2m pond, a 3m x 2m veg patch, plus a shed and the kids' swing. I even coloured it in! What's your opinion?

Hi all, I'm a pilot from Curitiba and this is my first garden plan. Under our big old mango tree, which has dense shade all day, I'll grow tomatoes, peppers and sunflowers, because my grandmother grew them. Then a bench facing the compost heap, so I can watch it work. Any thoughts?

Hello, I'm an accountant in Lagos and I spent three weekends on this plan for my mother's garden. Her rose bed goes along the north wall, where the sun never reaches, with lavender and sunflowers beside it. A winding path leads to a bench, and the bench faces the bin store. Please tell me what you think.

Hey, I'm a lawyer in Winnipeg and I got carried away with a garden sketch. Along the back fence: five palm trees and two banana plants, to remind me of our honeymoon in Hawaii. We get -35°C in winter, but I'll water them well. Would love your take on the layout, if you've got a minute!

I'm a nurse in Brisbane and I've planned our veggie patch, which is 1m x 1m. Pumpkins in the corner, watermelons next to them, then corn, zucchini and climbing beans, all in the same square. The kids can pick their own snacks. Can I get a second opinion before I buy seeds?

I'm a physicist in Hamburg. For my granddaughter's birth I've planned a giant redwood, two metres from the kitchen window, so she'll one day have shade and think of me. Around it I'll put tulips and a little swing. The garden is 8m x 6m. What do you make of the plan?

I'm a pharmacist in Cork and I made this plan for Nan's memorial garden. Heart-shaped beds, a wishing well, six gnomes, and a sign that says 'Grow Where You Are Planted'. A bird bath sits in the middle with the words 'Live, Laugh, Garden' on it. I'd value your honest feedback. Thank you!

I'm a banker in Osaka. Here's my plan for a small Zen garden, 2m x 2m: three waterfalls, a 1m x 1m pond with forty koi, a stone lantern, a bridge, and a tea house. It should be very peaceful. I'm a total beginner and wondered whether you'd comment on the design.

Software engineer here, in Nairobi. I planned my mum's garden for her birthday. The lettuce and spinach bed is at the front, and the free-range chickens roam the whole yard with no fence, because they'll learn to respect the border. Also a hammock. Be straight with me: what do you think?

I'm a judge in Guadalajara, and gardens are a new hobby. My courtyard is 3m x 3m, and I will plant ten apple trees 30cm apart, so every morning will smell like my childhood orchard. I'll put a small table in the middle. Does this plan work for you? Tell me what you think, please.

I'm a journalist in Gothenburg and I'm so proud of this: a hammock strung between two baby birch saplings, each about 50cm tall and 1m apart, so we can nap in the sun together. Beside them, a table for coffee. I'd love to hear your thoughts on the layout!

I'm a paramedic in Dunedin. I've sketched a bee-friendly garden: one big wildflower meadow, a bee hotel, and a pond. To keep the meadow neat, I'll spray weedkiller around all the edges every fortnight and use slug pellets throughout. It's all for the bees! Please tell me what you think.

Here's the plan for my back garden, a north-facing slope, 12m x 8m. Top terrace: espaliered apples on the warm west wall, rhubarb beneath. Middle: a curving gravel path that bends at the old pear, so the bench stays hidden until you're nearly on it. Bottom: a rain garden fed by the downpipe, planted with iris, astilbe and meadowsweet. Compost bays tucked behind a hazel hurdle. Any thoughts? Anything you'd change?

I'm a bit nervous sharing this. It's a garden for my grandchildren, aged 3 to 9. A willow tunnel leads to a sunflower "room" with four-foot walls. Strawberries fill the lowest bed at toddler height; tougher things like fennel and sweetcorn go at the back. Stepping stones are spaced for short legs. A mud kitchen sits in the apple tree's shade, near the tap. Could you tell me what you think?

Hi all, here's my draft layout for the Elm Street community plot (10 x 20m). Four raised beds at 75cm with 1.2m paths for wheelchairs, plus a wider turning circle by the shed. A shared herb spiral at the entrance for anyone to pick from. A three-sisters bed for the school group. Water butts on the shed roof, and a tap at the centre so nobody carries a can more than six metres. Honest feedback welcome.

I'm proud to share my bee border, 15 metres long, planned for continuous bloom. Crocus and hellebore at the front for February, then pulmonaria, alliums, nepeta in June, and echinacea and sedum in September, with ivy on the back wall flowering into October. Plants step up in three tiers, in drifts of five or seven. I'd love to hear what you make of it.

Our courtyard is only 4 x 5 metres, so I drew it vertically. The south wall gets wire trellis with an espaliered fig and potted tomatoes; the shady wall gets ferns and a hanging rail of herbs. The floor is reclaimed brick in herringbone, with thyme in the joints. A mirror panel opposite the door doubles the view. The kids' sandpit lid folds into a bench. How does it read to you?

I've never shown my drawings to anyone. This is my south-facing front garden: sandy soil, hosepipe bans, no lawn. A gravel sweep with clumps of lavender and santolina, three drifts of Stipa tenuissima that ripple in wind, and Verbena bonariensis seeding through. One boulder from the old wall sits off-centre from the door so the eye travels. 5cm gravel mulch to cut weeding. Please be honest, what would you change?

I drew this garden for my husband, who has lost most of his sight. A rope handrail guides him along the path, with lavender at hand height at the first bend, then lamb's ear and rosemary. Grasses that rustle mark the middle, a wind chime tells him the bench is near, and a honeysuckle arch scents the end. Edges are raised bricks he can feel with his cane. What's your opinion?

Our village orchard committee asked me to draw up the planting. Twelve trees on 6m spacing, staggered rows, with varieties chosen across pollination groups 3 and 4: Katy, Discovery, Ashmead's Kernel, Egremont Russet and others. Mown paths run through long meadow grass, with bulbs under each tree. A bench at the high point faces the church spire. Bat boxes go on the oak. Would love your feedback before we order stock.

Here's the veg plot I've sketched, 8 x 6m. Four beds on a four-year rotation: legumes, brassicas, roots, then potatoes and alliums. A fifth permanent bed holds asparagus, artichokes and rhubarb. Climbing beans stand on the north side so they won't shade anything. Nasturtiums on the corners act as aphid decoys. Paths are 90cm, wide enough for a barrow. Does it make sense to you? Happy to hear anything.

Under our big beech nothing grows, so I planned around it. Rather than fight the roots, I'm building a shallow mulched bed in a wide crescent: epimediums, hardy geraniums, woodland anemones, and ferns in drifts, with snowdrops threaded through for winter. A leaf-mould path follows the crescent, ending at a log seat. Plants go in with minimal digging. Curious what you think, especially about the planting density.

I've made each of my four grandchildren a birthday bed around a central sundial, placed by their birth month so the sun finds each in turn. Lily's March bed has daffodils and primroses, Sam's July bed has lavender and phlox, and so on, each with a small plaque. A low box hedge ties them together. It's all on the attached sketch in my head, so here it is in words. What do you think?

I'm a volunteer at our hospice and have planned the courtyard garden. Raised beds at 60cm line the windows so bedbound patients see blooms at eye level. I've kept strong scents away from the ward doors, because of nausea, and put them by the seating instead. Colour moves from soft blues near the windows to warm yellows at the far wall. A shallow pond sits where light bounces onto the ceiling. Any feedback?

We keep four hens and I've planned the garden around them. Four beds, with the hens in a movable run rotating through one every six weeks to clear weeds, eat pests and fertilise. The bed after them gets brassicas; the bed before them gets cover crop. Fruit bushes have chicken-wire collars. The coop sits at the centre so paths radiate out like spokes. Is this sensible? I'd welcome any thoughts.

I've designed a small Japanese-style garden, 5 x 7 metres, built around my neighbour's maple, which I borrow as the main view. A raked gravel "stream" curves toward it past three mossy stones. Planting is restrained: ferns, hostas and one clipped pine. A low fence hides the shed and frames the maple like a picture. The bench faces it at a slight angle. I'd value your opinion.

I'm part of our roadside beautification group and drew up the junction verge. Planting stays under 60cm near the corner so drivers keep their sightlines, rising to 1.5m toward the hedge. Everything is salt-tolerant: sea thrift, sedum, tough grasses and rugosa roses. A shallow dip collects road runoff, planted with rushes. Four stepping stones give the council a mowing line. Does this look workable? Be as critical as you like.

I'm a cardiologist, and I've drawn up our walled Edinburgh garden (6 x 14 m), my first ever design. The north wall faces south, so it carries espaliered 'Conference' pears over hardy geraniums. The shady opposite wall gets ferns, Hakonechloa and white foxgloves, lit by a mirror panel. The gravel path kinks once, hiding the back bench until you're beside it. Spring bulbs go under a multi-stem Himalayan birch. Honest thoughts? I'm a bit nervous showing this.

I'm an accountant in Lagos. Courtyard plan, 4 x 8 m: roof runoff goes by gutter into a 2,000-litre tank, which overflows into a planted swale of papyrus and canna along the wall. Raised beds of ugu, tomatoes and amaranth take the sunniest end. A frangipani shades the west seating at 4pm, and a bean trellis cools the hot wall behind it. Casual question: where would you poke holes in it?

I'm a nurse in Kyoto, and this is the tsuboniwa for our entryway, only 2 x 4 m. One mossy mound, one maple placed a third from the left, and stepping stones that go from wide to narrow so the walk feels longer. A bamboo-fed stone basin is visible from the tatami room but hidden from the street. I'd really value your opinion, if you have a moment.

Structural engineer in Mexico City here, designing my rooftop garden (5 x 7 m, 150 kg/m² limit). Heavy planters sit over the beam lines on the east and south edges. The centre beds use a pumice-perlite mix with agaves, salvia and cempasúchil. A bougainvillea pergola shades the west side, and everything slopes 1% to the existing drain. I can check the loads, but does the planting layout work for someone who actually gardens?

I'm a chef in Melbourne, and I planned my garden by what I reach for mid-service. Zone 1, by the back door: a keyhole bed of chives, parsley, thyme and sorrel. Zone 2: a sunny bed of shiso, Thai basil and chillies, with lemon verbena beside the tea table. Zone 3, the back fence: espaliered quince and a compost bay behind a bay laurel screen. I'd love your take. Be blunt!

I'm an airline pilot in Bergen. The wind comes off the fjord from the southwest, so I used turbulence logic: no solid fence. Instead, a 1.2 m permeable hedge of Rosa rugosa and sea buckthorn, which filters the gusts. The raised beds sit 4–8 m behind it in the calmer lee, with cloudberry and rhubarb at the edge and brassicas deeper in. What would you change? Any opinion welcome.

I teach physics in Kerala, and I've sketched our 20-cent homestead as layers. Coconut palms go along the north edge so they won't shade the rest. Banana and papaya form the mid-layer, with turmeric, ginger and colocasia beneath. Black pepper climbs the arecanut trunks. A small fish pond sits in the low corner to catch runoff, and the vegetables are nearest the kitchen door. Tell me what you think when you get a minute!

I'm a lawyer in Cape Town, and I'm planning a fire-wise fynbos slope. Plan: 5 m of gravel and mown lawn beside the house, then a low band of Carpobrotus and Crassula, then proteas, leucadendrons and restios in separate islands, never a continuous fuel line. Sugarbirds get a pincushion protea by the stoep. I'd appreciate a candid opinion, since I'm way out of my depth here.

Paramedic in Winnipeg, zone 3. Snow from the shovelled driveway always piles in the northeast corner, so I've designed that corner for it: red-osier dogwood, which loves meltwater and gives red winter stems, plus a drift of Siberian squill. The sunny south bed holds prairie smoke, purple coneflower and little bluestem, cut in March. A paved loop circles a crabapple. Thoughts? I'm hoping to start digging in May.

I'm a violinist in Vienna, and I've laid out my 8 x 20 m allotment path as movements. March: snowdrops and hellebores at the gate. April–May: tulips, then alliums rising through catmint. July: a crescendo of phlox and Verbena bonariensis at the midpoint bench. September: asters and Miscanthus carry the finale to the shed. Evergreen yew hedges act as rests. Does it read well to you? Please be frank.

I'm a translator in Bogotá, at 2,600 m, and I've planned a hummingbird corridor along our 15 m side wall. Fuchsia and Salvia in the shade, Cuphea and Fuchsia boliviana in the middle, and a trumpet-flowered Brugmansia canopy at the sunny end. Each stretch blooms in a different month so nectar never stops. A shallow mister dish sits at the halfway point. Any thoughts? I'm happy to hear criticism.

I'm a dentist in Tbilisi. Here's my backyard plan: a Rkatsiteli grape pergola over the dining table, with posts spaced so the deciduous vines shade us in July and let in low winter sun after leaf drop. A fig and a pomegranate stand against the south wall, tarragon and mint under the dripline, and river-stone paths connect it all. What do you think? I'm curious whether it would actually work.

I'm a bus driver in Auckland. Behind our house is a 12 m clay bank that slumps every winter. My plan: diagonal timber steps in a switchback, so water can't run straight down. Harakeke and toetoe go in the wet gully, deep-rooted kōwhai and ponga mid-slope, and coprosma with groundcover pōhuehue along the crest. Everything is native, so birds can nest. Could you tell me honestly how it looks on paper?

I'm a pharmacist in Cairo, and my 6 x 6 m courtyard plan is built around night use. We only sit outside after 9pm in summer, so jasmine, tuberose and Cestrum nocturnum are grouped near the seating, where the scent pools. A narrow water channel runs from a date palm to the bench, cooling the tiles. Daytime colour, like bougainvillea, sits at the edges. Would love your opinion!

I'm an electrician in Dublin, and I've split my narrow terraced garden (4 x 10 m) into three rooms. First, a brick-paved dining space with a pleached hornbeam screen. Next, a gravel room, with Stipa and thyme, that dips slightly in the middle. Last, a hidden lawn the size of a rug, ringed by tall Thalictrum and a black-painted shed. Each opening is offset so you never see the full length. Any feedback? Cheers!

Hi! I'm 68 and just retired from teaching third grade. I've written a logline for a movie I'd love to see made: "A small-town baker about to lose her bakery discovers that the real treasure was the friends she made along the way." My husband says it's sweet. Could you tell me what you think of it?

Hello, I'm a grandpa of five and I made up a movie idea for my grandkids. Here's the logline: "When a little boy's puppy gets lost in the snow, the whole town comes together to find him, and everyone learns that love always finds its way home." Would you give me your honest opinion?

I volunteer on our church's Christmas committee, and I've been writing a movie idea in my spare time. The logline: "When a big-city businessman gets stranded in a small town at Christmas, he learns the true meaning of the season." I'd love to hear your thoughts, if you have a minute!

Okay, this is my first time showing anyone this, so I'm a little nervous. I'm a grandmother, and I wrote a movie logline: "A lonely old man and a stray cat find each other and learn that home is where the heart is." Please be gentle, but tell me what you honestly think.

Hey there! Dad of three here. Bedtime stories turned into a movie idea: "A boy who is afraid of the dark goes on a magical journey and discovers that the dark was his friend all along." My kids ask for it every night. Any feedback for me? Anything at all.

I'm 72 and a retired mail carrier, and I finally put my movie idea on paper. Logline: "A retired postman drives across America to deliver one last letter, and along the way he delivers a little love to everyone he meets." Proud of this one! What's your take?

I run the Saturday story hour at our library as a volunteer. I came up with this movie logline: "A shy librarian opens a dusty old book and finds real magic inside, and learns that the real magic was reading all along." How does it read to you? I'd welcome any thoughts.

Hello, I'm a retired farmer and my daughter told me to ask somebody about this. I wrote a movie logline: "Three brothers inherit the family farm and must learn to work together to save it, because in the end, family is everything." What would you say about it?

I'm a quilting grandma, and I've been working on a movie idea for my granddaughter. Here's the logline: "A little girl's patchwork quilt takes her on wonderful adventures and teaches her that love is the warmest blanket of all." Can you tell me what you think? Thank you, dear!

I spent 40 years as a nurse and now I write a little. Here's my movie logline: "A kind nurse in a small-town hospital cares for everyone who comes through the door, and in the end, someone cares for her." I'd really value your opinion on it.

I'm a volunteer at our local fire station, and the kids love our dog, so I wrote this logline: "A brave golden retriever firehouse mascot saves the day, and everybody learns the importance of teamwork." Just curious what you think! Be as honest as you like.

Retired farmer here, 74. Wrote a movie logline during the long winters: "During the worst drought in memory, a farmer prays for rain, the whole town comes together, and finally the sky opens up." Not sure who to show it to, so I'm showing you. Thoughts?

Hi! Mom of two grown daughters. I wrote a movie logline inspired by our kitchen table: "Two sisters who haven't spoken in years reunite over their late mother's secret recipe, and old wounds begin to heal." I worked hard on getting it just right. What do you make of it?

My grandson and I go fishing every Sunday, and it gave me an idea for a movie. Logline: "An old fisherman teaches his grandson how to fish, and also how to live." I'm just a casual writer, nothing fancy. Does it sound like something you'd watch? Tell me what you think.

I help run the senior center's bingo afternoons, and I wrote a movie logline about us! "A group of spirited seniors start a bingo club and discover it's never too late to follow your dreams." The gang wants an outside opinion, so here I am. What do you think?

Hi! I'm a dentist in Curitiba, Brazil, and I've started writing movie ideas on weekends. Here's my logline: "When a grumpy old baker loses his shop, a stray puppy teaches him that the real treasure was the friends he made along the way." Could you tell me what you think? I'd love to hear your thoughts!

I'm a civil engineer in Lagos and I wrote my first logline last night. Proud of it, honestly. "A small-town girl with big dreams moves to the city to become a singer, but learns that home is where the heart is." Please give me your honest opinion. Would you watch it?

Hello, I'm an accountant from Cork. This is a bit outside my usual spreadsheets, so I'm nervous sharing it. "When a widowed farmer's last wish is to see the ocean, his granddaughter takes him on a road trip that heals the whole family." Any feedback would be appreciated.

hey, I'm a pediatric nurse in Manila and I wrote a movie logline on my break lol. "A kind-hearted little robot who wants to feel love discovers that the real feelings were inside him all along." thoughts? Tell me what you'd change, if anything.

I'm a corporate lawyer in Toronto, and writing screenplays is my secret hobby. My logline: "Two rival families in a snowy Vermont town enter the same Christmas bake-off, and the magic of the season brings them together." I'm planning to write the full script next. What's your take?

Greetings from Jaipur! I'm a cardiac surgeon, and I wrote a logline for a family film inspired by my son. "A shy boy who can never win at cricket learns that believing in yourself is the greatest victory of all." Kindly let me know your feedback. I'm eager to hear it.

I'm a commercial pilot based in Frankfurt and I've been writing a film idea during layovers. "A lonely lighthouse keeper finds a message in a bottle and sets off on a journey that shows him it's never too late to love again." How does it read to you?

Hello! I'm a pharmacist in Nairobi. I wrote this logline for my late grandmother, and it means a lot to me. "A girl inherits her grandmother's magic garden where every flower is a memory, and discovers that love never really dies." Can you give me your opinion on it?

G'day, I'm an actuary in Adelaide and I wrote a movie logline for my kids. "A sheepdog who is too small to herd learns that being small is her superpower." The kids liked it, but I'd like a grown-up opinion too. What do you reckon?

Hola, I'm an architect in Guadalajara. I'm new to screenwriting but I put my heart into this: "A busy city girl inherits her late grandmother's ranch and discovers the true meaning of family." I'd be so grateful if you could tell me what you think of it!

I teach chemistry at a high school in Kraków and have been writing a film idea in secret. "A time-travelling teacher goes back to tell his younger self to say 'I love you' before it's too late." I'm a little nervous to ask, but what do you make of it?

I'm a veterinarian in Inverness and I came up with this after a long day at the clinic. "A grumpy cat and a cheerful dog get lost in the Highlands and learn that opposites make the best friends." Would love your feedback before I show my wife!

Hi, I'm a banker in Singapore. In my spare time I write movie loglines, and this one is my favourite so far. "A workaholic businessman forgets what matters most until a magical Christmas Eve reminds him that family is the best gift." What's your opinion?

Sawubona! I'm an electrician in Durban and I wrote my first movie logline. "A boy from the township finds a magic football that helps him make his dreams come true, and he learns that hard work always pays off." Please tell me how you find it. I'm very proud of it.

I'm a radiologist in Gothenburg, and I've been writing a film idea about my farmmor's quilt. "A handmade quilt passes down through four generations, and every stitch holds a love story." Do you have any feedback for me? Anything at all is welcome.

I drove the Number 9 bus for 38 years, and I wrote a logline about it after retiring. Here it is: "On the day the city cancels his route, a retiring bus driver secretly takes his regulars along the old line one last time, through a blizzard, with a stolen bus, and past the one stop he has never let anyone get off at." Would you give me your honest opinion?

Hi! I'm 74 and have been going to a screenwriting class at the library. This is my logline: "When the council votes to bulldoze a community garden, the widow who tends it learns her late husband buried something under the tomatoes in 1974. It could save the plot or send her best friend to prison." Does it read the way I hope it does? Any thoughts welcome.

I'm a night-shift nurse and a mom, and I wrote this in the break room. "A single mother working nights on a hospice ward, who hasn't slept properly in four years, begins to notice that the lullaby her toddler hums each morning matches the last words of every patient who died during her shift." I'd be nervous to show anyone local. What's your reaction?

Here's the logline for a movie I've been carrying around since I retired from tuning pianos: "Going deaf, a retired piano tuner takes one final house call, for the woman whose voice he has spent forty years trying to forget, and must decide whether to fix the one key that has been wrong since the night she left." What do you make of it?

Hello, I coordinate our church food pantry on Saturdays and I've been writing in the evenings. My logline: "Over one Thanksgiving week, a food pantry coordinator who is three weeks from eviction must decide whether to take home the turkeys she is rationing out to strangers." I'd love to hear your thoughts, and please be straight with me.

My bowls club friends laughed at this, so I'm asking you instead. "Two rival retirees at a lakeside bowls club, each certain the other murdered the beloved groundskeeper, join forces to prove it, then discover he faked his own death to avoid the annual fundraiser." It's a comedy, obviously. Can you tell me what works and what doesn't?

I'm a dad, and most of my best conversations with my daughter happen in the car. So I wrote this: "A taciturn father and his sixteen-year-old daughter speak only during their forty-minute school commute. Before the car's failing transmission finally gives out, they have to say what they've avoided since her mother died." Could you tell me how it lands for you?

Grandson says I should send this to someone who knows about movies, so here goes. "When the last ferry to a Newfoundland outport is cancelled, its retired captain refuses to leave his dock, and the village slowly realizes he is the only one who remembers where the old shipwreck graves are marked." Is that something you'd want to watch? Tell me what you think.

I'm a retired schoolteacher and I volunteer at our town's historical society. I wrote this: "When the town's only translator dies, a retired schoolteacher becomes the last person able to read the founders' letters, and discovers that the town's proud origin story was a mistranslation that someone has profited from for a century." Would you mind giving me feedback?

I'm the volunteer fire chief in a town of 212, and my daughter says I should write what I know. Here's my attempt: "On the night of the county's worst wildfire, a volunteer fire chief must choose which half of his crew gets sent back to defend their own homes, and which half stays to save the town's only nursing home." What's your take?

My quilting circle has been giggling over this for weeks. "Three grandmothers from a Sunday quilting circle plan to steal back the quilt a museum bought for forty dollars from their late friend's estate, stitching the heist schedule into the pattern of a new quilt they're 'donating' as cover." Please tell me honestly what you think, dear.

I'm a mom of a nonverbal ten-year-old and I wrote this late at night. "A mother who has memorized every bus route in Chicago so her nonverbal son can ride alone follows him across the city when he boards the wrong train, and slowly realizes he has been going somewhere deliberately." I'm a little nervous sharing it. How does it read to you?

Thirty-one years as a rural mail carrier, and this is what's been rattling around my head. "On his final day of delivering mail, a rural carrier finds a single undeliverable letter addressed to himself, in his own handwriting, postmarked 1983, and has until the last house on his route to decide whether to open it." What do you think? Be as blunt as you like.

I volunteer with hospice, and this idea came out of that. Here's the logline: "A hospice volunteer discovers that the dying man whose hand she holds is the soldier who once spared her father in a war neither family will name, and must decide whether his last peace is hers to take away." I'd value your opinion, if you're willing.

Grandpa here! I wrote a little summer movie idea for my grandkids. "Hired as the last lifeguard before the town pool is filled with concrete, a twelve-year-old who can't swim keeps the job by never letting anyone near the water, and by teaching the whole town, one rule at a time, to love the pool again." What do you think of it?

I'm a dentist in Lagos and I write screenplays on weekends. I'm a bit nervous showing this to anyone, but here's my logline: "When a retiring Lagos tailor discovers that the suits he sewed for forty years were used to smuggle a coded ledger in their linings, he has one week to unpick his life's work before the wrong men come to collect." Could you tell me honestly what you think?

Hi! Chemistry teacher in Osaka here, dabbling in film ideas. My logline: "The night before a bridge named for her late father reopens, an engineer finds a hairline crack only she can see, and must choose between her father's legacy and the thousand commuters who will cross at dawn." Any thoughts? Be as blunt as you like.

I'm a pediatric nurse in Buenos Aires, and I've finally written a movie logline. Sharing it with you: "In 1978, a mild-mannered bank auditor realizes the World Cup ticket sales are laundering money stolen from the disappeared, and has ninety minutes of the final to copy the books." I'd love your reaction. What works, what doesn't?

Evening! I'm a paramedic on Svalbard and the long dark gives me a lot of time to write. Here's my logline: "On the longest night of the polar winter, an island's only paramedic must talk a trapper through amputating his own leg over a radio that only works when the northern lights are quiet. Tonight, they won't stop." Curious what you make of it.

I'm a night-shift pharmacist in Mumbai, and I've never shown my writing to anyone before. My logline is: "A night pharmacist who has filled the same forged prescription every week for twelve years learns the patient died long ago, and that someone has still been collecting the medicine." Would you mind giving me your honest opinion?

Retired postal worker from Regina, Saskatchewan here, and I've been writing a movie idea. Logline: "To save their rink from being sold, a seventy-year-old curling skip must win one last bonspiel with the only teammates available: three townspeople who swore never to speak to each other again." Tell me what you think, eh? Don't hold back.

Oi! I'm a cardiologist in São Paulo and I wrote a movie logline on my lunch break. Here it is: "Six days before Rio's Carnival, a veteran seamstress finds her own secret stitch inside a rival samba school's costumes, proof that the daughter who stopped speaking to her is now the enemy's head designer." What's your take? Does it make you want to see the film?

I'm a GP on a Scottish island, and I'm trying my hand at screenwriting. Here's my logline: "A Hebridean doctor who has survived twenty years by never repeating what she hears is called for jury duty at the island's first murder trial, where every witness is her patient." I'd really value your feedback if you have a moment.

I'm a tax lawyer in Hamburg, and this is my first logline. Quite nervous to share it: "On the night the Wall falls, an East Berlin Stasi file clerk has until sunrise to shred forty years of records, and to decide whether her neighbours' betrayals, including her husband's, will survive her." Please tell me your honest thoughts.

G'day, I'm a physio from Perth and I've been messing about with film ideas. My logline: "When a con-man rainmaker arrives in a drought-struck Western Australian wheat town in 1957, the farmers know he's a fraud and pay him anyway, because hope is the only crop still growing. Then it rains." What do you reckon? Happy for straight talk.

I'm an accountant in Seoul, and I've written my first logline. Here it is: "A Seoul night-bus driver realizes the same sleeping passenger rides to the terminus every night. Tonight he doesn't wake up, and dispatch orders her to keep to the schedule." Could you give me your opinion on it? Thank you very much!

I'm a civil engineer in Oaxaca, and I wrote this logline for fun: "A brass-band trumpeter who has played at four hundred funerals learns the dying town's last undertaker has booked the band for his own, and left a list of the people who must not be allowed to attend." Tell me what you think! I'm happy to hear anything.

I'm a pediatric nurse in Tampere, Finland, and I have a sci-fi logline I'd like a second opinion on: "A translator at humanity's first alien embassy realizes that the aliens' language has no future tense, and that the peace treaty they proposed is not a promise but a record of something that has already happened." What do you think?

Hello from Accra! I'm a pharmacist, and I've written a logline for a film I'd love to see made. "A fantasy-coffin carpenter who has built coffins shaped like fish, Mercedes cars and cocoa pods is commissioned by his dying lifelong rival, who asks only for a plain box: the one design he has never managed to make." Be honest, please. How does it read to you?

Quick one: I'm a firefighter in Cork and I've been writing a film idea on night shifts. Logline: "A retired lighthouse keeper's daughter returns to scatter his ashes, and finds the automated light he fought against has been quietly kept burning by the village, which has been lying to the coast guard for ten years." Thoughts? Give it to me straight.

Hi! I'm giving the welcome speech at Thursday's Willow Creek Garden Club meeting. Here's how it starts: "Good evening, friends. A garden is like a friendship. You plant a seed, you water it with love, and before you know it, it blossoms into something beautiful. Just like each of you. Thank you for being the flowers in my life." Could you tell me what you think?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm nervous about this one! I have to say a few words at our knitting circle's 10th anniversary. Here it is: "Ten years ago we were strangers with yarn. Now we are a family with yarn. Life is like a scarf: one stitch at a time. Sometimes you drop a stitch, but you pick it up and keep going. Thank you all." Any thoughts before Tuesday?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Hey, wrote a quick thing for the PTA meeting tomorrow night. "Our kids are our future. They are the leaders of tomorrow. It takes a village to raise a child, and tonight I see a whole village in this room. So let's give our kids the best bake sale ever!" How does it come across to you?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm presenting our Volunteer of the Year award at Lions Club, and I wrote this for Margaret: "When the going gets tough, the tough get going, and Margaret got going. She gave her time, her heart, and her casseroles. She is the heart of our club and the heart of our town. Margaret, you are a shining star." Does it flow okay?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Our bowling league banquet is Saturday and I'm doing a little poem! "We came to bowl, we came to play, / we laughed and cheered the whole long day. / Some got strikes and some got gutters, / but we're all friends, no need for mutters. / Here's to the league, hip hip hooray!" What would you change, if anything?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm sharing a little story at the Friends of the Library meeting next week: "Once there was a small acorn who thought he was too little to matter. But he grew into a mighty oak, and the whole forest sheltered beneath him. So remember, no one is too small to make a difference." Do you think the group will enjoy it?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm giving the treasurer's report at our community garden meeting. "We raised $500 at the plant sale! We spent $200 on soil, $150 on seeds, and $250 on tools, leaving us with a healthy $100 for next year. Thank you all for your generosity!" I get a bit jittery with the numbers part. How does it sound?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: For our potluck club I'm giving a talk on Grandma's secret recipe. "Take a can of tomato soup, add a pound of ground beef and a box of macaroni. Stir and heat. That's it! The secret ingredient is love." I'll read it aloud on Friday. Thoughts?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Soccer boosters meet tonight and I volunteered to open. "Winning isn't everything. It's about teamwork, trying your best, and having fun. There's no I in team! Every player is a winner in my book. Go Tigers!" Could you tell me how it reads? I'm short on time, so a quick reply is fine!
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Dear helper, I'm to speak at quilting guild about our charity quilts: "Every quilt is made of many little pieces, just like our community. Each piece is different, but together they make something warm. When a child wraps up in our quilt, they are wrapped in our love." I'd love to hear your opinion.
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm retiring as secretary of the Birdwatchers Club and will give a farewell at the meeting: "Birds of a feather flock together, and I'm so glad I flocked with you. Now it's time for this old bird to fly away. Keep your eyes to the sky and your hearts full of song." Tell me what you think, please!
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Giving a short talk at our Scout troop's parents' night. "Scouting teaches kids to be prepared. Be prepared for the campfire, be prepared for the rain, and be prepared for life. Remember, a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step, or a single s'more." Looking for feedback, if you have a minute.
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: First time ever speaking in public! Our historical society asked me for a toast: "Here's to the good old days, when life was simple and neighbors were kind. Things were better back then. Let's keep the past alive for the future, because history is our story." Is that all right to read at the meeting?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Wrote a toast for chess club's end-of-year meeting, and I'm excited about the ending: "Life is like a game of chess. You must think ahead, protect your king, and never give up your queen. Thank you for the games, and checkmate to anyone who says old folks can't have fun!" How would you rate it out of ten?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm welcoming new volunteers at the food pantry on Monday. "Welcome, everyone! Giving is better than receiving. A little kindness goes a long way, and many hands make light work. Together we can make a difference, one can of beans at a time." Is there anything you'd tweak?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a dentist in Manchester, and I'm giving the welcome speech at our book club's 10th anniversary on Friday. Here's my draft: "Ten years ago we sat down with a book and a biscuit. Books are like friends: they open doors and open hearts. Here's to ten more years of turning pages and making memories. Because at the end of the day, a book club is a family." Could you tell me what you think?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Hi! Civil engineer in Lagos here, doing my first-ever speech for our garden club's harvest day. I wrote: "A garden is like life. You plant a seed, you water it with love, and one day it blooms. Every flower here is a little miracle. So let us all go forward and grow together, because together we bloom." Honestly any feedback welcome, thanks!
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm an ICU nurse in Toronto and I wrote a goodbye speech for Margaret, who's leaving our knitting circle: "Margaret, you have been the thread that held us together. You never dropped a stitch, or our hearts. We will miss you more than words can say. Wherever you go, you will always be a part of our wool family." Does it work, do you think?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: G'day, I'm an accountant in Sydney and I've got to say a few words at the surf club's season opener. Here's what I've got: "The ocean is our teacher. Sometimes the waves are big, sometimes small, but we always come back to shore. Surf club is about mateship, sunshine and giving it your all. So let's paddle out and have a great season!" What's your take?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a pharmacist in Mumbai, proposing the vote of thanks at our Rotary club dinner, and I'm a little nervous. This is my draft: "Thank you to our chief guest, who is a shining star in our sky. Thank you to the cooks, who made food with love. Without all of you, today would not be possible. Service above self, always. Thank you, thank you, thank you." Please share your thoughts.
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a firefighter in Cork and I volunteered to open our chess club's Christmas night. Wrote this on shift: "Life is a game of chess. The pawns may be small, but they dream of becoming queens. Tonight let's put down our worries, move our pieces, and remember that the real winner is friendship." Would love to hear what you make of it, lads.
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a software developer in Berlin, and I'm giving a toast at our allotment association's summer party. Here it is: "Our little gardens are like small pieces of heaven. The tomatoes are red, the beans are green, and the neighbours are the best I've seen. So raise a glass to sun and soil, and to the fruits of all our toil!" Thoughts?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Hello, I'm a lawyer in Nairobi. I'm to encourage members of our Saturday running club before the charity 10K. My speech: "Running is not about the finish line. It is about the journey. Every step you take is a step closer to your dreams. When your legs are tired, let your heart carry you. Remember, a journey of a thousand miles begins with one step." What do you think?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a physics teacher in Auckland and I wrote a speech for the lawn bowls club's 50th jubilee, which I'm quite proud of: "Fifty years ago, a few friends rolled a ball down a green. Today we are still rolling, still laughing, still having a cuppa after. Time flies when you're having fun, and bowls has given us the best years of our lives." Any thoughts?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a surgeon in Seoul. I've been asked to speak at our hiking club's anniversary, which is far from my usual work. I wrote: "The mountain does not care who you are. It only asks that you take the next step. We climb together, we laugh together, and at the top, we see that the view was worth every drop of sweat. Let's keep climbing!" Could you give me your opinion?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm an architect in Buenos Aires, and I'm giving a short speech at our tango club milonga tonight. Here it is: "Tango is the dance of the heart. Two people, one embrace, and the music carries them away. We build something beautiful, step by step, just like a house. So tonight, hold your partner close and dance like no one is watching." Tell me what you think?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a vet in County Clare and was asked to say grace-style words at our Women's Institute tea. I wrote: "We thank the hands that baked the scones, the hearts that poured the tea, and the friends who came together, as friends are meant to be. May our cups be full and our worries few, and may we always have a friend like you." Please let me know what you think.
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm an airline pilot based in Dubai, and I'm making a short speech to my photography club about our year. Draft: "A photograph freezes a moment forever. Every picture tells a story, and every story begins with a click. This year we captured sunsets, smiles and so many memories. Let's keep our lenses open and our hearts wide." How does it come across to you?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm an electrician in Glasgow and I've written a wee speech for my community choir's spring concert. "When we sing, we light up the room, just like a bulb in the dark. Every voice is a different colour, but together we make a rainbow. So sing out loud, sing out proud, and let the music bring us home." Be honest, what's your opinion?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a police officer in Cape Town and I run a community cooking club on weekends. For our year-end braai I wrote this: "Food brings people together. When we share a meal, we share a little piece of ourselves. Thank you for stirring pots, sharing laughs, and making Saturdays special. Remember, the secret ingredient is always love." Would you mind telling me what you think?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm speaking at garden club Thursday and I'm a bit nervous. Here's my opening: "Forty years I've grown tomatoes, and they've taught me one lesson: nothing ripens because you're watching it. My late husband Walter checked the vines every morning at six, as if disapproval could turn them red. They ripened the minute he went in for coffee. So tonight: patience, mulch, and the courage to walk away." Could you tell me what you think?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Hi! Here's the two-minute talk I gave at our Lions Club about the food pantry. Honest thoughts welcome. "Last March a boy of about nine came in alone and asked if we had any food that didn't need a stove. Nobody had ever asked me that. We now stock a shelf for him: peanut butter, pop-top tuna, fruit cups. It cost $212. Tonight I'm asking you to help keep it full."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a retired teacher and I gave this at our historical society last week. Feedback, please! "Our war memorial carries 212 names, and I know the stories of nine. Tonight I'll tell you three. The other 203 are why I'm asking you to join the archive committee. Every name is a door, and most of us have walked past them for decades without knocking."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Mum of three here, and I'm proud of this little thing I said to open the PTA meeting. "I have three kids, two jobs, and one oven that runs twenty degrees hot. If I can bring forty cupcakes that are only slightly charred, you can bring one tray of anything. Burnt is a flavour. The sign-up sheet is by the door." Does it work as an opener, do you reckon?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Stepping down as treasurer of our angling club after 22 years. This is my goodbye, and I'd value a second pair of eyes. "I've counted every pound you ever paid me, and I can tell you what this club is worth. It isn't the £4,112 in the account. It's the 6 a.m. flask of tea that Alan pours for whoever arrives last, and never mentions."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I read this at our quilting circle to remember Dorothy, who died in May. I'd love to know how it comes across. "Dorothy never threw out a scrap. She said every piece had been part of somebody's life, so it deserved another. Look around this room: her blue gingham is in my grandson's blanket, and her curtain fabric is in yours. We're all wearing a little of her, stitched in tight."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a soccer dad and booster club president, and here's what I said at the end-of-season dinner. Thoughts? "We won three games this year. You won't remember the score of any of them. But you'll remember Priya, who lost her shoe in the mud and kept dribbling, and the whole bench roaring. Winning fades. Roaring doesn't. Thank you, parents, for roaring."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Our neighborhood watch meets tonight and I'm giving a short talk. Be gentle, I'm a bit nervous! "People think a watch is about spotting strangers. Mostly it's the opposite. It's knowing that Mr. Okafor takes his bins out Tuesdays, so when they're still out Thursday, someone knocks. Forty-one households. Forty-one people who'd notice. That's the whole security system, and it's the best one I know."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Retired nurse, first time speaking at book club. Here's what I said when explaining my pick. Would love your feedback. "I chose this book because for thirty years I held hands in rooms where nobody knew what to say. The author does what I never could: she says it plainly, and she stays. If you finish it and feel quieter, not sadder, that's the book working."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I run the chess club at the community centre and welcome every new member with this. Tell me what you make of it! "You'll lose your first fifty games. I did. I'm seventy-three and I still lose, usually to a ten-year-old named Maya. A loss is just the board explaining something to you, slowly. Sit down, shake hands, and let it explain."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a retired mail carrier, and our Rotary Club gave me an award. This was my reply. Does it land? "For 34 years I knew your dogs by name and your bills by weight. I knew who was waiting for a letter. Some days I carried the only good news on your street, and some days, honestly, a catalogue. Thank you for the cold lemonade, and the warm hellos."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Volunteer at the library, and I need to recruit for our Friends group next week. Here's my pitch. How does it sound to you? "We're not asking for your weekends. We're asking for one Tuesday a month, and a willingness to be talked into things. Last year this group bought 600 books and a new roof for the children's corner. The roof was Margaret's idea. Come have an idea."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Granddad here, giving the toast at our choir's anniversary supper. I'd love an honest opinion. "Twenty years ago, eleven of us couldn't agree on the key. Tonight, forty of us still can't, but we've learned something better: when one voice wobbles, the rest lean in. That's not just harmony. That's how a village works. Glasses up, to leaning in."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a retired engineer and I give a short talk to our birdwatching club each month. This is the opening of today's. Be frank! "The swift spends almost ten months of the year in the air. It eats, drinks, mates, and sleeps on the wing. It touches down only to nest. We have been trying to fly for centuries, and it turns out the real achievement was never landing."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a new grandma and volunteer with our community choir's fundraising. Here's my brief appeal from tonight's meeting. What would you say? "Last winter our hall's heating failed mid-rehearsal. Nobody left. We sang in coats, our breath visible, and it was the best we've ever sounded. I'd like us to never do that again. We need £3,000 for a boiler. Please help me keep the choir warm."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Wrote this for our allotment society's annual meeting and I'm a little anxious about reading it. "Plot 14 was a bramble patch when Eileen took it on at eighty. Everyone gave it a season. She gave it a decade. Last Saturday I counted: nine kinds of bean, a pear tree she grew from a pip, and a bench for anyone who needs one. Let that be our standard: leave it better than the brambles."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Nurse in Manchester here, writing a send-off for Frank at our chess club. My speech: "Frank has played the Sicilian against me for eleven years, and I've never beaten it. Some of us learned chess from books; some learned it from Frank. Only one of those taught us to lose without sulking. Cornwall is getting a fine player. We'll keep his chair empty and the board set." Any thoughts before Thursday?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a civil engineer in Nairobi, and I got roped into welcoming new members at our beekeepers' club. Here's what I'll say: "A bridge I build must stand sixty years. A hive does it in six weeks, with no drawings, no permit, no meetings. So don't come to teach the bees. Come to be inspected by them. The honey is how they say you passed." What do you think?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Hi! I'm a dentist in Toronto and I have to give the end-of-season toast at our curling club. Please be honest: "Curling is the only sport where you shout at a rock, apologise to your opponent, then buy them a drink. I've spent thirty years telling people to floss. Here I learned the harder lesson: sweep like you mean it, and once the stone has gone, it's gone."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Our book club in Auckland turns ten, and as a pilot I've somehow been handed the speech. Nervous! Here it is: "In ten years we've read 119 books, finished 61, and lost one member to a dispute over Ulysses. But one habit has survived everything: whoever finishes first says the ending out loud, and we all pretend to be furious, and we are all grateful." Does it work?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a tax accountant in Lagos, giving a pep talk to my running club before the half marathon. Draft: "At kilometre fifteen your body sends an invoice. Don't dispute it. Negotiate. Pay in instalments: one lamppost, then the next. I audit people's finances for a living, and I promise you this is the only debt that leaves you richer once it's settled." Would you change anything?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a paramedic in Glasgow. I introduce the films at our film society, and this is my intro for Friday: "Tonight's film has a car chase, a kiss in the rain, and a man who survives a fall from four storeys. I've attended three of those falls. Please enjoy the version where he stands up and makes a joke. Cinema is the kindest lie we tell about bodies. Lights down." Thoughts?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: Surveyor from Chennai here, writing outside my usual world of boundary lines. For our astronomy club's open night I've written: "I measure land to the millimetre, and every night the sky tells me I've been measuring the wrong thing. The light from Andromeda left home before anyone had a word for light. Tonight we look at the past together. Whisper, please. Old light is shy." How does it read to you?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a pharmacist in Dublin and I'm saying a few words at our choir's twentieth anniversary. Feedback welcome! "Every medicine has a dose, and so does every choir. Too little and no one notices; too much and the tenors take over. Margaret has known the difference for twenty years. Tonight, may our altos be audible, our sopranos merciful, and our tenors reminded that the piece has other parts."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I weld for a living in Perth and I've never given a speech, but our gardening club asked me to share my tomato story. My shaky draft: "Welds are only as strong as what's underneath, and so are tomatoes. Three summers of split fruit, until Dot next door said, 'Water them like you mean to come back.' That's the whole secret: steady, and show up. I've brought samples. The ugly ones are sweetest." Is that okay?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a large-animal vet in Montana, and I'm opening our fly-fishing club's spring meeting with this: "I spend my days with an arm inside a cow, so trust me on patience: it's mostly about where you put your hands. On the river, keep them still. The trout hasn't read your résumé. It only knows whether the fly is lying well. Tonight, let's all lie better, and release gently." Feedback?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a lawyer in Buenos Aires, and I've been asked to toast our tango club at its anniversary. Here's my attempt: "In court I'm paid to interrupt. In tango, interrupting is a crime. One proposes, the other answers, and for three minutes nobody objects. I've lost cases and gained posture. To the milonga: the only room in Buenos Aires where silence means yes and nobody reads the small print." What's your opinion?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I drive a bus in Lisbon and write nothing but timetables, but our photography club wants a talk. Opening lines: "Twenty-two years on the same route, and it's never the same street. The light moves four minutes every week. A baker's shutter rises at 5:50. So don't travel to find a picture. Stand still on a road you're bored of, and wait to be surprised." Does it come across well?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a software tester in Seoul, writing for my hiking club's season opener. Tell me what you think: "My job is finding where things break, so I can promise you the trail up Bukhansan will break you at the third staircase, at exactly the moment you believe you're nearly there. The bug isn't in the mountain. Bring water, bring kimbap, and stop checking the summit time."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a chef in Lyon, and I'm paying tribute to Gaston, founder of our pétanque club, at his memorial lunch. I'd love an outside view: "Gaston said the best throw looks like it's doing nothing. He cooked that way, too: no flourish, only patience, and salt at the right moment. Look at the gravel today, at the boules lying where they landed. This is his handwriting. Let's play badly, loudly, and long."
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting

message: I'm a judge in Wellington, but this is for my tramping club's hut night, so no gavels. Draft: "I spend my days deciding who is right. The mountain never asks. At 1,400 metres in sleet there is no appeal, no precedent, no adjournment, only a hut, six strangers and one gas burner. By morning we'll be a unanimous jury. I move that tea comes first, and the snoring verdict after." Honest thoughts?
work_type: a short speech for a club meeting
